An oral hearing took place before the Copenhagen City Court (Københavns Byret - hereafter ‘the City Court’) in 1996. Five co-accused in the case were also arrested and interviewed from 1996 to 1998. The applicant was released on 22 December 1995 after being released from solitary confinement. The investigation was concluded in 1996 and an indictment could be expected at the beginning of 1996. The case was brought against the applicant by the police in Copenhagen. The trial is ongoing and the accused is being represented by a legal team.

The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Les Salles Sur Verdon, France. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases’ (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. The persons involved were usually intricately interconnected and collaborated in their economic criminal activities, which concerned very large amounts of money. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. The trade in inactive, solvent companies largely ceased in the summer of 1993.

It related mainly to a criminal activity whereby the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud. According to a survey conducted by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. It also made an order excluding him from Swiss territory for ten years. On the other hand, the applicant was acquitted by the jury on 672 counts of fraud. The offences to which the convictions related had been committed between 1973 and 1981. The applicant lodged an application with the Court of Justice of the Canton of Geneva for the conviction in absentia to be set aside, under Article 331 of the Geneva Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 42 below) He maintained that good cause had been shown for his absence at the hearing on 17 April 1989, as he had been compelled to comply with the enforceable decision of the American court – which clearly constituted a reason beyond his control. The applicant was also held to be at fault for having delayed in appealing against the decision of the American court. The appeal had been lodged on 26 April 1989, that is to say a week after his trial had actually begun, and his application for an adjournment had been dismissed. It held that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention did not preclude a trial being held in the defendant's absence if the defendant refused to attend or was unable to attend through his or her own fault. It considered that the applicant had misled the American court by making inaccurate statements, notably regarding Swiss procedure, in order to secure a judgment. The applicant was arrested at Munich Airport (Germany) on his way to a conference. He was extradited to Switzerland and transferred to Champ-Dollon Prison. The defendants withdrew their appeals on points of law, thereby confirming the judgment against them. The judgment convicting the three co-defendants ..., who were likewise sentenced to several years’ imprisonment, has become final. The defence's submissions again provide nothing to support the hypothesis that the proceedings were moving towards an acquittal. The quotations from the trial court’s judgment are taken out of context. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand, pursuant to section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. In view of the reasons given for the judgment, it was much more likely, having regard to the adverse financial position of the Stumm holding company, that if the proceedings had continued, the defendant would have been convicted on the counts in question. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. The Regional Court disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. On 28 December 1981, the Bochum public prosecutor submitted that, having regard to the state of the proceedings, there was every likelihood (hohe Wahrscheinlichkeit) that the conviction would have been upheld. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss), a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) claiming a breach of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “1. The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted’ 2. The refusal of the applications for an order that the Treasury should bear the deceased defendant’s necessary costs and expenses is based on Article 467 § 3, second sentence, sub-paragraph 2, of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded merely as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36801/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the administrative appellate courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to her request for disability benefits. She claimed that, due to her health problems, she had incurred, and still incurred, extra costs for, inter alia, medication, doctors’ visits, treatment, travel expenses, special clothes and shoes, special soap and creams, and for supplementary vitamins and minerals. She had calculated that these extra costs amounted, in total, to SEK 75,314 (approximately EUR 8,150) per year. The applicant's extra costs per year amounted to no more than SEK 7,300 from September 1999, SEK 8,900 from January 2000 and SEK 6,800 from January 2001. The Office concluded that the applicant’s extra costs did not reach the minimum level established for each year to be granted disability benefits. The decision was based on Sections 5 and 6 of the Act on Disability Benefits and Care Allowance (Lagen om handikappersättning och vårdbidrag, Act no. 1998:703) The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Blekinge, requesting that the decision be set aside. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Jönköping, insisting that she was in need of assistance for one hour per day. She alleged that she had to buy custom-made clothes and special shoes due to her deformities caused by the lymphatic oedema and hip problems. All these extra costs should, in her view, be included in the calculation to grant her disability benefits. The court concluded, in an overall assessment of the applicant’s need of help and of her extra costs, that the conditions for granting disability benefits were not fulfilled and that the applicant was not eligible for a disability allowance. The applicant asked for an oral hearing to clarify certain unclear points of the case. The court, consisting of five judges including two lay judges, found it established that lymphatic drainage treatment of the kind the applicant needed was to be regarded as medical treatment. The County Council was responsible for costs of such treatment to the extent that it could be considered medically motivated. Accordingly, when. assessing the application for disability benefits, the applicant was not entitled to include extra costs for lymphatic. drainage treatment. In the light of this and as the court also shared the County Administrative Court’s assessment concerning the remainder of the subject‑matter, the case could be decided on the case file as it stood. In 2005 the applicant made a further appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), requesting that the Administrative Court of Appeal’s judgment be repealed and the case returned for renewed examination. She referred to Article 6 of the Convention and claimed that an oral hearing was necessary in order to clarify the case. In the alternative, the applicant requested that the court grant her disability benefits. On 17 May 2006 the Supreme. Administrative Court refused leave to appeal. The judgment was unanimous and the. appeal was to be rejected. The appeal was settled in August 2006 and the application was dismissed. The case was decided in favour of the applicant.

The court stated that the failure to call and hear evidence from six eyewitnesses, Belarus nationals, had been a serious shortcoming justifying a retrial. The trial court had not made efforts to secure their presence at the hearing or to make use of a rogatory letter in order to have them heard as witnesses by the Belarus authorities. Furthermore, as regards the anonymous witness, the court of first instance had failed to make efforts to capture his whereabouts. The applicant’s detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It considered that the facts of the case had been duly established and the rules of criminal procedure, as well as guarantees of a fair trial, had been respected. Despite the authorities’ efforts, the court could not secure his presence at the hearing. Consequently, it was necessary to take into account evidence given by him in the investigation. The Supreme Court of Poland ruled in favour of the applicant in the case.

The right to silence under section 52 of the Constitution is not limited to public officials. The right to be silent can be extended to anyone in the public, even if it is a private person. It can also be extended beyond the bounds of the law to include non-government officials, such as the police. The freedom of speech and expression is not subject to the right to the silence of the public. The law does not prevent the public from being able to speak out on issues that are of concern to them. The public can speak out if they feel it is in their best interests to do so, especially if they believe that they are in danger of being misled.

Section 52 of the Constitution provides for the right to be silent on matters of national security. The right to silence includes the right not to reveal the identity of a person. It does not include the right, however, to give information that is not in the public interest. Section 52 is intended to be a stop-gap measure, not a permanent law. The law is not intended to prevent future use of the right by members of the public to disclose information that would be beneficial to the public, but to ensure the safety of the nation's security. It is meant to provide the public with a way of knowing what is going on in the country and to protect the public.

The right to silence under section 52 of the Constitution is not unlimited. The right to remain silent can be extended to include the right to not be required to provide information to a person that is in need of it. The freedom of speech and freedom of the press is also not unlimited, the Supreme Court has ruled. The Supreme Court ruled that the freedom to speak to those who need it should not be limited to the duration of a person's sentence or the length of a period of time it takes to provide that information. It also ruled that it was not necessary for a person to give information to the police before being released to the general public. The court ruled that such information should be made public.

The Supreme Court concluded that the restriction in section 52 was proportionate to the State's entitlement to protect itself. The applicants' appeal to the Court of Criminal Appeal in relation to their conviction under section 52 of the 1939 Act has been adjourned generally pending the outcome of the present application. The entitlement of those with something relevant to disclose concerning the commission of a crime to remain silent must be regarded as of an even lesser order. and to assert his or her constitutional rights. The Government contested this argument and stated that the applicant was brought for the first time before the Public Prosecutor on 23 July 1994. The applicant was not seen by a doctor before being questioned by the Prosecutor on 23 July 1994 and consequently he does not have any medical evidence concerning the torture he was subjected to. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7070/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In her statement the applicant admitted to having engaged in activities on behalf of the PKK0. The President of the Court's Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was charged with membership of an illegal organisation, namely the PKK. Edirne Magistrates' Court, which ordered her pre-trial detention in prison. In two statements made during meetings with the prosecutor and the judge the applicant admitted to being a member of the PKK and did not want to be represented by a lawyer during the questioning. The applicant rejected the allegations against her and alleged that she had been told by the gendarmes that if she did not accept the accusations before the judge and the prosecutor she would be taken back to the gendarmerie station and tortured again. When asked by the trial court what she had to say about the medical report of 9 March 2000 in which it was stated that her body bore no signs of ill-treatment, the applicant replied that the report had been prepared before she was beaten up by gendarme officers. In 2001 the applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. The applicant appealed against her conviction and argued that the decision of the trial court had not been adequately reasoned. On 8 July 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's conviction. The trial court asked to hear a “cassette of the questioning” of the applicant which had apparently been mentioned in a document drawn up by the gendarmerie. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs requested the Ministry of Justice to obtain the cassette so that it could be submitted to the Court. The Government was requested to submit a copy of the cassette of questioning.  domestic judicial authorities to produce the cassette, stated in their letter of 21 May 2008 that they had “no records of the cassette being handed over to the Edirne prosecutor”. The cassette was never handed to the prosecutor. The case has been referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg, France. The ECHR ruled that the tapes should be returned to the parents of the victims, and ordered the release of the tape to the mother of the victim. The father of one of the children on the tape died in a car crash in 2008. The mother died in 2009 and the son was taken to hospital.

Reference was made to the United States Supreme Court which had rejected a challenge to the Californian Constitution’s disenfranchisements of convicted prisoners. Some considerable attention was given to Canadian precedents.

Canadian Supreme Court struck down the disenfranchisement of all prisoners as too widely drawn and infringing the minimum impairment rule. The Federal Court of Appeal upheld the subsequent legislative provision restricting the ban to prisoners serving a sentence of two years or more in a correctional institution. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded: “... I return to what was said by the European Court in paragraph 52 of its judgment in Mathieu-Mohin’”. The cases before the European Commission of Human Rights and this Court were also reviewed, the Divisional Court noting that the Commission had been consistent in its approach in accepting restrictions on persons convicted and detained. The Working Group said that such prisoners had lost the moral authority to vote.

The cases before the European Commission of Human Rights and this Court were also reviewed. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded: “... I return to what was said by the European Court in paragraph 52 of its judgment in Mathieu-Mohin. Perhaps the best course is that suggested by Linden JA, namely to leave to philosophers the true nature of this disenfranchisement whilst recognising that the legislation does different things.” It seems to me to be appropriate for this Court to defer to the legislature.

The United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum. Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned. In course of time this position may move, either by way of further fine tuning, as was recently done in relation to remand prisoners and others, or more radically. But its position in the spectrum is plainly a matter for Parliament not for the courts. That applies even to the ‘hard cases’ of post-tariff discretionary life sentence prisoners. They have all been convicted and if, for example, Parliament were to have said that all those sentenced to life imprisonment lose the franchise for life the apparent anomaly of their position would disappear.

Parliament in this country could have provided differently in order to meet the objectives which it discerned, and like McLachlin J in Canada, I would accept that the tailoring process seldom admits of perfection. As [counsel for the Secretary of State] submits, there is a broad spectrum of approaches among democratic societies, and the United Kingdom falls into the middle of the spectrum. Civil proceedings against a trustee in bankruptcy of “Westa” Insurance Company were dismissed in July 2003. The appeal against this decision was dismissed in June 2004. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. The trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when the prosecutor was reading the bill of indictments. The Court of Appeal instructed the trial court to hold more than 3 hearings per month. On 11 September 2002 the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw from the trial. The Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the judges and lay members of the trial court to withdraw. The Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant and his 17 co-defendants be kept in custody until 30 June 2003. On 1 September 2003 a new legal-aid counsel was appointed for the applicant. The previous counsel was discharged from his duties at his own request and following a number of complaints. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the trial could not have been terminated due to obstructiveness on the part of the defendants who had filed numerous requests for the trial to be terminated. The appeal was dismissed again on 30 July 2003. Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. In all those decisions the Court of Appeal stated that the grounds previously given for his detention were still valid. The trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses. The applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. He maintained that the length of his detention was excessive and that the charges against him lacked a basis for them. The decision of 27 July 2005 dismissing the applicant’s appeal against the decision of 22 June 2005 justified his continued detention. It also held that keeping the applicant in custody was necessary in order to prevent him from interfering with the trial. The case is still pending before the first-instance court. The applicant was released on 19 October 2005. The trial court made a further severance order and divided the case into eleven separate cases. After 20 June 2005 no hearing was held due to the serious illness of the judge rapporteur. On 21 September 2005 the President of the IV Criminal. Section of the Gdańsk Regional Court assigned a new judge. rapporteur Consequently, the trial had to commence de novo. The Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. It also imposed on him a prohibition on leaving the country.

Whether the applicant had acted in good faith and in the public interest or believed that the statement had been true did not influence the illegality of his action. The court considered that making an untrue statement that offended the personal rights of a person would always be contrary to the law. The interpretation of the law adopted by the lower courts was correct.

The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The French Government were invited to intervene in the proceedings. However, by a letter of 10 October 2006, they informed the Registry that they did not wish to exercise their right to intervene.

The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in Ferney-Voltaire, France. He married K.P., a Polish national, on 15 March 2001. They initially lived in Kraków, but on 3 July 2001 they moved to France. Their two children were born in September 2001 and October 2002 respectively. It appears that following the applicant's departure for France the court sent him summonses in connection with the private prosecution but received no response. The court ordered the police to execute that decision and to serve a copy of it on the applicant immediately after his arrest and to inform him that he could appeal. The information that a wanted notice had been issued in respect of the applicant was subsequently entered in a central criminal register.

The applicant is an artist who lives in Ferney-Voltaire, France. He married K.P., a Polish national, on 15 March 2001. They initially lived in Kraków, but on 3 July 2001 they moved to France. Their two children were born in September 2001 and October 2002 respectively. A certain B.M., an administrator of the building in which the applicant's wife had a flat, brought a private prosecution against the applicant for slander (zniewaga) under Article 216 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 15 July 2002 the District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody for a period of three months. The information that a wanted notice had been issued in respect of the applicant was subsequently entered in a central criminal register.

The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in Ferney-Voltaire, France. He married K.P., a Polish national, on 15 March 2001. They initially lived in Kraków, but on 3 July 2001 they moved to France. Their two children were born in September 2001 and October 2002 respectively. The applicant is an artist and runs a small business in France which provides the only support for the family. A wanted notice (list gończy) was issued with a view to locating and detaining him. The District Court ordered the police to execute that decision and to serve a copy of it on the applicant immediately after his arrest.

The case was heard at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. The judge ruled that the man had not been properly informed of his rights. The man and his family were detained while on holiday in Słubice. He was released without charge on January 6, 2003. The court is still considering whether the case should be re-examined and whether the man should be charged with a crime. The case is expected to be heard again in April 2014. The trial will be heard by a panel of three judges, including the judge who issued the original detention order, on 16 July 2002. The jury will decide whether or not to order the release of the man.

The case was brought by the son of a French man who was detained in Poland in 2002. He was held at a border station for two hours while his wife and two children waited in the car. The family appealed the detention and the case was eventually dismissed. The father-of-two was released on a bail bond of £1,000. The case is now before the European Court of Human Rights, which will decide if the father-in-law should be extradited to France or released on bail. The appeal will be heard in January 2015. The judge will decide whether to extradite the father of the child to France, which he says would be illegal.

The man was arrested at the Słubice border on 3 January 2003. He was not told why he was being held. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The man's wife appealed the decision, which was overturned. The judge ruled that he had not been informed of his rights and had been denied access to a lawyer. The court also ruled that the man was not entitled to a court-appointed lawyer to argue against his detention. The father of two young children was not allowed to see his children while he was held in custody. The two children had to stay in the car with the heating on as the temperature was below zero.

The court imposed a fine of PLN 10,000, which it considered proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of the applicant’s guilt. By using insulting words in respect of the district officials, Maciej Ziembiński intended to derive satisfaction from doing them moral harm. By doing so in a newspaper, he fell within the scope of Article 216 § 2 of the Criminal Code, acting unlawfully, reprehensibly, and, in the absence of circumstances capable of precluding or mitigating his guilt. Piotrków Trybunalski Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It ordered the applicant to pay PLN 1,000 (approx. EUR 256) in respect of the costs of the appeal proceedings. The Regional Court held that the lower court had correctly established the facts of the case. It endorsed the trial court’s findings that the words used in the article had been insulting and harmful to the private prosecutors’ dignity. It further held that, although fair criticism of public authorities and officials was socially desirable and legally accepted, the protection afforded by law did not extend to the use of insulting words which offended human dignity.

The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. As presented by the applicants the case was not decided on the merits. Policemen, armed with truncheons and guarded by police dogs, entered the house, woke up the other occupants and ordered them to stand against the wall. No information was provided about the grounds, purpose or legal basis for the search. During this time the police showered abuse on the students. The applicants requested to be examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheon. The Wrocław District Prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The atmosphere was tense. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. As D. S. was unruly and continued to express objections, the policemen decided to arrest him. While he was being taken into custody by the police, he hit one of them in the face. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. He had not obeyed the police requests to calm down and the verbal exchange between him and the police officer A. C. had become increasingly heated. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. Therefore, the submissions of the other persons could not be considered credible. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. The right to receive and impart information, including information concerning acts of officials, was fundamental in a democratic society. The children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. The case involves a woman who tried to enter Turkey illegally using a forged passport. She was arrested on the ground that she had entered Turkey using a forge passport. The applicant was taken into custody and underwent a virginity examination. After a few days she was released from detention with the help of her family. She later lodged an asylum application with the Aliens Department. The police rejected her application as it had been submitted out of time. She eventually was accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul after the intervention of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) She was sent back to Iran. She has since been accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul after the intervention of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) the case is still pending. On 16 February 1998 a woman was granted a stay of deportation under the Geneva Convention. She feared she would be sent back to her native Iran. The court found that there was no need to suspend the order as it did not cause any harm to her. The case was eventually dismissed by the Supreme Court of Turkey. The decision was made on the basis that it was not an act of unlawful destruction of human rights. The U.S. Embassy in Ankara said the decision was not based on any grounds other than that the woman had been given permission to leave the country and that it would be in the public interest to have her case heard in court.

The case is the first in a long line of cases involving the deportation of a woman from the European Union to the United States. The case was decided by the Ankara Administrative Court, not by the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled that the woman did not have the right to be removed from the EU without a court order. The decision was upheld on appeal by the High Court of Justice, which said there was no need for the stay of execution as the woman had been allowed to stay in the EU. The woman was able to return to the U.S. after the case was settled by the Supreme Court of Appeal. She was allowed to go back to work.

The case was settled under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) in 1998. The European Court of Human Rights ruled there was no need for the stay. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the case was not a matter of law, but of international humanitarian law. The court ruled that the decision was not an issue of law and that the ruling was based on the ECHR's own decision. The decision was upheld by the High Court of Justice, which ruled the case could be re-admitted to the ECHR. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Appeal, which found that the stay of deportation was not in breach of the Constitution.

Turkey has ratified the Geneva Convention and the 1967 Protocol thereto. It has exercised the geographic preference option under the 1951 Convention in order to limit the grant of refugee status to asylum-seekers from European countries. For humanitarian reasons, Turkey issues temporary residence permits to non-European countries who are recognised by the UNHCR as refugees pending their resettlement in a third country by that organisation. An asylum-seeker whose application has been refused may now appeal within fifteen days of the refusal to the competent governorship. The appeal is to be assessed by the superior of the official who took the initial decision to refuse asylum. A person who enters Turkey illegally and does not apply to the Turkish authorities within five days of his or her entry cannot be accepted as a refugee.

The law and practice governing asylum-seekers in Turkey is outlined in this article. Turkey has ratified the Geneva Convention and the 1967 Protocol thereto. Foreign nationals arriving in Turkey to seek asylum must submit their asylum application to the police within five days of their arrival in Turkey. Those who enter illegally are required to submit their application at the border town nearest the point where they entered the country. An asylum-seeker whose application has been refused may now appeal within fifteen days of the refusal to the competent governorship. The appeal is to be assessed by the superior of the official who took the initial decision to refuse asylum. Asylum requests are examined by the Ministry of the Interior. Non-European Asylum-seekers who receive a positive decision may then submit their cases for resettlement.

The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The father of the first child died on 12 March 1986. He had left his wife and four children a sum of money. The first child wanted the money to go to the rest of the family. The court ruled that the money should go to his wife, not to the other children. The decision was overturned by a court of appeal in 2007. The second child now has the money back and is able to live with his wife. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court of France, where they are fighting for the right to keep the money they received from the father's death. The judge ruled that they are entitled to the money as part of a settlement. The first applicant was an illegitimate child who had been conceived when her father was bound by marriage to a person other than her mother. Under the terms of the deed of division, she was required to pay an equalising balance to the other heirs in the French franc equivalent of 236,187 euros (EUR) The second applicant sold her home to pay that balance on behalf of her daughter, who had no property of her own. The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation. In a judgment of 3 May 2000, the court dismissed the applicants' appeal. following that judgment, the equalisingbalance was duly paid to theOther heirs. The first applicant completed her studies in December 1993.

In a judgment of 7 February 1984 the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance dismissed the applicants' main application for an order that the forename 'Fleur' be added as their daughter's first forename. But it granted their application made in the alternative for the addition of “Fleur-Marie’ It held as follows: “Although a forename may be composed of up to two names already in use, it cannot consist of a combination of two names linked by a preposition’

The Guillots chose to give their daughter the forenames ‘Fleur de Marie, Armine, Angèle’ The registrar of births, deaths and marriages refused to register the first of these names on the ground that it did not appear in any calendar of saints' days. The court granted their application made in the alternative for the addition of “Fleur-Marie’. The case was heard at the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance in February 1984. The Guillots won the case, and their daughter was born on 7 April 1983, with the forename 'Fleur' as her first name.

Mr and Mrs Guillot appealed to the Versailles Court of Appeal. The case has been described as a landmark in the history of French law.

Mr and Mrs Guillot appealed to the Versailles Court of Appeal, which on 18 September 1984 upheld the judgment of the court below in the following terms: “(...) Although in spite of the mandatory requirements of the Law of 11 Germinal Year XI, which provides that forenames must be chosen from the various calendars in use, case-law is tending towards a more liberal approach. It is necessary to prevent parents from choosing forenames which are excessively whimsical and so eccentric that the child is likely to be the first victim. This is the case with the forename 'Fleur de Marie', notwithstanding that it was the name of the heroine of a famous literary work. On the other hand, there is no reason not to allow the claim made in the alternative that the fore name should consist of the two forenames ‘Fleur’ and ‘Marie’ juxtaposed.

'Fleur de Marie' is composed of two forenames recognised by French law, which when linked by the preposition 'de' form the name of the heroine of Eugène Sue's Mystères de Paris. A forename may be composed of up to two names already in use, it cannot consist of a combination of two names linked by a preposition since it would cease to be a mere reuse of a traditional boy's or girl's name. It is necessary to prevent parents from choosing forenames which are excessively whimsical and so eccentric that the child is likely to be the first victim. This is the case with the forename 'Fleur de Marie', notwithstanding that it was the name of the heroine of a famous literary work. The applicant was born in 1987 and lives in Van. He was disbanded from the army as he was diagnosed with a psychotic illness by the Van Military Hospital. On 7 October 2008 he initiated compensation proceedings, claiming that he had become ill during his military service as a result of the degrading treatment he had been subjected to in the army. He requested a total of 150,000 Turkish liras (TRY) (approximately 80,000 euros (EUR) at the time) in both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. He also requested legal aid for the court fees, presenting a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtar) attesting to his poverty. The Supreme Military Administrative Court decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicant had not paid the necessary court fees.

He was convicted and sentenced to six years and three months in prison. The Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court in May 2011. He has since been released on bail and is awaiting a further court hearing on a second charge of ill-treatment of a police officer on the basis of a medical report. The appeal was dismissed again on the ground that the doctor involved had not found any new signs of physical violence since the previous reports.

name: Fikret Doğan
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. Mr Rıza Türmen, the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case. The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Gölcüklü to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a ‘reasonable time’ He also alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning hisright to aFair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal.

The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible.

The Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) was accused of trying to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed under judicial guardianship. His case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) in 1995. It was upheld on appeal in 1996 and he was freed on bail on 22 July 1991. He was released on bail again on 28 November 1989.

The Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) was an illegal armed organisation. Its object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment, permanently debarred from employment in public service and placed under judicial guardianship. The Court of Cassation (yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and the file was transmitted to it. The case was appealed and upheld in 1995, but the applicant was never released from custody. The application has been dismissed by the Turkish Supreme Court of Justice.

The case of the Dev-Yol was brought before the Ankara Martial Law Court. The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation. He was also accused of involvement in the killing of three persons, the attempt to kill another person, opening fire and organising bomb attacks on several premises. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court acquitted the applicant of other charges. It sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The Court of Cassation (yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case and the file was transmitted to it.

On a motion lodged by the applicant, the Director of the Nowy Targ District Office ordered the neighbours to demolish the building by 30 January 1998. On an unknown date in 2004 the applicant complained to the Małopolski Regional Inspector of Construction Supervision, alleging that the length of the enforcement proceedings had been excessive. The complaint was referred to the Cracow Regional Administrative Court. On 25 May 2006, in response to the complaint, the Regional Administrative court delivered a judgment. It ordered the Sucha Beskidzka District Inspector to take all the necessary measures with a view to enforcing the decision.

The complaint was referred to the Cracow Regional Administrative Court. In May 2006, in response, the Cragow Regional. Administrative Court delivered a judgment.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 27770/08) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. The application was communicated to the Government on 25 May 2009. On 7 December 2010 the Acting President of the Section to which the case was allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court. The Court decided that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings that the applicant should not be expelled to Somalia pending the Court’s decision. The applicant had claimed to be a member of the Isaaq tribe, which comes from Somaliland, an autonomous region in north-west Somalia. He claimed that his parents were born in Hargeisa, although it was accepted that he was born in Mogadishu. As the applicant did not co-operate with the provision of bio-data, the Government decided that it would be preferable to remove him to Somalia. In November 2004 the applicant refused a formal request to sign such a disclaimer. In July 2006 the Government concluded an agreement with African Express Airlines which made enforced removals to Somalia possible. The first enforced removal to Somalia took place on 30 November 2006. In September 2006 the applicant was granted permission to apply for judicial review. Mr Justice Calvert-Smith ruled that the Secretary of State for the Home Department could only detain a person that he intended to deport for what amounted to a reasonable period. The period of detention from 3 December 2004, which was the date of the applicant’s first review following his refusal to return voluntarily, to 30 June 2006 was found to be unlawful because of its length, the impossibility during that period of achieving removal, and the misleading statements which had misled decision-makers both inside and outside the Home Dept. Both the applicant and the secretary of state were granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant was issued with removal directions set for 29 November 2006 and sought leave to apply for judicial review of the removal directions. The applicant was granted permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal on 18 December 2009. The applicant remains in immigration detention pending removal. On 6 December 2010 the applicant was issued with removal directions to Somalia. The removal was to take place on 8 December 2010. The Court granted the applicant interim measures under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his removal. The current application is only concerned with the first period of detention. 30 June 2006 should have been held to be unlawful. On 13 April 2007 the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal had ordered that he be released from detention on bail. He was released early the following week but was re-detained on 3 April 2008 after breaching his bail conditions. In April 2006 the Home Office introduced a ‘secret’ policy creating a presumption in favour of the detention of Foreign National Prisoners pending their deportation. The policy was not disclosed until mid-2008 and was not formally published until September 2008. The lawfulness of this policy was considered by the Supreme Court in the cases of Walumba Lumba and Kadian Mighty v. Secretary of State for the Home Department [2011] UKSC 12 (see paragraph 37, below) The Supreme Court ruled that the policy constituted a “near blanket ban” on release. The applicant was held from 3 September 2003 to 13 April 2007. During this period there were monthly reviews of the applicant’s detention. The reviews were carried out in November 2003, March 2004, June 2004, September 2004, October 2004 and November 2004.

He claimed he had sold the house for GBP 50,000 in order to clear this debt and had used the GBP 12,000 residue from the sale to purchase the newsagents premises for his parents because he owed them money too. When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones; this was the source of the GBL 17,000 he had in his building society account. He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name, claiming variously that each had been purchased and sold on behalf of a friend or stolen without insurance. The applicant was convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32621/11) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention following the expiry of his tariff was unlawful in light of the failure of the authorities to put in place the necessary resources to enable him to demonstrate to the Parole Board that his risk had reduced. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ms M. Addis, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The application was heard on 23 September 2013 and the complaint under Article 5 § 1 was communicated to the Government. A number of other complaints were declared inadmissible. In September 2009 the applicant was transferred to HMP Acklington. He claims that he had been informed that the extended SOTP was available at that prison. A Parole Board review on 7 September 2009 said that much offending work still had to be done in order to reduce the applicant’s risk and that he should therefore remain in closed conditions. On 27 August 2010 the applicant completed the Thinking Skills Programme (“TSP”) at HMP Acklington. In January 2011 a pre-tariff-expiry paper Parole board review took place. The applicant was informed that he was not recommended for release and his request for an oral hearing was refused. The applicant’s tariff period expired on 26 April 2011. On 22 September 2011 he was transferred to HMP Whatton. He requested confirmation that he would be prioritised for the extended SOTP. The extended programme lasts 5 months. A SARN report will then have to be completed within 26 weeks of treatment being completed. The report will identify any further treatment that is necessary. Mr Dillon will be considered for one of these programmes, if he is found suitable. The review was scheduled to commence in March 2012 and conclude in November 2012, with an oral hearing in September. He sought advice on possible judicial review proceedings in respect of the delay in providing access. The applicant was reassessed for participation in the extended SOTP. In a report dated 6 February 2012 he was found not to be sufficiently motivated to undertake the course. The Parole Board notified the applicant of its decision on the papers not to direct his release or to recommend his transfer to open conditions. It considered that he had breached the trust placed in him and expressed concern that this might not bode well for the applicant’s likely compliance with licence conditions. The applicant subsequently pursued a request for a place on an extended SotP scheduled to commence in August 2012. It was recommended that the applicant complete individual work with his offender supervisor to consider, inter alia, the costs and benefits. The Parole Board agreed that the applicant posed a high risk of harm to children. The applicant was reassessed for the extended SOTP in July 2012. He was found to be suitable to participate in the programme and was advised that a SARN report would be completed within the next six months to identify any further work that needed to be done. Ms Leslie Stubbings was born on 29 January 1957. She was placed by a local authority in the care of Mr and Mrs Webb when she was nearly two years old. She alleges that she was sexually assaulted by Mr Webb and committed acts of indecency at his instigation on a number of occasions between 1959 and 1971. The defendants applied to have the claim dismissed as time-barred under the Limitation Act 1980 (“the 1980 Act“: see paragraph 35 below). The High Court found in favour of the defendants, ruling that Ms Stubbments’ “date of knowledge“ was September 1984. Both the High Court and the Court of Appeal which considered the case were bound by earlier authority.

Ms Leslie Stubbings alleges she was sexually assaulted by her adoptive parents. The High Court found in favour of the defendants, ruling that Ms Stubblings’ “date of knowledge“ was too recent to be a breach of duty. The Court of Appeal ruled that the claim was based on a “breach of duty’ within the meaning of section 11 of the 1980 Act.

Ms J.L. alleges that between 1968 and 1979 she was frequently abused by her father, who took pornographic photographs of her and subjected her to serious assaults of a sexual nature. In 1990 she began to have nightmares about her childhood abuse and asked her doctor for help and he referred her to a psychologist. At this time, she allegedly gained insight into the connection between the abuse and her mental health problems for the first time. In January 1991 she consulted solicitors with a view to commencing proceedings for damages against her father. Legal aid was granted and a writ was issued on 26 March 1991. A medical report prepared in May 1991 for the purposes of the litigation described her as suffering from severe psychological damage, which manifested itself in an inability to trust others.

The rifle lacked a breech-block and there was never any ammunition. [The applicant] does not consider himself to be the owner of the rifle since it is his mother, now 82 years old, who is the formal owner of it. The court finds that [the applicant] cannot avoid being held responsible for the possession of the weapon, but that the violation of the Weapons Act is of a minor character.“ The court sentenced him to 30 day-fines (dagsböter) of 10 kronor each, i.e. 300 Swedish kroner in total. The Court of Appeal ruled that the case could be dealt with without a hearing. The applicant had asked for the appointment of a defence lawyer under the free legal aid scheme. The case was adjourned until the end of March 1985. The judge ruled that he would not insist on calling witnesses because it was no longer disputed that the breech-block was missing. The application was dismissed by the judge and the case was dismissed. The appeal was upheld by the Supreme Court in May 1986. The Appeal Court returned a decision to the lower court with a verdict of not guilty. The lower court ordered the applicant to pay a fine of £1,000. He was sentenced to six months in jail and fined £500. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s request for a trial hearing as this was found to be manifestly unnecessary. The matter was referred to the Supreme Court (högsta domstolen), which refused him such leave on 19 June 1985. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 3 March 1986. The request for confiscation of the rifle is therefore rejected. The applicant is therefore found guilty of having violated the Weapons Act. The sentence should be the one determined by the City Court. No such action has been taken in this case. An action for confiscating the rifle should be directed against the owner of the Rifle in accordance with Section 17 of the Act of 1946 on promulgation of new Code of Judicial Procedure. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 13 September 1991 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 13071/87) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 29 September 1986. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 June 1992. The Court heard addresses by Mr Pannick for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by Mr Clarke and Mr Campbell for the applicant. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. The jury’s decision was by a majority verdict of ten to two. He received a sentence of ten years for the robbery, and two sentences of eight years each for the burglary offences. All three sentences were to be served concurrently. Leave to appeal against the sentence was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal on 5 February 1985. On 21 May 1985 the substantive appeal against sentence was dismissed by the full court. In February 1986, the Director of Public Prosecutions decided that there was insufficient evidence to support criminal charges against three police officers. At the disciplinary hearing, on 13 to 15 June 1988, the tribunal decided there was no case to answer and dismissed the charges. An independent police investigation was ordered in the course of which certain facts came to the attention of the police. The report was requested by the Home Department but its disclosure was refused on the grounds of public interest immunity. The applicant submitted to the Court of Appeal that the verdict should be set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case, in particular, that certain information had been withheld by the police. At the trial one of the police witnesses had stated under cross-examination that no fingerprints were found at the scene of the crime. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. The applicant had not been informed of this by the prosecution before his trial. A further shortcoming complained of by the applicant related to the fact that the police had shown two volumes of photographs of possible burglars (including a photograph of the applicant) to the elderly victim of the robbery. Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. Court concluded that there was some slipshod police work in the present case, no doubt because they took the view that here was a man who had admitted these crimes fully, and consequently there was very little need for them to indulge in a further verification of whether what he said was true. Although this is a matter which perhaps casts the police in a somewhat lazy or idle light, we do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions. Consequently, treating this matter as we have to according to section 17 of the Act, we think this appeal fails and must be dismissed.

The applicant was asked to give information about the location of his sawmill. He refused to do so and the Enforcement Authority asked the District Court to detain him. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal (Högsta domstolen) on 9 November 2010. The Enforcement Authority contacted the applicant in order to plan the sale of the attached sawmill. In his reply a few days later, the applicant stated that he had removed the sawmill from his property and hidden it. The Authority also handed the applicant a summons for questioning on its premises. On 17 May 2010 the Enforcement Authority requested the District Court to detain the applicant because he had refused to cooperate and give the required information. On 27 May 2010, after having held an oral hearing, the Court held a hearing and ordered the applicant to return the saw mill to the Authority. The sawmill was returned to its owner on 28 May 2010. The Court of Appeal found that there were extraordinary reasons to detain the applicant and that detention was proportionate to the aim pursued. The Enforcement Authority appealed to the Court of appeal, maintaining its claims and adding that, according to the preparatory works of the Enforcement Code, it was only necessary that the debtor had received an injunction but refused to comply with it. It further submitted that having regard to the applicant’s stance on the matter, the imposition of a conditional fine would most likely have no effect. Lastly, the Authority stated that it had reported the applicant to the police on the ground that he had committed a breach of an official order when he had removed and hidden the sawmill. The Court of Appeal held an oral hearing on 30 June 2010 and decided to maintain its earlier decision. On 13 July 2010 the District Court reviewed the applicant’s detention and held a new hearing in the case. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the applicant should be kept in detention since he still had not given any information about the location of the sawmill. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal since a new decision had already been taken by the District court at that time. The applicant appealed to the Court of appeal which, on 20 July 2010, rejected the appeal. The appeal was dismissed on 23 July 2010 and the applicant was detained. The applicant had sought compensation for the suffering he had endured during the 42 days he was deprived of his liberty. He also demanded to be reimbursed SEK 2,940 for costs which had been deducted from his pension during his time in detention. On 15 October 2012 the Chancellor of Justice rejected the claim. The Chancellor noted that the decision to detain the applicant had been taken by a court of law, in accordance with relevant legal provisions. The applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision was dismissed on 23 July 1998. In his speech, Lord Steyn held that section 35(2) of the 1991 Act conferred a wide administrative discretion on the Secretary of State to decide upon the release on licence of mandatory life prisoners. He expressly repeated Lord Bingham's concern that the imposition of a substantial term of imprisonment by exercise of administrative discretion was hard to reconcile with ordinary concepts of the rule of law. On 22 December 1998 the applicant was released on licence by the Secretary. of State. The applicant was sentenced to 12 years in prison, suspended for 12 years, with the possibility of an early release. He was also fined £1,000.

The applicant alleged that his detention after recall on life licence had ceased to be justified by the original sentence. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 29 May 2001 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr J.-P. Costa, President, Mr W. Fuhrmann, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr K. Jungwiert, Sir Nicolas Bratza and Mr. Traja. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1967. He was released on licence in April 1979. His licence required him to cooperate with his probation officer and to remain in the United Kingdom. In September 1980 his licence was revoked and thereafter he was continuously ‘unlawfully at large’ In April 1989 he returned from South Africa in possession of a false passport. He remained in custody, however, due to the revocation of the life licence. In July 1993 he was arrested and remanded in custody on counterfeiting charges. On 19 July 1994 he was convicted on two counts of conspiracy to forge travellers' cheques and passports and sentenced to six years' imprisonment. In 1996 the Parole Board conducted a formal review of the applicant's case and recommended his release on life licence. In 1997 the Secretary of State rejected the Board's recommendation in the following terms. The applicant was granted leave to seek judicial review. On 1 July 1997, but for the revocation of his life licence, the applicant would have been released from prison on the expiry of the sentence for fraud, pursuant to provisions whereby prisoners serving determinate sentences of more than more than 10 years are eligible for release. On 10 June 1997 the applicant was given leave to appeal the decision. The application was successful on the grounds that the conditions of his licence had been breached and he was entitled to a full review. The applicant is now serving the equivalent of a determinate sentence of about five years, albeit in open conditions. This term has not been imposed on him by way of punishment, because he has already served the punitive terms which his previous, very serious, offences have been thought to merit. The term has been imposed because he is thought to present danger to the public, because that is not suggested. It is not submitted that the term imposed bears any relation to the gravity of any future imprisonable offence which the applicant might commit. The imposition of what is in effect a substantial term of imprisonment by the exercise of executive discretion, without trial, lies uneasily with ordinary concepts of the rule of law.” The House of Lords dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Court of Appeal's decision. Lord Buxton, concurring with the latter remarks, added: “The category of imprisonable offence is extremely wide, and can encompass many matters that are wholly unrelated, both in nature and seriousness, to the reasons for the life sentence prisoner being within the power of the State in the first place’” On 16 December 1997 the applicant was moved to open conditions. The applicant was released on licence on 22 December 1998.

The first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000) and had been met by his family. The trial judge said: “With regard to a defendant’s costs you [Counsel] are right, the costs should and almost invariably would follow the event. I cannot think of another case in my 35 years’ experience in which costs have been expended on defending him on charges for which he has been found not guilty” On 14 February 2007 the jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. The first applicant has since been cleared of all charges against him by a jury at the Crown Court in London.

The trial judge’s summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. ... We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken” The jury acquitted the applicant of the three remaining charges. When the first applicant applied for his costs (which exceeded GBP 100,000 and had been met by his family) his counsel stated: ‘This is a case in which [the first applicant] was inevitably going to be charged with a criminal offence, I do not doubt that for a moment’ The trial judge refused the application, saying costs should and almost invariably would follow the event.

The trial judge's summing up to the jury contained the following direction: “We all know this is a horrific, a disgusting episode. We all know that, and we all know – there has not been any argument about this, has there? – where moral responsibility lies but we are a court of law, we are not here to dish out admonitions for immoral conduct, disgusting behaviour. ... We are here to judge whether a crime has been committed, whether the criminal law of the land has been broken. In order to do that you have to be objective. You have to stand back from the feelings of disgust and revulsion that come from the facts of this case and be objective”

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 32771/96) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. He was also indicted on another count of cheating the public revenue and pleaded guilty to that charge too. The applicant was convicted of fraud and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. He appealed to the Court of Appeal Criminal Division seeking leave to appeal against sentence. The applicant did not maintain in his application that he had been unable to understand the proceedings at the trial or to communicate effectively in court. In his application, the applicant was represented by the same legal team that had defended him at trial. The judge asked whether anyone in court who was fluent in both English and Italian could provide interpretation for the applicant. The court agreed to make use of the applicant's brother, but he was never requested to translate any statement during the course of the hearing. Leave to appeal was refused by the Single Judge on 3 May 1996 and by the full Court of Appeal on 15 July 1996. He wrote to the Home Secretary, admitting that he had not declared GBP 2,000 per week for staff wages due to the recession, and claiming that the real amount of the fraud was GBP 140,000 and not GBP 800,000. He further complained that his counsel had failed to secure him the services of an interpreter at the trial on 26 January 1996 and that this was of “paramount importance” for the purposes of the plea in mitigation. The Court declared the application admissible on 26 October 2004. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and the case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicants claimed that they had left Syria legally, flying from Damascus to Turkey and then on to Stockholm. They had travelled using their own passports but had destroyed them upon their arrival in Sweden. The Migration Board rejected the family's application for asylum and their request for residence permits and ordered their deportation to Syria. The applicants appealed to the Aliens Appeals Board (Utlänningsnämnden), relying on the same grounds as they had before the Migration Board and adding that Kurds were being persecuted and discriminated against in Syria. On 16 September 2003 the Aliens appeals Board dismissed the appeal on theSame grounds as the Migration board, stating that the new reasons advanced by the applicants did not alter the position. The first applicant had been convicted of threatening behaviour against his four-year-old daughter and a brother-in-law. He appealed to the Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of Skåne and Blekinge, which on 24 February 2004 upheld the conviction and the suspended sentence. In January 2004 the family lodged a new application for asylum to the Aliens Appeals Board and requested a stay of execution of the deportation order. They referred to a judgment that had been delivered on 17 November 2003 by the Regional Court in Aleppo which stated that the first applicant was convicted, in absentia, of complicity in a murder. They were also ordered to pay 1,000,000 Syrian pounds to the victim's family. The Aliens Appeals Board requested the Swedish embassy in Syria to verify whether the judgment was authentic. They further enquired if a reprieve was possible and whether death sentences were normally carried out in Syria. A local lawyer (förtroendeadvokat) they had engaged had confirmed that the judgement was authentic and had carried out research into the Syrian criminal law on sentences for murder and manslaughter. The embassy said that the lawyer had also stated that it was not unusual for the Syrian courts to impose the maximum sentence possible when an accused failed to appear for trial after being summoned to do so. It added that, according to their sources, it appeared that the accused had to be present in person in order to obtain a retrial. The court rejected the application for asylum on the basis that it was unlikely that it would be granted. The court also ruled that the first applicant would not be granted asylum if he returned to Syria. The case was settled on the grounds that the man had been married to another person. The first applicant was sentenced to death by lethal injection, but it was overturned on appeal. The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the sentence was not justified. The judge said that the case was the result of a miscarriage of justice, and that the death penalty was not available to the man. The trial was thrown out on appeal, but the judge said it was likely the case would be re-filed. The stay of execution of the deportation order until further notice is still in force. The dissenting member of the Aliens Appeals Board considered that, having regard to all the facts of the case, the applicants did have a well-founded fear that the first applicant would be executed if returned to Syria. The family should therefore be granted residence permits in Sweden. On 19 April 2004, following the Court's indication under Rule 39, the Migration Board granted a stay of Execution of the Deportation Order until further Notice. The stay is currently in force and remains in place until the family can apply for a permanent residence permit to stay in Sweden again.
