Court of Appeal ruled that section 2 (1)(b) of the 1969 Act was not in itself incompatible with Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal continued as follows: “Nor does the principle of the presumption of innocence prevent the prosecuting authorities from suspecting someone of having committed an offence.” The trial court thus rightly held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible. Snjezana Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Sejdo Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was in the end disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence.

Court of Appeal: “Nor does the principle of the presumption of innocence prevent the prosecuting authorities from suspecting someone of having committed an offence.” “By section 2(1)(b) of the [ 1969 Act], refusal of a claim [for compensation] depends not on proven guilt but on the possibility that the person concerned may have committed the offence and therefore on a (persisting) suspicion...” The trial court thus rightly held that the testimony given by the parents of the appellant, whose alibi related to the night of 31 March to 1 April 1996, was not credible; and Snjezana Vostic’s own testimony to the effect that she had last seen Sejdo Nadarevic in mid-February 1996 was disproved by the witnesses who gave evidence at the trial.

Alexander Findlay is a British citizen who was born in 1961 in Kilmarnock, Scotland. In 1982 he took part in the Falklands campaign. During the battle of Mount Tumbledown he witnessed the death and mutilation of several of his friends and was himself injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (“PTSD”) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. Lance-sergeant, who had become a lance-Sergeant, was sent with his regiment to Northern Ireland. On 29 July 1990, after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested. On 31 July 1990 an ex-naval psychiatrist, Dr McKinnon, examined Mr Findlay and found that he was responsible for his actions at the time of the incident. However, a combination of stresses (including his back injury and posting to. Northern Ireland) together with his heavy drinking on the day, had led to an “almost inevitable’ event. He was acquitted of all charges against him by the jury on 22 July 1991. Mr Findlay appeared before the general court martial, at Regent’s Park Barracks in London, on 11 November 1991. He pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence), two charges of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline (a military offence) He was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, reduction from the original sentence of two years. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 13258/09) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Two Norwegian nationals, Mr Lars Lillo-Stenberg and Mrs Andrine Sæther (“the applicants”), alleged that their right under Article 8 had been breached by a Supreme Court judgment of 2 September 2008. On 20 August 2005, the applicants married in a private ceremony which took place outdoors on an islet in the municipality of Tjøme in the Oslo fjord. In the last photograph, the bride was barefoot with her wedding dress raised above her knees to avoid getting the dress wet. The applicants brought compensation proceedings against the magazine before Oslo District Court. The magazine appealed to the Supreme Court (Høyesterett), which by judgment of 2 September 2008 found against the applicants, by three votes to two. Mr Justice U.S. gave the following reasons, which in the main were endorsed by the two other members of the majority: “I have concluded that the appeal should be allowed.’’ “The provision in section 3-6 refers, at any rate primarily, to violation of section 390. In my view, there is no need to consider whether, as contended by [the applicants], there is a need to redress for violation of privacy.” The couple had not been informed beforehand that there were plans to publicise the wedding, nor were they asked for their consent. The article as a whole contains information about the couple and their child. The relationships between the family and their friends are clearly of a personal nature. There would have been no question of violation of privacy if consent to publication had been obtained. The next question is whether the article was unlawful. This question must be decided on the basis of an overall evaluation of the article, cf. paragraph 64 of the Big Brother judgment with further references.. In my assessment of legality I also refer, as was done in the Plata judgment, paragraphs 57 and 58: ‘... When the penal provision applies to violation of Privacy, this necessarily implies that the issue that arises is that of legality’ The European Convention on Human Rights is incorporated into internal Norwegian law in the Human Rights Act. Both Article 8 relating to respect for private and family life and Article 10 relating to the right to freedom of expression are central to the present case. The article in question clearly has a purely entertainment value. In the assessment of legality, protection under Article 8 is the most relevant principle to be weighed. (40) I will now examine the circumstances in the present Case in relation to the issue of legality. The issue is whether in spite of this there are grounds for saying there is no right to publication of details of the subjects’ private life. A wedding is a public affirmation that two persons intend to live together and has legal consequences in many different sectors of society. Information about a wedding does not in itself involve a violation of privacy if it is given in a neutral form and based on a reliable source. The Court reiterates the fundamental importance of protecting private life from the point of view of the development of every human being’s personality. That protection extends beyond the private family circle and also includes a social dimension. It considers that anyone, even if they are known to the general public, must be able to enjoy a ‘legitimate expectation’ of protection of and respect for their private life. Se og Hør ran several articles featuring photos taken from different sources together with speculation and gossip. The magazine also described the relationship between the parties during their life together, which was an invasion of their private life as a couple. A wedding is a very significant personal experience for the bridal couple, an experience that includes their families, friends and other persons close to them. The wedding ceremony and celebrations are therefore clearly part of private and family life and thus in principle should be protected. But in my opinion this consideration is only one aspect of the case. I shall now examine more closely the way the wedding was conducted. The bride arrived at the islet in a rowing boat, with six bridesmaids on board. There she was greeted by her future husband and by a men. The wedding was organised in a very unusual way and took place in an area accessible to the public under the Outdoor Recreation Act. After the ceremony the bride and groom had to step from rock to rock in order to reach the shore, which the bride accomplished in bare feet. The situation would not have been any better if the photography had taken place somewhere closer, or from a place where the photographer and journalist could have been seen by the wedding party. This could have disturbed the whole wedding. Nor was the photographing in the nature of a breach of confidence, as it would have been if for example any of the participants had published personal photos taken during or in connection with the wedding. Mr Justice T. gave the following reasons which in the main were endorsed by the other member of the minority: “(58) I am substantially in agreement with the first-voting judge’s general interpretation of section 3-6 of the Damages Act and section 390 of the Penal Code. (59) I will first examine whether the subject of the article in Se og Hør can be considered to be ‘a personal matter’ in the meaning of section 390. (60) The case raises difficult and uncertain legal questions, clarification of which is in the public interest, cf. section 20-2, third paragraph, a, of the Code of Civil Procedure. Weddings have always been a subject of general interest. It is not unusual for the couple to wish to share their wedding and its arrangements only with those closest to them. In my view the desire to hold a private wedding should be respected in the sense that the wedding ceremony should be regarded as a personal matter within the meaning of section 390. The wedding party was held at a hotel on Tjøme, which in this context is clearly a private area. The islet where the events reported by Se og Hør, and the marriage itself, took place is a relatively short walk away and directly linked with the hotel’s property. The article included a description of the guests and the couple’s families, together with the names of well-known figures. The names of guests with children were also given, and pictures were shown. I regard these as the personal touch that the bridal couple had wished to give their wedding. I agree with the first-voting judge that the publication of personal matters is justified in cases where it does not contribute to public debate. However, when matters of a personal nature such as those in question here are published, they must have at least a minimum of public interest if the invasion of privacy is to be considered legitimate. Although the desire to entertain is in itself legitimate, its nature does not justify overriding the affected parties’ desire to protect their privacy. The opposite parties have demanded that the amount decided by the Court of Appeal should be maintained. I am of the opinion that the article in Se og Hør cannot be justified on the basis of an assessment of legality. Since I know that I am in the minority, I will not formulate a final conclusion. I have no objections to the amounts decided on. (70) For these reasons, the opposite parties are entitled to redress for pain and suffering from the appellants.” The amount decided on by the court of appeal is to be maintained at the same level as the original amount. The amount to be paid to the opposite party has not yet been decided.

In Lord Bingham’s view both errors resulted from a misreading of Pinochet (No. 3) (see paragraph 44-56 below) Lord Hoffmann, concurring in the judgment, considered that there was no automatic conflict between the jus cogens prohibition on torture and the law of State immunity. Saudi Arabia, in claiming immunity, was not justifying torture but merely objecting to the jurisdiction of the English courts in deciding whether it had used torture or not. The distinction between criminal proceedings (which were the subject of universal jurisdiction) and civil proceedings ( which were not) was “fundamental” and one that could not be “wished away”. Lord Hoffmann found Lord Justice Mance’s conclusion that the Convention against Torture did not lend acts of torture any official character to be unsatisfactory. He also considered inappropriate the Court of Appeal's proposed approach to the exercise of jurisdiction. He concluded that it would be “invidious in the extreme for the judicial branch of government to decide that it will allow the investigation of allegations of torture against the officials of one foreign state but not against those of another” He considered that it was necessary to show that international law did not require immunity against civil suit to be accorded to officials who were alleged to have committed torture.

The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. It imposes on the other party an obligation to enter into negotiations, to attend meetings for negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. The case originated in an application against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission by two Swedish subjects on 9 June 1972. The President of the Court deemed it conducive to the proper administration of justice to constitute a single Chamber to consider both the present case and that of the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union. The five judges so selected were Mr H. Mosler, Mr E. Rodenbourg, Mr. A. Favre, Mr G. Wiarda and Mr. P. O’Donoghue. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building in Strasbourg on 25 September 1975. There appeared before the Court: Mr. H. DANELIUS, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr. B. HÅRDEFELT, Chief Legal Adviser at the. Ministry of Finance. The Commission produced the document recently called for by the Court. The Court heard the addresses of Mr. Fawcett, Mr. Schmidt for the Commission and Mr. Danelius for the Government, as well as their replies to questions put by the. Court and several judges. Swedish workers and employers in the private sector have traditionally enjoyed the right to form and join trade unions and associations. In 1971, after expiry of one collective agreement and during negotiations for a new agreement, the applicants’ unions called selective strikes not affecting the sectors in which worked the applicants, who thus did not come out on strike. Mr. Schmidt and Mr. Dahlström complain that they, as members of the “belligerent“ unions, were denied certain retroactive benefits paid to members of other trade union and to non-union employees who had not participated in the strikes. The case will be heard by the Labour Court. The Act of 1936 guarantees two distinct rights to the parties on the labour market. The right to organise is defined in Section 3 of the Act as being the right of employers and employees to belong to an employers’ organisation or a trade union. It imposes on the other party an obligation to enter into negotiations, to attend meetings for negotiations and, where necessary, to make proposals for the settlement of the issues involved. This provision is applicable to all trade unions. As from 1 January 1966, the 1965 State Officials Act (statstjänstemannalag) has virtually assimilated State employees to employees in the private sector. The Act made the 1928 Collective Agreement Act, the 1928 Labour Court Act and the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate applicable in the public sector. The Act provided for collective agreements to be concluded, subject to certain exceptions, between the National Collective Bargaining Office (Statens Avtalsverk) and the organisations of State employees. The Ministry of Finance has a nominee on the governing board of the Office. The few independent trade unions represent only about 2,000 State employees in all. Insofar as they are union members at all, university teachers and army officers generally belong to SACO and SR respectively. Negotiations in the public sector of the labour market are centralised in that they are conducted by the federations on behalf of their member unions. Collective agreements in Sweden are normally concluded for a period of two or three years. For various reasons, however, the new collective agreement is often concluded some time after the previous agreement has expired. The new agreement has often specifically provided that its terms shall apply retroactively as from the date of expiry of previous agreement. In the case of a strike during the bargaining period, employers have customarily refused to grant retroactive benefits in order to deter unions from taking industrial action in the future.  collective action may not be taken by the different trade unions independently but rather on the basis of a decision by, or after receiving the approval of, the federation concerned. The question whether an individual employee has any means of challenging his union’s decision to go on strike is a matter exclusively governed by the internal rules of the union concerned. These may provide for a right to ask for a secret ballot or for other rights to object to the union's decisions to take industrial action. The law described above at paragraphs 10 to 17 has in recent years undergone various changes which, being subsequent to the facts at issue, are not relevant for the present case. Previous collective agreement was reinstated on 13 March 1971 for a period of six weeks. All strikes and lock-outs terminated forthwith. In June 1971 in a new global agreement for the years 1971 to 1973. According to this agreement, certain posts were upgraded and the salary scales were generally increased retroactively as from 1 January 1971. Clause 18, however, provided for an exception in this respect: “Officials who were members between 1 January and 12 March 1971 (or any part of this period) of organisations that organised industrial action... shall not be entitled to the increased wage benefits applicable under the agreement, unless the Collective Bargaining Office decides otherwise” SACO and SR brought an action against the State under the 1936 Act on the Right to Organise and Negotiate. Mr. Dahlström, who was upgraded under the new agreement, was affected for the whole period up to 12 March 1971. During these periods the applicants performed work for a lower salary than that paid to other employees who were in the same salary brackets but not members of SACO or SR. Their financial losses amounted to Kr. 300 and Kr. 1,000 respectively. In its judgment of 22 December 1971, the Labour Court unanimously rejected the claim of the applicants’ unions. The Court first confirmed the parties’ common view that the right to organise did not exclude the possibility for strikes. The Court found that no such purpose on the part of the State could be established. No support had appeared for the idea that the State intended to induce members of SACO and SR to switch over to TCO-S and SF. The Court assumed that the latter organisations would also have been refused retroactivity if they had organised industrial action during the process of negotiations. Any procedure designed to refuse the benefit of retroactivity generally to non-union employees in sectors where SACo and SR were dominant or representative could have become very complicated and time-consuming. The State would be barred from upholding the principle that a strike destroys retroactivity in any other way than by refusing retroactive validity for agreements with respect to all employee organisations. The applicants complained that in the particular circumstances the Government’s policy regarding payment of retroactive benefits had amounted to preferential treatment. The Commission declared the application admissible by a decision of 18 October 1972. In its report of 17 July 1974, the Commission: (i) confirmed its opinion, previously expressed in the report in the Swedish Engine Drivers’ Union case, that Article 11 para. 1 (art. 11-1) may legitimately extend to cover State responsibility in the field of labour-management relations and thus to provide some protection for unions against interference by employers. (ii) expressed the opinion: ‘In view of the preceding finding, the. Commission was not called upon to examine whether the action complained of was justified under Article 11. para. 2.’ The report found that the differential treatment complained of was in the circumstances justified as an industrial relations policy. The report contains a separate concurring opinion. It found that there had been no violation of Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 11 para. 1 (art. 14+11-1). The report also found that it had been justified as a matter of industrial relations. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for further action. The ECHR ruled that the case should be referred back to the ECH for further proceedings. The decision was upheld and the case was adjourned until January 24, 2015.

The flights which determine the NNI at any point on the ground are those which take place between 06.00 and 18.00 hours Greenwich Mean Time during the three busy summer months. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours (high noise-annoyance zone) It is to be noted that the NNI calculation reflects a logarithmic element in the PNdB scale, which has the result that every increase of 10 in that scale represents approximately a doubling of the loudness. The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Hundested. She suffered severe problems with her jaw, resulting in her being able to open her mouth only 5 millimetres. On 19 April 1988 at a hospital in Hillerød the applicant underwent a jaw operation which entailed implanting Teflon in both her jaw-joints. She continued to experience problems, and on 20 February 1992, alleging malpractice, she complained to the National Patients' Complaints Board. The applicant claimed compensation for her medical costs, loss of working capacity and disablement. The National Board of Health found against the applicant on 16 February 1994.

A binding-over order requires the person bound over to enter into a ‘recognisance’ or undertaking secured by a sum of money fixed by the court. In 2005 criminal proceedings on suspicion of aggravated theft, aggravated fraud and embezzlement were opened against the applicant and a number of other persons by the Vienna Regional Criminal Court. On 21 February 2006 the investigating judge issued a search warrant for the applicant’s premises. The warrant authorised the search and seizure of the following items: “Documents, personal computers and discs, savings books, bank documents, deeds of gift and wills in favour of Dr Heinz Robathin, and any files concerning R. [name of one person] and G. [ name of another person].” The search warrant stated that the applicant was suspected of having taken furniture, pictures and silver worth more than 50,000 euros (EUR) from Mr R. in December 2003 for personal enrichment.

Criminal proceedings on suspicion of aggravated theft, aggravated fraud and embezzlement were opened against the applicant and a number of other persons in 2005. The applicant was suspected of having taken furniture, pictures and silver worth more than 50,000 euros (EUR) from Mr R. in December 2003 for personal enrichment. The police officers proceeded to search the applicant’s computer system, copying all files to disc. The representative of the Vienna Bar Association opposed this as being disproportionate since it was technically possible, by using appropriate search criteria, to search for and copy only those files which corresponded to the criteria set out in the search warrant.

The applicant is a practising lawyer by profession and runs his law office with a partner. In 2005 criminal proceedings on suspicion of aggravated theft, aggravated fraud and embezzlement were opened against the applicant and a number of other persons. The search of the applicant’s business premises was carried out by police officers of the Federal Ministry of the Interior on 21 February 2006. The police officers copied all data returned by a search for the names ‘R.’ and ‘G’ to one disc and all other data to separate discs. The representative of the Vienna Bar Association opposed this as being disproportionate since it was technically possible, by using appropriate search criteria, to search for and copy only those files which corresponded to the criteria set out in the warrant.

The applicant opposed the search of the data. The Review Chamber (Ratskammer), a panel of three judges, of the Vienna Regional Criminal Court was called upon to decide whether they were to be examined or returned. On 3 March 2006 the Review Chamber authorised the examination of all the files. It repeated that there were grounds for suspecting the applicant of the offences described in the search warrant. The data in issue had been seized in the context of the preliminary investigations in respect of the applicant and other persons. A lawyer could not rely on his duty of professional secrecy and the attendant guarantees of Article 152 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure when he himself was the suspect.

The Vienna Bar Association contacted the Procurator General, suggesting that he lodge a plea of nullity for the preservation of the law. It submitted, in particular, that a search of a lawyer’s business premises risked impinging on his duty of professional secrecy. In sum, the examination of the seized files was necessary in order to investigate the offences described in the search warrant. The search warrant did not extend to the seizure of all the law office's data. In fact, most lawyers also had all their files in electronic form. Standard software for law offices allowed full-text searches for any name or word and thus made it easy to narrow the search of data. The same applied to searches of electronic data.

Vienna Bar Association contacted Procurator General, suggesting that he lodge a plea of nullity for the preservation of the law (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde zur Wahrung des Gesetzes) in the applicant’s case. It submitted, in particular, that a search of a lawyer's business premises risked impinging on his duty of professional secrecy. In sum, the examination of the seized files was necessary in order to investigate the offences. The Review Chamber (Ratskammer), a panel of three judges, of the Vienna Regional Criminal Court was called upon to decide whether they were to be examined or returned.

The Bar Association argued that the seizure of all the data and the Review Chamber’s decision to permit the examination thereof had been excessive and therefore unlawful. The Review Chamber had failed to give any specific reasons why an examination of the data relating to Mr R. and Mr G. would not be sufficient. The applicant's duty of professional secrecy could only be lifted in relation to the suspicion against him concerning two of his clients but not in respect of all his lawyer-client relationships. Moreover, the partner in his law office was not under any suspicion. The court sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, two of which were suspended on probation.

The case originated in an application (no. 25154/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by a British citizen, Mrs Jane Smith (“the applicant”), on 4 May 1994. The applicant alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against her in respect of her occupation of her land in her caravans violated her right to respect for home, her family and private life. The applicant and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from European Roma Rights Centre. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 May 2000. The applicant is a gypsy by birth. Since her birth she has travelled constantly, mainly in the Surrey area, with her family in search of work. They regard travelling as detrimental to both the health of their family and to the education of their children. They have five children, born in 1975, 1977, 1982, 1989 and 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Drabble and Mr Pannick. In 1988, the High Court had granted a declaration that Surrey County Council was in breach of its duty under section 6 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 to provide provision for gypsies. In March 1993, the applicant bought land known as 111A Almners Road, Runnymede. It was a portion of a garden in a Green Belt area where there was already some residential development. The applicant moved a mobile home onto the land and took up residence with her family. In 1996 the applicant’s uncle, Jasper Smith, a member of the Gypsy Council, stated that he had attempted on numerous occasions prior to 1993 to obtain a site on an official site on behalf of the applicant without success. The previous owner of 111A Almners Road, also a gypsy, had been refused planning permission in January 1993 to live on the land in a caravan. The Council considered that the stationing of a caravan would be detrimental to the character of the Green Belt. The applicant was aware of this situation and the fact that the previous owner had appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment against the refusal of planning permission and the enforcement order. An Inspector appointed by the Department of Environment heard evidence and representations from the applicant and the Council. By a letter dated 3 June 1993, the Inspector dismissed the appeal. “10. The mobile home is situated on an enclosed plot of land fronting Almners road, adjacent to No. 111. This land is separated from the adjacent house by a screen fence, which continues along the rear boundary of the appeal site’ The appeals site lies within the south west sector of the Metropolitan Green Belt. Structure Plan 1989 and policy PE2 of the Replacement Structure Plan 1992 provide that gypsy caravan sites may be appropriate and necessary in the green belt, but they will not be considered acceptable as of right. Despite the support of some nearby residents, I consider that the discernible presence of the unauthorised development on the appeals site is harmful to the appearance of this mainly rural location. … In light of this and its particular impact on the aims of green belt policy, I conclude … that the use of the land for a residential caravan site for a mobile home and associated operational development is not appropriate to this part of the Met. There are no plans to change the status of the green belt. There is no need to change it because it is already there. There are plans to make it more accessible to people who need it. The green belt is a place to live, not a place for people to live. It is an important place to work and to raise a family. It has been around for a long time, and it is good to see it being used again and again. It's a good place to raise children, but it is not a great place for a family to live and work. However, the earliest date that the trial judge would be available was the week beginning 30 October 2000. There was no evidence of any enquiry from 24 March 2000 onwards into whether a space could be found for the confiscated hearing during the six-month period. Neither had there been any analysis of any factors which might amount to exceptional circumstances. The trial judge had also “candidly acknowledged more than once” that there were no exceptional circumstances to justify the imposition of a confiscation order. The Court of Appeal certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decisions. The House of Lords observed that the core problem before it was whether, as a matter of statutory construction, failure to comply with a statutory time-limit would have the effect of invalidating an act. In London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v. Aberdeen District Council [1980] 1 WLR 182, 189E-190C, Lord Hailsham had emphasised that it was within the courts’ inherently discretionary jurisdiction to determine the nature of a particular statutory requirement. The prime purpose behind the statutory provision for confiscation orders was to recover any financial benefit that an offender might have obtained from his criminal conduct. In October 2005 the Court of Appeal re-imposed the confiscation orders and sentences of imprisonment in default on the applicants. The prejudice to the applicants was not significant and was outweighed by the countervailing public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for what were no more than bona fide errors in the judicial process. In any event, there would always be the safeguard of judicial review should there be an apparent abuse of process. The Crown Court had postponed its final decision on confiscation Orders in good faith. In the present case, the Crown court had postponed the final decision in goodfaith. The public interest was outweighing the prejudice to applicants and they were not prejudiced by the prejudice. The court could not have intended to disable a court from making a confiscation order after sentence.

The applicants were born in 1972 and 1958 respectively. The first applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. The Court heard addresses by the Government, Mr J. Perry QC, Mr A. Dodsworth, Mr F. Krause and Ms E. Abrahamson. The case was heard at the High Court in London, where it is expected to be heard for the next three months. The applicants sought leave to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s decision. On 29 July 2003 the High Court refused leave on the papers. The High Court ruled that it would not be in the public interest to provide artificial insemination facilities in a particular case. The judges ruled that the case was not a miscarriage of justice, but rather a case of miscarriage of the principle of free speech. He pointed to the similarity of the arguments put by the applicants in the present case and in the Mellor case. The starting point of the policy is that deprivation of facilities for artificial insemination may prevent conception altogether. The finishing point is whether there are exceptional circumstances for not applying the policy. He then noted that on occasions the Secretary of. State had “dis-applied” the Policy when the circumstances had merited it. The other judges also relied on the judgment in Mellor. Mance LJ said the following: “The case of Mellor is also clear authority that considerations and potential consequences of public interest over and above a narrow view of the requirements of good order and security in prison can play a role in a decision whether or not to permit such artificial insemination’” The first applicant was transferred to the open side of another prison as a Category D prisoner. The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. On 28 June 2003 two police officers went to the Beşiktaş district of Istanbul following a complaint by a woman. Subsequently, the policemen and the taxi driver commenced a verbal dispute in the presence of the applicant, who is also a taxi driver. The applicant told the police officers that he would pay the fine on his friend’s behalf. The police officers then pushed the applicant to the ground, handcuffed him and began kicking and punching him. He was subsequently put in the police car. One of the officers closed the car door on the applicant's leg. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination, his right leg was broken as a result of the incident.

The applicant was arrested and taken to the Beşiktaş police station by the officers, as he was accused of having insulted them. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination of the applicant, his right leg was broken as a result of the incident. The applicant lodged a petition with the trial court and requested that the police officers be punished for ill-treating him. On 31 January 2005 the 12th Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court acquitted the applicant of the charges against him in respect of one of the officers. As regards the second officer, who had closed the car door on the applicant’s leg, the court found that the officer was not at fault.

The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. On 28 June 2003 two police officers went to the Beşiktaş district of Istanbul following a complaint by a woman, and imposed an administrative fine on a taxi driver. Subsequently, the policemen and the taxi driver commenced a verbal dispute in the presence of the applicant. The applicant told the police officers that he would pay the fine on his friend’s behalf. The police officers then pushed the applicant to the ground, handcuffed him and began kicking and punching him. He was subsequently put in the police car and one of the officers closed the car door on the applicant's leg. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination, his right leg was broken.

On 23 December 2008 the 1st Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court convicted the police officers as charged. The court found, in the light of the medical reports that it had obtained, plus the witness statements and the submissions of the accused and the applicant, that the officers had beaten the applicant and had closed the car door on his leg. However, since the officer had overstepped his authority by his actions, the court decided not to convict the applicant. The applicant lodged an objection to the judgment of the first-instance court. In his petition, the applicant noted that he would make more detailed submissions after he had been provided with a copy of the reasons for judgment. On 21 April 2009 the Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection of 29 December 2008.

The Istanbul public prosecutor filed an indictment with the 1st Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court against the police officers, charging them with ill-treatment of the applicant. The court sentenced the accused police officers to two months and fifteen days’ imprisonment. The applicant lodged an objection to the judgment of the first-instance court. On 21 April 2009 the Istanbul Assize Court dismissed the applicant’s objection of 29 December 2008. As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, this decision was final. The judge suspended the pronouncement of the judgment for a period of five years, pursuant to Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Law no. 5271).

According to the arrest and search protocols, the applicants were arrested in the course of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the DHKP‑C (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party-Front) The applicants had been considered to be involved in the activities of this organisation at the university in Antalya. The applicants' representative alleged that they had been subjected to different types of ill-treatment while in custody. The applicants were brought before a doctor, who noted that there were no signs of ill treatment on their bodies. They were charged with membership of the DHKP-C under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713. On 24 January 2002 the Diyarbakır State Security Court acquitted the applicants of the charges against them. The application was dismissed on 21 March 2002 as neither the public prosecutor nor the applicants filed an appeal against it. The court ruled that the relevant evidence had been collected and that the applicants were students and had to take their exams. Court awarded 500,000,000 Turkish liras (TRL) each to Ali Kemal Mart, Göksel Avcı, Ertuğrul Saraçoğlu and M.D. in respect of non-pecuniary compensation. 10 December 2003 the court awarded the men around 300 euros each for their part in the incident. The court also awarded a further TRL to a third of the men for their role in the case. The case was settled out of court in 2005, and the verdicts were returned to the court on November 6, 2007, and December 10, 2007. The men were awarded an additional TRL of about $500,000 each.

It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was discharged from the army in 1992 and awarded a sixth-degree disability pension. In 2004 a CT scan revealed an unidentified metallic object in the left orbital area of the applicant's head. In 2007, the applicant was admitted to the neurosurgery department of the GATA Military Hospital and he had a bullet in his head, measuring 15 x 10 mm. The doctors stated that removing the bullet was potentially life-threatening. The judge ruled that the bullet in the applicant’s head had remained unnoticed and that he had sustained further pecuniary damage. The Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1), his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. A rectification request was lodged by the applicant in April 2009. On 22 April 2009 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected a rectification request lodged by. the applicant. A decision to rectify the rectification was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009.

The decision followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic to follow on from Ahmet Necdet Sezer before the expiry of his single seven-year term of office. Fourteen political parties took part in the elections, which were marked by two characteristics. A strong mobilisation of the electorate was observed following the presidential crisis, since the participation rate rose to 84%. Secondly, political parties used two pre-electoral strategies to circumvent the national 10% threshold. With 46.58% of the votes cast, the AKP won 341 seats, 62 per cent of the total.

The strong showing by independent candidates was one of the main features of the elections of 22 July 2007. The Higher Electoral Council dismissed the applicant’s request, on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298. It pointed out that this provision could only be modified by a fresh legislative amendment. An earlier version of this article stated that the applicant had applied to have his application dismissed. We are happy to make clear that this was not the case and that the application was made as part of the normal course of proceedings. We apologise for any confusion.

Application no. 37920/07 was made before the June 22, 2007 parliamentary elections. The applicant argued that the large number of independent candidates standing in the election was caused by dissatisfaction with political parties. The application was dismissed on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298 on Elections, which stated that this provision could only be modified by a fresh legislative amendment. The Higher Electoral Council oversaw the implementation of the Law, which laid down sanctions for infringements of the provisions on election broadcasts. A new application was made in July 2007, but the application was rejected before it could be heard by the Court of Appeal. A fresh application was heard in July 2008, but it was denied.

The applicant alleged a violation of Articles 10 and 14 of the. Convention respectively, in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and a violation. of Article 13. The Court considers it useful to outline the circumstances under which the parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007 took place. In early May 2007 the Turkish Parliament decided to hold early parliamentary elections. This followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic. In the elections the AKP, the CHP and the MHP managed to get over the 10% threshold. More than sixty independent candidates stood for election in about forty provincial constituencies. The strong showing by independent candidates was one of the main features of the elections of 22 July 2007. There were none in the National Assembly in 1980 but 1999 saw them return, when there were three. In 2002 nine independent MPs were elected from a national total of 260 independent candidates. In the elections in July 2007, twenty-seven independent MP were elected, and more than twenty ‘thousand hopes’ candidates were elected after obtaining approximately 2.23% of the votes cast. The applicant lodged with the Higher Electoral Council a request for the annulment of the Decree du 27 May 2007. Election broadcasts were authorised from 15 to 21 July 2007, that is to say during the week before the elections. The applicant stressed that one peculiarity of the 22 July 2007 elections had been the large number of independent candidates standing. He considered that this unprecedented phenomenon had stemmed, firstly, from the 10% electoral threshold imposed during the parliamentary elections, and secondly, from dissatisfaction felt by most people at the material time with the performance of the political parties, whether in power or in opposition. The application was dismissed on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298.

The compensation proceedings were settled in December 1997. The application was dismissed by the Security Court in July 2003. The case was reopened in April 2009 and the applicants are still seeking compensation. The Ministry of the Interior appealed, arguing that it had not failed in that obligation because the reason for the killing and the identity of its perpetrators had not yet been established. For the public authorities to be said to have failed in their obligation, it was necessary to establish that they had either not performed their duties at all, or failed to perform them in a timely manner, or had performed them in an unsatisfactory fashion. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision and argued that a citizen need not officially seek protection from the authorities in order to trigger the State's obligation to protect such a citizen’s life. The appeal lodged by the applicants was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 17 April 2003. The applicants maintained that the authorities had failed to take the necessary steps to prevent the attack on their relative and to find the perpetrators. The Ministry was therefore responsible for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the failures on its part. The final decision was served on the applicants on 3 January 2006. The fact that some eight years after the killing the perpetrators had still not been identified was an indication that the public Authorities had failed in their duties. The appeal was rejected and the case was returned to the Appeals Court.

The applicant, a housewife, was born in 1953 and lives in Bursa. She was taken to the Görükle gendarmerie station where she was beaten with a truncheon and sworn at by a gendarme. On the same day, at 3.45 p.m., the applicant was examined by a doctor who noted that she had ecchymoses of 20x10 cm on her left shoulder and arm. The doctor considered that the injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for ten days. The applicant filed an official complaint with the public prosecutor about the above events and requested the prosecution of those responsible. On 21 April 1999 the prosecutor questioned the accused gendar me, Mr T.Ü, who denied the allegations.

They were arrested and taken into police custody where they remained until their release the following day. The applicants allege that they were subjected to ill-treatment during their arrest and their detention in custody. They claim that the intervention of a number of police officers and the force used by those police officers against them in a demonstration in which they were taking part had been in violation of their rights under Articles 3 and 11 of the Convention. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the. Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicants were brought before the Bakırköy prosecutor. With the exception of the third applicant, the applicants complained of ill-treatment. The applicants told the prosecutor that by attending the demonstration they had been exercising their democratic rights. They also alleged that the police had arrested them without any previous warnings. The fourth applicant complained that he had been beaten up by the police officers. Ten police officers denied having been at the demonstration or having seen any of the demonstrators. The remaining officer, police chief M.T., said he had not taken part in the dispersal of the demonstration but had questioned the applicants in a police station. On 14 April 2004 the Bakırköy prosecutor decided to close the investigation into the applicants’ allegations of ill-treatment. He denied having ill-treated any of the arrestees or having sworn at them. The applicants' objection against the prosecutor’s decision was rejected by the Eyüp Assize Court on 8 December 2004. On 28 January 2008 the BakTurkish Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicants, holding that they had exercised their democratic rights and not committed any offences. This decision stated that it was to be served on the applicants. According to a hand-written note on this decision, it was communicated to the applicants on 9 February 2005.

The case was brought by a woman who says she was forced to wear the headscarf because she was a Muslim. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled that the woman was entitled to wear a head scarf as long as it did not interfere with her constitutional rights. The woman was able to continue wearing the head scarf for a further four years. She was allowed to wear it for another four years, but was not allowed to leave the university campus unless she showed up for a lecture. In the end, the court found her not guilty of any crime and allowed her to continue to wear her head scarf. The judge ruled that she was not entitled to be a member of the university. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health, again for the same reason. She lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress in order to maintain order. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. On 19 April 2001 the Supreme Administrative court dismissed an appeal by the applicant on points of law. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for a semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. Istanbul University argued that the disciplinary penalty was lawful as the reason for the applicant’s one-semester suspension. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's application to have the penalty quashed. The applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. On 28 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court held that the aforementioned legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1999. The application was dismissed on the grounds that there was no case on the merits.

The Sami have, since ancient times, inhabited the northern parts of Scandinavia and the Kola Peninsula. Their historical use of the land has given rise to a special right to real estate, the reindeer herding right (renskötselrätten) Presently regulated in Sweden by the Reindeer Husbandry Act (Rennäringslagen, 1971:437), it comprises the right to use land and water for the Sami's own sustenance and that of his reindeers. The right may only be exercised by the members of a Sami village. Such villages are both geographical grazing areas and economic entities. They do not have any public legal status.

ECJ: Discrimination based on sexual orientation is to be prohibited, just as is discrimination based on the fact that a person belongs to a particular sex. But it does not apply to differences of treatment based on a person’s sexual orientation. The refusal by an employer to allow travel concessions to the person of the same sex with whom a worker has a stable relationship, does not constitute discrimination prohibited by Article 119 of the Treaty or Directive 75/117. It should be observed, however, that the Treaty of Amsterdam amending the Treaty on European Union, the Treaties establishing the European Communities and certain related acts, signed on 2 October 1997, provides for the insertion in the EC Treaty of an Article 6a.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’s) on 12 April 1989 and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation (‘the Government’) on 3 July 1989. It originated in an application (no. 11034/84) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Franz Weber, on 15 May 1984. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 and Article 10. Franz Weber, a Swiss journalist, lives at Clarens, in the Canton of Vaud. The applicant and one of the associations he runs, Helvetia Nostra, lodged a complaint alleging defamation against R.M., who had written a letter published in the letters column of the. newspaper L’Est vaudois under the headline ‘Franz. Weber is fooling you’. The Court heard addresses by Mr Boillat and Mr Vautier for the Government, by Mr Trechsel for the Commission and by Mr Schaller for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. R.M. was charged with defamation and committed for trial in 1982, but the case was dismissed. R.M.'s behaviour borders on the 'criminal', says the former head of Helvetia Nostra. He says the list of municipal taxpayers is not published and it is easy to hide behind that sort of censorship and live by devious means. ‘We have had enough of playing into the hands of people who sponge off us,’ he writes. “You would be amazed at the distrust of the whole country’s democratically - and how democratically! - elected authorities,” he adds. On 3 March 1982 the daily newspapers Gazette de Lausanne, 24 heures and Tribune/Le Matin reported what the applicant had said. Mr Weber had already divulged the first three items of information at a press conference in Berne on 11 May 1981, during which he denounced “the plot hatched against him by the Vaud authorities in order to intimidate him’ The President of the Cassation Division imposed a fine of 300 Swiss francs on him, together with a probationary period of a year for the purposes of deletion of the fine from the cantonal register. He also stated that he had lodged a challenge and a complaint against the investigating judge. The court in Vaud ruled that Mr Weber's disclosure of criminal complaints had been lodged was not information about an investigation. The court said that disclosure of a criminal complaint is not caught by Article 185 CC, more particularly where it has been decided to take no action on the complaint. Mr Weber himself admits that the breach of the confidentiality of the investigation was intentional. The proceedings in the Criminal Cassation Division of the Vaud Cantonal Court were dismissed on 15 October 1982. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that there was no need to deal with it in the present proceedings as criminal proceedings will shortly be time-barred. The matter which was to be kept confidential was known to a limited or indefinite number of people because confidentiality had already been breached. Mr Weber lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. He relied on Articles 10 and 6 (art. 10, art. 6) of the Convention. In his view, Article 6 applied because of the criminal nature of the fine. On this point cantonal law differed from federal law. The appellant was therefore rightly convicted. ...“ Finally, the Criminal Cassation Division set aside of its own motion the entry of thefine in the cantonal register.’’. The proceedings in the Federal. Court were held at the Court of Appeal in Lausanne, Switzerland. The hearing was held at the Court of cassation, which is located at the Prosecutor’s Office. The applicant maintained that Article 185 of the Vaud Code of Criminal Procedure (Vaud CCP) violates freedom of expression. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 November 1983. It noted in particular that such restrictions are "permissible where they are necessary in a democratic society" The rule enacted in Article 185 Vaud CCP clearly conforms to these principles. A weighing of the competing interests at stake leads to the same conclusions. The prohibition against communicating information about an investigation until its completion and the penalties attaching to the offence are undoubtedly consistent with the proportionality principle. The applicant had grounds for rebelling against the sometimes unorthodox course taken by the proceedings against him. He successfully availed himself of the usual remedies. The fine was convertible into ten days’ imprisonment under Article 12 of the Vaud Order on the recovery of fines and their conversion into imprisonment. The possibility of conversion into a custodial sentence makes no difference, since conversion is possible only in the event of the appellant’s refusing to pay the fine out of sheer unwillingness. The safeguards provided for in Article 6 § 1 (art. 6-1) ECHR were therefore not applicable in the instant case. The fine imposed was not a negligible one, but it nonetheless came into the category of penalties which by their nature, duration or manner of execution are deemed not to be appreciably detrimental.

Pierre-André Melin, a French national, lives off private means and resides at Courbevoie. He formerly practised as a lawyer. On 6 May 1985 the Nanterre Criminal Court convicted him of fraud and sentenced him to a suspended term of sixteen months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed immediately to the Versailles Court of Appeal, which, giving judgment on 15 January 1986, upheld the lower court’s guilty verdict. On the other hand, it deferred pronouncement of sentence until 25 June 1986 as the accused had undertaken to reimburse the victim within six months if the court were to find him guilty. This aspect of the proceedings is not in issue.

Mr Melin had conducted his own defence, though he had been assisted by a lawyer at first instance. He complained that the judge-rapporteur had failed to communicate to him a time-limit for the submission of a memorial. On 4 July the Chief Registrar replied to him that, as the judgment of the Court of Cassation was final, he could not appeal against it. The case was settled in July 1986 and Mr Melin was awarded the damages of £150,000. The sentence was quashed on the grounds that it was disproportionate to the crime, and he was not entitled to appeal against the verdict.

Section 42 of the new Austrian Penal Code is aimed at avoiding criminal trials in trivial cases. Manuel Tejedor García was an officer in the national police force and lived in Barcelona. While off duty, he was in Gallur (Saragossa) to celebrate his niece’s first communion. He noted the presence of Mr Karamo Jarra, a Gambian national, and Mr Leonel Pajucides Falçao, a Portuguese national. He asked them for their identity papers, which they agreed to produce. But he did not consider the documents satisfactory and drew his revolver. He fired a shot into the ceiling of the café; approximately twenty people were present and left the premises in a frightened state.

Mr Tejedor García, who was born in 1948, now lives in Saragossa. At the material time, he was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró. On 21 May 1989, while off duty, he joined members of his family and friends to celebrate his niece’s first communion. At about 8.30 p.m., after a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, in addition to the wine that. accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of. the wine, he drank two glasses of cognac. Manuel Tejedor García, who was dressed in plain clothing, did not consider the documents satisfactory and, showing his police identification, fired a shot into the ceiling of the café. He then kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them, using the psychological pressure of the gun, to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. On 29 May 1989 the investigating judge sent the case file to the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial, competent for criminal proceedings regarding members of the security forces. On 18 September 1989 the ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. Following a judgment of the Constitutional Court declaring unconstitutional the provision by which criminal offences by security forces should be tried, the case was sent back. On 12 November 1991 Mr Tejedor García appealed on points of law on the ground, inter alia, that the public prosecutor's application against the decision of 10 September 1990 had been made out of time. The case involved the expropriation of shares in the RUMASA group by the Spanish government. The aim was to protect the public interest because the group's banks had taken risks considered to be disproportionate in relation to their solvency. The Constitutional Court dismissed the deputies’ appeal by a judgment of 2 December 1983, adopted with the President’s casting vote. In a dissenting opinion, six members of the court expressed the view that the Expropriation procedure followed was contrary to the Constitution. The case led to the creation of the Spanish Bankruptcy Court, which now has the power to seize the assets of Spanish banks.

The argument in favour of increasing procedural safeguards for the alleged victims of sexual offence is the danger of the court proceedings causing damage and traumatisation to the victim. However, it would also appear to be in the interest of victims aged over 14 for them to be questioned only once, as making a statement places a heavy mental burden on them. The European Court of Justice has ruled that particularly vulnerable victims receive ‘specific treatment best suited to their circumstances’ The aim is to ensure that victims are questioned “only insofar as necessary for the purpose of criminal proceedings’ ‘Victims may be entitled to testify in a manner enabling that objective to be achieved, by any appropriate means compatible with its basic legal principles,’ the court ruled. ‘A court should be able, in respect ofparticularly vulnerable victims, to use a special procedure if it best corresponds to the situation of the victims’‘ ‘The hearing arrangements must be capable of guaranteeing to all victims treatment which pays due respect to their individual dignity and gives them the opportunity to be heard and to supply evidence’

In the early 19th century, the majority of Irish schools were owned by the Catholic Church. In the late 1800s, the Church began to take control of the schools. In 1900, the Irish government began to privatise some of these schools. The Catholic Church was able to take full control of schools, but the state was left to pick up the tab for the rest. In 1950, the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the public schools, not the Catholic churches. In 2000, the High Court ruled that the public school system was not responsible for the maintenance of the school system. In 2003, the Court of Appeal ruled in favor of the Public Education Act. The High Court of Ireland ordered the state to provide free education to all children in all schools.

The Supreme Court of Ireland ruled that the state was not liable for the acts of L.H. and the public school system. The High Court ruled that it was the duty of the public schools to provide children with the education they needed. The decision was the result of an appeal by the Supreme Court to the High Court of Justice of the Republic of Ireland. The Supreme Court found that there was no evidence that the public was at risk of being injured by the actions of the state in the case. The court also found that the government had not failed to provide the public with the information it needed to make a fair decision. The case was the first of its kind to be heard by the Court.

The Court of Appeal ruled that the state did not have to pay for the education of children in Irish schools. The court ruled in favour of the parents of children who had been left out of the education system. The Supreme Court also ruled in favor of the mother and father who had to pay the children's school fees for their education. The case was decided by a majority of 8 to 1 vote in favour, with the second vote by the majority of 3 to 1. The decision was the result of an appeal by the father of one of the children, who was the mother of the other, to the Supreme Court from the High Court of Ireland.

Hardiman J described the Irish Free State as a ‘managerial’ system. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. A few were under the control of other denominations, and even fewer were controlled by non-denominational groups. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire’ of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. The provision of free primary education was placed on a statutory basis by the Act of 1998. But the rules did not govern the activities of any individual teacher. He said this was due to the fact that the rules were ‘general in nature’.

In the 1950s, the Irish Free State had 3,000 schools under the control of the Catholic Church. The Irish Constitution provided for free primary education, but it was overseen by the Church. In the 1960s, a union was asked to manage the schools, but was told it would interfere with the Church's role. Now, the provision of free primary school education has been put on a statutory basis by the 1998 Education Act. But the Church still has the power to run the schools and could not be removed from the charge of the education system, the court was told. The case will be heard at the Irish Court of Appeal in Dublin on May 16 and 17.

The current law is the result of a long-running legal battle between the state and the Catholic church. The case is currently being heard by the Irish Court of Appeal, which is expected to deliver its verdict in the coming weeks. The decision will be the first in the case to be heard by a full bench, and it is likely to be the most significant.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant mainly complained under Article 3 that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also declared admissible the remaining complaints. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The applicant and the Government each filed further observations on the merits. The Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice had been given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure and their submissions to the Chamber were admitted to the Grand Chamber file. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2013 (Rule 59 § 3). In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. Those allegations were not reported at that time. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. While she had significant psychological difficulties, she did not associate those with the abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School. In 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (‘the Minister’) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965. An initial award (44,814.14 euros (EUR) was made by a single judge. The applicant appealed to a CICT panel. She claimed that the CICT gave her the option of continuing her appeal (at the risk of finding that her CICT application would be rejected as out of time) or of accepting the initial offer. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later. The High Court awarded the applicant damages in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.H. The State Defendants applied for a direction to strike out the case. The High Court judge, in response to the applicant’s complaint regarding the absence of a State system for adverting to and addressing sexual abuse in national schools, asked Counsel for the applicant as follows: “What evidence do I have, or what should I have deduce[d] from the evidence that has been given?” The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application in March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fennley J agreed), the appeal was dismissed. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Those churches were “remarkably successful” in achieving this aim. State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons and managers. The Catholic Church had responded that there could be no interference whatever with the “inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling”. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and the case is now mooted for a new generation. Hardiman J referred to the ‘urgent desire’ of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers, a few were underThe control of other denominations and even fewer were controlled by non-denominational groups. Hardiman J noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.]” Hardiman J: The Minister can hardly be responsible for a failure to ‘cease’ a course of action of whose existence he was quite unaware. Kenny J: In my view the Constitution specifically envisages, not indeed a delegation but a ceding of the actual running of schools to the interests represented by the patron and the manager. Fennelly J: Cases of sexual abuse had preoccupied the criminal courts and the Supreme Court for many years and it was surprising that that court was confronted for the first time with questions relating to the liability of institutions including the State for sexual abuse of schoolchildren in a national school by a teacher. Fennelly J said the system was not a State system but rather a “State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint to the State.Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. He considered that, for all practical purposes, most primary education in Ireland took the form of a joint enterprise between Church and State. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. The Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. She was awarded damages of more than £30,000.

Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The application was declared partly inadmissible pursuant to Article 35 §§ 3 (a) and 4 of the convention as being manifestly ill-founded.

The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency.

The applicants are the sons of the late David Gray (hereinafter referred to as “Mr Gray” or “the deceased”) who died in the evening of 16 February 2008 at his home in Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom. Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now” (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. In the instant case, the deceased had on some of these occasions been injected with 10mg doses of the opiate diamorphine, contained in a sealed palliative care box.

U. arrived in the United Kingdom on Friday, 15 February 2008 for his first shift as a locum doctor scheduled for the coming weekend. According to an induction report established by a TCN doctor there had not been sufficient time to assess U’s professional competence prior to his first assignment the next day. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Some two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray's partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed that Mr Gray had died.

Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. He had applied to be admitted to one of the Medical Performers Lists maintained by each of the local PCTs. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection. Two hours after U. had left, Mr Gray’s partner realised that he was no longer breathing and called an ambulance. The attending emergency services confirmed Mr Gray had died.

U., at the time aged 65, had qualified as a doctor in Germany in 1972 where he was practising as an aesthetic surgeon. Once a GP is admitted to a PCT’s Performers List he may work in the area of any other PCT in England. U. administered 100mg of diamorphine from the respective ampoule included in the palliative care box by intra‑muscular injection.

On 16 February 2008 TCN suspended U. from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany. Subsequently, two other incidents were reported where U. on the occasion of home visits had failed to administer the appropriate medical treatment. He explained that when treating the deceased he had committed a grave mistake with fatal outcome that had resulted from the confusion between the drugs pethidine and diamorphine. The latter being a drug not used by on-call services in Germany and with which he had been unfamiliar. On the day of the incident he had further been overtired following his journey from Germany to the United Kingdom and had found himself in a tremendous stress situation.

On 16 February 2008 TCN suspended U. from duty, terminated his engagement with immediate effect and advised him to return to Germany. Subsequently, two other incidents were reported where U. on the occasion of home visits had failed to administer the appropriate medical treatment. U. apologised for the medical malpractice in connection with the deceased’s treatment and again explained that he had confused the opiates and referred to the stress situation he was subject to when making the mistake. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United Kingdom established as the cause of Mr Gray's death diamorphine poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication.
