The diamorphine injection had more than minimally contributed to the death and that in view of the large dose administered there was no need to necessarily invoke the additional effect of alcohol in causing death. A post mortem report issued on 25 June 2008 by a forensic pathologist in the United Kingdom established as the cause of Mr Gray’S death diamorphines poisoning in association with alcohol intoxication as well as hypertensive heart disease and myocardial fibrosis.

Cambridgeshire police commenced criminal investigations against U. for manslaughter by gross negligence. German authorities were asked to provide information with respect to U.’s medical qualifications and the authenticity of the related certificates submitted by him to the British authorities when applying to be admitted as a locum doctor. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany. U. was suspended from the medical register in London where his suspension was confirmed. The criminal proceedings were instituted against U in the United Kingdom and Germany in 2008. The investigation was launched in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of manslaughter.

Cambridgeshire police commenced criminal investigations against U. for manslaughter by gross negligence following Mr Gray’s death. The Bochum Chief Public Prosecutor ex officio initiated preliminary criminal proceedings (Ermittlungsverfahren) against U in Germany under file no. 49 Js 174/08 on suspicion of suspicion of manslaughter. The CPS asked the German authorities to carry out the respective investigations and to arrange for hearings of the relevant witnesses in Germany in the presence of representatives of Cambridgesbury Constabulary. The German authorities were asked to provide the requested information by mid-March 2008.

The criminal proceedings against U. in the United Kingdom and Germany were instituted following Mr Gray’s death. Cambridgeshire Constabulary, through Interpol London, made an application for assistance to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation (Bundeskriminalamt) on 5 March 2008. U. was suspended from the medical register in London where his suspension was confirmed. In July 2008 German and British police officers visited U. at his surgery in Witten, Germany, and informed him that criminal investigations were pending against him. U. availed himself of his right not to testify. He also declined a subsequent request by the Cambridgeshire police to be interviewed in the United Kingdom. A forensic expert opinion was obtained from a professor of Essen university hospital on the question whether the treatment of the deceased by U. had complied with medical standards. In his final report issued on 18 September 2008 the expert confirmed that the cause of Mr Gray’s death was the death by ‘negligent causing’.

Mr Gray suffered from kidney stones and from 2004 on he had regularly been attended at home by his doctor, a General Practitioner. The GP had routinely administered injections of opiates, in particular pethidine at a dosage of 100mg, for pain relief. On several occasions between 2006 and 2008 Mr Gray had recourse to out-of-hours medical services by “Take Care Now’ (“TCN”), a private agency that recruits locum doctors within the United Kingdom or from abroad. Dr U., a German national, had recently been recruited by TCN through an agency on a self-employed basis to provide out-of-hours care. The applicant alleged that the principle of equality of arms had been violated because the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal had taken decisions on 3 and 25 February 2011 relating to the continuation of his detention. The German Government were represented by one of their Agents, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. On 16 March 2016 the complaint concerning Article 5 § 4 of the convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The applicant was convicted of smuggling drugs into Germany and trafficking (dealt with as a single offence instead of two separate offences) and sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment. On 13 December 2010 he lodged an appeal against the judgment. On 28 January 2011 the Düsseldorf Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office (Generalstaatsanwaltschaft – “the prosecution authorities”) submitted written observations to the Court of Appeal, requesting the dismissal of the appeal of 5 January 2011. On 25 February 2011 the Court. of Appeal dismissed the request for a subsequent hearing as inadmissible. The decision of the Court of Appeal was based on the fact that there had been no opportunity to respond to the request for an inquiry. The decision was not based on facts, but on the lack of opportunity to comment on the request. The court's decision was made on the basis that the request had been made without sufficient information. The Court's decision is therefore the result of a legal challenge to the decision made by the court, which was upheld by the Supreme Court. The case was settled in the High Court of Justice on July 31, 2011. The appeal was upheld on August 6, 2011, and the decision is now on its way to the European Court of Appeals.

In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud (CPP/VD), all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The reason for the confidentiality of judicial investigations is the need to protect the interests of the criminal proceedings by anticipating risks of collusion and the danger of evidence being tampered with or destroyed. The present case therefore concerns secrecy imposed by the law rather than by an official decision. However, disclosure to friends or relatives by the parties or their lawyer is not punishable (see Article 185a CPP/VD).

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 56925/08) against the Swiss Confederation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the fine imposed on him in criminal proceedings for having published information covered by the secrecy of criminal investigations had violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52): 1 July 2014. On 29 September 2014 the Government requested that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber under Article 43. On 17 November 2014 a panel of the Grand chamber accepted that request. The joint dissenting opinion of Judges Karakaş, Keller and Lemmens was annexed to the judgment. The applicant is a journalist by profession. He published an article in the weekly magazine L’Illustré entitled ‘Drame du Grand-Pont à Lausanne – la version du chauffard – l’interrogatoire du conducteur fou’ The article in question concerned a set of criminal proceedings against M.B., a motorist who had been remanded in custody after an incident on 8 July 2003 in which he had rammed his car into pedestrians. The incident, in which three people had died and eight others had been injured, had caused much emotion and controversy in Switzerland. The Court heard addresses by Mr Poncet, Mr Schürmann and Mr Hoffmann. M.B. had been ‘charged with premeditated murder [assassinat] and, in the alternative, with murder [meurtre], grievous bodily harm, endangering life and serious traffic offences’ He ‘appear[ed] to show no remorse’, according to an article in the Tribune de Genève. ‘On being taken into custody he asked for his watch to be returned and requested a cup for his coffee, some dried fruit and chocolate.’ ‘I would like to phone my big brother in Algeria’ he begged. He finally announced on 11 August that he had come to a ‘final decision’: he dismissed his lawyer, Mr M.B., on grounds of ‘lack of trust’ M.B. was sentenced to one month’s imprisonment, suspended for one year. The Lausanne Police Court replaced the prison sentence with a fine of 4,000 Swiss francs (CHF) (approximately 2,667 euros) The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law. His appeal was dismissed on 30 January 2006 by the Criminal Court of Cassation of the Canton of Vaud. He also lodged a public-law appeal and an appeal for nullity with the Federal Court, which on 29 April 2008 dismissed the appeals. Its decision was served on the applicant on 9 May 2008. The relevant passages from the decision follow. “In short, the appellant submits that his conviction for a breach of Article 293 of the Criminal Code is contrary to federal law.” Anyone who makes public all or part of documents, investigations or deliberations of an authority which are secret by law or by virtue of a decision taken by that authority, acting within its powers, will be punished by a fine. The court may decide not to impose any penalties if the secret thus made public is of minor importance. According to case-law, this provision proceeds from a formal conception of secrecy. In its Stoll v. Switzerland judgment of 10 December 2007, the European Court of Human Rights confirmed that this formal conception. of secrecy was not contrary to Article 10 ECHR inasmuch as it did not prevent it from being applied. The Federal Court was asked to determine whether the interference in issue was compatible with Article 10 ECHR. In pursuance of Article 184 of the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Canton of Vaud, all investigations must remain secret until their final conclusion. The secrecy requirement relates to all the evidence uncovered by the investigation itself as well as all non-public decisions and investigative measures. The law also specifies that the following are bound by secrecy vis-à-vis anyone who does not have access to the case file: the judges, judicial staff, and also the parties, their friends and relatives, their lawyers, the latter’s associates, consultants and staff. The present case concerns secrecy imposed by the law rather than by an official decision. The aim is to maintain the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights has already had occasion to deem such a purpose legitimate in itself. This is the inescapable conclusion as regards the records of interviews of the accused. It would be inadmissible to allow such documents to be analysed in the public sphere, before the conclusion of the investigation. The evidence can validly be classified secret, by prohibiting public access to it, as provided by the legislation of the Canton of Vaud. It is also the only possible conclusion as. regards the letters sent by the accused to the investigating judge, which focused on practical problems and criticisms of his lawyer (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 7). Journalist published details of his interviews and correspondence with the investigating judge. The content of the correspondence is not disputed, but the only issue is the existence of a justification for publication. The appellant submits that he had the professional duty (under former Article 32 of the Criminal Code) as a journalist to publish the information in question because of what he describes as the obvious interest in the ‘Lausanne Bridge’ case for the population of French-speaking Switzerland. He considers that in the light of European case-law, the basic assumption should be that publication is justified in principle unless there is a pressing social need to maintain secrecy. He submits he is not responsible for the indiscretion committed by a third party. The cantonal court found that while the accident of 8 July 2003, the circumstances of which were undoubtedly unusual, had triggered a great deal of public emotion, it had nevertheless, in legal terms, been simply a road accident with fatal consequences. It is true that the ‘Lausanne Bridge case’ attracted extensive media coverage (see Police Court judgment, point 4, p. 8, to which the cantonal judgment refers) However, this circumstance alone, alongside the unusual nature of the accident, is insufficient to substantiate a major public interest in publishing the confidential information in question. Unless it can be justified per se, the interest aroused among the public by media coverage of events cannot constitute apublic interest in the disclosure of classified information. The cantonal court ruled that the tone adopted by the appellant in his article showed that his main concern was not, as he claims, to inform the general public about the State’s conduct of the criminal investigation. The headline of the article (‘Questioning of the mad driver’, ‘the reckless driver's version’) already lacked objectivity. It suggested that the case had already been tried in the author's view, in the sense that the fatalities on the Lausanne Bridge had been caused not by an ordinary motorist but by a mad driver. The European Court of Human Rights reiterates that neither it, nor the domestic courts for that matter, should substitute their own views for those of the press. Journalist wrote that the driver was doing his best to ‘make himself impossible to defend’ The manner in which he quoted the excerpts from the records of interviews and reproduced the letters sent by the defendant to the judge pointed to the motives of the author of the impugned article. Readers of this highly biased publication would have formed an opinion and subjectively prejudged the future action to be taken by the courts regarding this case. The cantonal court concluded that this factor did not indicate that the public interest in receiving information prevailed. That court cannot be criticised on that account. The appellant did not explicitly criticise the amount of the fine imposed on him. Nor did he challenge the refusal to grant him a probationary period after which the fine would be struck out. The fine does not exceed half the amount of the appellant’s monthly income at the material time (see Police Court judgment, point 1, p. 5), and there is nothing to suggest that his freelance status at the time of the first-instance judgment led to any significant drop in his earnings. The sanction for the offence with which the appellant is charged did not prevent him from expressing his views, since it was imposed after the article had been published. It is unclear, in view of the nature of the offence charged (the least serious in the classification set out in the Swiss Criminal Code), how the sanction imposed on the applicant could be regarded as a form of censorship.

Josef Felix Müller was invited to take part in an exhibition of contemporary art in Fribourg in 1981. The exhibition, entitled “Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of Fribouring’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. In the space of three nights Josef Felix. Müller, who had been invited by one of the organisers, created three works of art in a total of three hours. One of the works was titled ‘Frisch’ (‘Crisp’) and the other two were called ‘Dorothea’ and ‘Eden’. The artist has exhibited his works in private galleries and in museums.

Josef Felix Müller is a painter from St Gall, Switzerland. He was invited to be part of an exhibition of contemporary art in Fribourg in 1981. His work was part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton's entry into the Swiss Confederation. He took part in the Sydney Biennial in Australia in 1984, as Switzerland’s representative. He has been awarded several prizes and has sold works to museums such as the Kunsthalle in Zürich. In the space of three nights Josef Felix Müller created nine works of art in his home town of St Gall. For more information on the exhibition, visit Fri-Art 81.

In 1981, the nine last-mentioned applicants mounted an exhibition of contemporary art in Fribourg at the former Grand Seminary, a building due to be demolished. The exhibition, entitled “Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of Friborg’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. The organisers invited several artists to take part, each of whom was allowed to invite another artist of his own choosing. The artists were meant to make free use of the space allocated to them. Their works, which they created on the spot from early August 1981 onwards, were to have been removed when the exhibition ended on 18 October 1981.

The investigating judge went to the exhibition on 4 September and had the disputed pictures removed and seized. On 24 February 1982, the court sentenced each of them to a fine of 300 Swiss francs for publishing obscene material.

President Ryssdal, who had assumed the office of President of the Chamber, consulted - through the Deputy Registrar - the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicants on the need for a written procedure. The Court decided to inspect the impugned paintings by Josef Felix Müller, as the Government had suggested, on 30 November 1987. They were duly shown, in camera, in the presence of those appearing before the Court, on 25 January 1988, before the hearing began. The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The first applicant, Josef Felix Müller, a painter born in 1955, lives in St. Gall. The other nine applicants are: Charles Descloux, art critic, born in 1939 and living in Fribourg. The artists were meant to make free use of the space allocated to them. Their works, which they created on the spot from early August 1981 onwards, were to have been removed when the exhibition ended on 18 October 1981. The exhibition, entitled “Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of Friburg’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. Josef Felix Müller produced three large paintings entitled “Drei Nächte, drei Bilder’ (“Three Nights, Three Pictures’) They were on show when the exhibition began on 21 August 1981. The prosecutor of the Canton of Fribourg reported to the investigating judge that the paintings appeared to come within the provisions of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The investigating judge went to the exhibition on 4 September and had the disputed pictures removed and seized. On 24 February 1982, the court sentenced each of them to a fine of 300 Swiss francs (SF) for publishing obscene material but acquitted them on the charge of infringing freedom of religious belief and worship. The court said the law did not define obscenity for the purposes of Article 204 CC [Criminal Code] The overall impression is of persons giving free rein to licentiousness and even perversion. The subjects - sodomy, fellatio, bestiality, the erect penis - are obviously morally offensive to the vast majority of the population. Although allowance has to be made for changes in the moral climate, even for the worse, what we have here would revolutionise it. The artistic merit of the three works exhibited in Fribourg is admittedly less obvious than is supposed by the witness Ammann’s testimony. The Art and History Museum of the Canton of Fribourg meets the requirements for preventing any further breach of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The three confiscated paintings will be deposited there. Müller is undoubtedly an artist of some accomplishment, particularly in the matter of composition and in the use of colour. The court would not disagree. that the paintings Müller exhibited in Basle were more ‘demanding’.“All the applicants appealed on points of law on 24 February 1982; in particular, they challenged the trial court’s interpretation as regards the obscenity of the relevant paintings.” Josef Felix Müller’s paintings aroused “repugnance and disgust’ “These are not works which, in treating a particular subject or scene, allude to sexual activity more or less discreetly“ “They place it in the foreground, depicting it not in the embrace of man and woman but in vulgar images of sodomy, fellatio between males, bestiality, erect penises and masturbation’. “The court is likewise unconvinced by the appellants’ contention that the paintings are symbolical. What counts is their face value, their effect on the observer, not some abstraction utterly unconnected with the visible image’ Several of the defendants admitted that the paintings had shocked them. As the trial court pointed out, the defendants at the very least acted recklessly. Similar pictures by Josef Felix Müller, moreover, had been exhibited in Basle in February 1982 and it had not occurred to anyone to regard them as being obscene. In their submission, the Fribourg Cantonal Court had wrongly interpreted Article 204 of the Criminal Code. It had taken no account of the scope of the freedom of artistic expression, guaranteed inter alia in Article 10 (art. 10) of the Convention. It should be possible to show pictures which, if they were displayed in the market-place, would fall foul of Article 204. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal on 26 January 1983 for the following reasons: “The paintings in issue show an orgy of unnatural sexual practices (sodomy, bestiality, petting), which is crudely depicted in large format; they are liable grossly to offend the sense of sexual propriety of persons of ordinary sensitivity. The content and scope of constitutional freedoms are determined on the basis of the federal law currently in force. eval_texts: The case originated in three applications lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The Court delivered its judgments on 27 February 2001 in Mr Adoud's and Mr Bosoni's case and on 26 April 2001 in the case of Mr Meftah. The court held unanimously that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of Article 25 of the Human Rights Convention, and that the French Republic had violated the rights of the three French nationals in the application. The Federal Constitutional Court ordered that all provisions declared incompatible with the Basic Law remained applicable until the entry into force of new legislation. In relation to detainees whose preventive detention had been prolonged or ordered retrospectively, the courts had to examine without delay whether the persons concerned were highly likely to commit the most serious crimes of violence or sexual offences. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. Upon the request of the applicants to secure the entire video material of the police operation, it was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. On 19 September 2011 the Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2 § 2, 19 § 4 and 103 § 1 of the German Basic Law (Gürgeserzwingungsverfahren) The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. The applications also filed criminal complaints in respect of assistance given in an official capacity in avoiding prosecution or punishment.

John Hemsworth died from a cerebral infarction on 1 January 1998. The RUC began an investigation supervised by the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (“ICPC”) On 2 February 2000 the Attorney General ordered the Coroner to hold an inquest. The applicants claimed that the original pathologist later expressed his agreement with these later two expert opinions. The Coroner opened a pre-inquest hearing, in 16 cases including into John Hemsworth’s death, to hear submissions on the implications of the judgments of this Court of 4 May 2001 in certain cases concerning deaths in Northern Ireland (Hugh Jordan v the United Kingdom, no. 24746/94, (extracts) The first applicant applied for legal aid for the inquest under the Lord Chancellor’s Extra-Statutory Scheme. On 5 June 2001 she began a judicial review action. On 7 January 2003 the High Court found against her as did the Court of Appeal (9 March 2005) The first applicant was legally represented, as she was for all domestic proceedings. The hearing was adjourned given the possibility of the referral of those cases to the Grand Chamber of this Court. The applicants claimed that, during that hearing, the Coroner advised that there was no evidence that the deceased had been struck by RUC officers. The first applicants applied for the Cor coroner to recuse himself. The inquest into the death of a soldier in Northern Ireland began on 21 September 2009. The Coroner had decided to take a statement from a possible eye-witness to the assault. On receipt of the statement, it emerged that Officer M, of the Police Service Northern Ireland, had taken the statement on the Coroner’s behalf. Officer M had been a member of the RUC at the time of the alleged assault. He was also the Deputy Investigation Officer and, in addition, he was due to be called as a witness. It emerged therefrom that Officer. M had interviewed a soldier (Private G) in 2000. Private G had told Officer M that, on the day of the assault, he had seen Officer M talking to Private G. The Coroner was advised by the Crown Solicitor’s Office that all documentation in relation to Private G was destroyed in August 2009. Private G had seen an officer in the RUC Blues OSU assaulting a civilian with a baton in an area close to the location of Mr Hemsworth's alleged assault. Given the time it would take to recall witnesses and to call Private G, the Coroner considered it preferable to discharge the jury and conduct the inquest afresh. The Coroner ordered the PSNI to prepare a paginated and indexed bundle of all material held by them. Officers unconnected with the original investigation should conduct this disclosure exercise. John Hemsworth died on 7 July 1997. The inquest jury found the medical causes of death to be cerebral infarction and thrombosis of the right internal carotid artery. The Coroner announced that he would refer the matter to the Director of Public Prosecutions (“DPP”) and ensured the production, from public funds, of a transcript of the inquest proceedings. On 3 February 2012 the DPP’s office acknowledged the referral. Further to the applicants’ queries, on 23 April 2012 the Coroner confirmed the referral and on 14 May 2012 the case was adjourned until the end of May 2012. The Government submitted that the matter was the subject of ‘active consideration’ by the DPP. The Police Ombudsman reviewed the police file but found no evidence that any RUC officer was responsible for John Hemsworth’s death. The applicant initiated civil proceedings against the PSNI and on 10 August 2011 a Notice of Intention to Proceed was served. The DPP acknowledged the referral on 3 July 2012 and the matter is currently under consideration by the Government. The application is now being considered by the Court of Appeal for a possible hearing in March 2015. The case is currently being heard at the Belfast Crown Court and is expected to be heard in May 2015.

Gibraltar is a dependent territory of the United Kingdom. It forms part of Her Majesty the Queen’s Dominions. The United Kingdom parliament has the ultimate authority to legislate for Gibraltar, but in practice exercises it rarely. The House of Assembly is the domestic legislature in Gibraltar. It has the right to make laws for Gibraltar on “defined domestic matters”, subject to, inter alia, a power in the Governor to refuse to assent to legislation. Gibraltar is excluded from certain parts of the EC Treaty by virtue of the Treaty of Accession. The provisions on free movement of goods do not apply; it is treated as a third country.

The European Union's "Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union" (ECO) is intended to be a framework for future cooperation between the EU and the rest of the world. The ECO provides for the creation of an EU Commission that can make decisions on matters relating to the EU. The European Court of Justice (ECoP) has the power to make changes to the ECO's rules, but not to impose them. The EU can also make its own rules on matters of national importance, such as the right of citizens of a member state to have a say in the EU’s foreign policy, or the right to sue the EU for any breach of the treaty.

The ECHR is responsible for the regulation of the EU's membership of the ECHR, the European Parliament and the Council of Europe. The ECHR has the power to amend the European Convention on Human Rights, which includes the right to a fair trial, a right to compensation, and the right of a person to be compensated for the loss of his or her property. It also has the ability to make changes to the laws of the EC, as well as to the rules and regulations of the Union.

The European Union’s Treaty of Functioning is made up of five articles. The first article gives the European Parliament the power to act as a “legislator” The second article is the “supremation of the Parliament’. The third article is “the right of the European Union to legislate”. The fourth and final Article is the right for the EU to make a law “on behalf of all its members”, but only if the law is in line with the fourth and fifth article. The fifth and final clause is the power for the European parliament to “make a law on behalf of” its members. The seventh and final article is that of the Council of Europe.

The lawyers were given leave by the President of the Grand Chamber, Mrs Palm, to use the German language (Rule 34 § 34). In 1992 a controversy arose between His Serene Highness Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein (“the Prince’s”) and the government on political competences. The matter was settled on the basis of a common declaration by the Prince, the Diet (Landtag) and government. The applicant had not stood for re-election in May 1993, and he was appointed President of the Liech tenstein Administrative Court (Verwaltungsbeschwerdeinstanz) in December 1993 for a fixed term of office (see paragraph 26 below) In February 1995, in the context of a series of lectures on questions of constitutional jurisdiction and fundamental rights, the applicant gave a public lecture. On 27 February 1995 the Prince addressed a letter to the applicant concerning the above lecture, as summarised in the article published in the Liechtensteiner Volksblatt. The applicant expressed the view that the Constitutional Court was competent to decide on the “interpretation of the Constitution in case of disagreement between the Prince (government) and the Diet”. The letter, written on heraldic letter paper, read as follows: “Vaduz, I was astonished to read the report in the 17 February issue of the. ‘Nature and Functions of the Lie chtenstein Constitutional Court’. I assume that the statements you made on the Court's areas of responsibility have been correctly reproduced in this report’ Prince Hans-Adam II of Liechtenstein wrote to Herbert Wille saying he had lost his confidence in the government. Wille was appointed President of the Administrative Court on the Diet’s recommendation. He said the court has no competence to decide as a court of interpretation in the event of a disagreement between the Prince and the people (the Diet) In my eyes your attitude, Dr Wille, makes you unsuitable for public office. I do not intend to get involved in a long public or private debate with you, but I should like to inform you in good time that I shall not appoint you again to a public office should you be proposed by the Diet or any other body. Sie werden sich bestimmt noch an die Auseinandersetzung zwischen der Regierung and mir vor dem 28. Oktober 1992 erinnern. Sie haben dazumal sinngemäss geantwortet, dass Sie mit diesen Teilen der Verfassung sowieso nicht einverstanden seien. "Ich habe diese unentschuldbare Haltung gegenüber unserer Verfassung eingesehen", sagt Dr. Wille. "Ich hoffe, dass sie mein Vertrauen verloren hat. Ich habe nicht die Absicht, mich mit Ihnen öffentlich üffentliches Amt. Leider muss ich aufgrund des Berichtes im Liechtensteiner Volksblatt nun feststellen, das Sie sich nach wie vor nicht an die Verfasung gebunden fühlen" "Ihre Auffassungen vertreten, die eindeutig geggen Sinn und Wortlaut der VerfAssung verstossen,    erzielt wurde", says Dr.Wille. Hans-Adam II. Fürst von Liechtenstein’s office as President of the Administrative Court was called into question. The applicant concluded that the declaration made by the Prince that he did not intend to appoint the applicant to a public office, amounted to an interference with his rights to freedom of opinion and to thought. He denied having ever made a statement to the effect that he. did not consider himself bound by the Constitution or parts thereof. He further explained his research on the competences of the Constitutional Court in constitutional matters. According to him, the expression of an opinion not shared by the. Prince could not be regarded as a failure to comply with the Constitution. The Prince had known Mr Wille for many years and considered it appropriate to state the reasons for his decision regarding him. The decision no longer to appoint him to the office of President of one of the highest courts, on account of his attitude in the past as well as the opinions expressed by him, did not amount to an interference with his rights to freedom of expression and to thought. All citizens were free to propose and to plead for amendments to constitutional or other legal provisions. However, MrWille, during his term of office as a member of the government and in his lecture, had not availed himself of such constitutional and democratic means, but had simply ignored those parts of the Constitution with which he disagreed. Confusing the terms “Government” and “Diet” with “Prince” or “people” would undermine the rule of law. In a democratic State based on the rule of law, a distinction had to be drawn between freedom of expression and the means used by an individual for imposing his views in such a society. The Prince considered that Mr Wille, having regard to his education and professional experience, knew that the terms ‘people’ (“Volk”), “Diet” (‘Landtag’) and “Prince” were clearly defined in the Constitution. The applicant’s contention that these terms were interchangeable would jeopardise the Constitution and the constitutional State as a whole, the Prince said. The applicant is currently employed as a researcher by the Liechtenstein-Institut. The Prince refused to accept the proposed appointment of Mr Wille as President of the Administrative Court. Roma marriage is not covered by Spanish legislation, in spite of that ethnic minority’s social and cultural roots in our country. The lack of regulation of the recognition of the civil effects of Roma marriage cannot hinder the protective action to which the State has committed itself by laying down social security norms. ... Directive 2000/43/EC implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin is applicable to the present case.

Roma marriage not registered in the Civil Register, as it is not a feature of the ethnic culture which has existed in our country for centuries. Spanish court rejects claims of discrimination against Roma couple. Court: ‘discrimination by absence of differentiation’ did not arise from Article 14. ‘No discriminatory treatment, whether direct or indirect, for racial or ethnic reasons, arises from the fact that the applicant’s partnership, in accordance with the rites and customs of the Roma community, has not been assimilated with marriage for the purposes of the said pension,’ the court said. Court said ‘there is no form of covert discrimination here against the Roma ethnic group. ... A supposed discrimination on social grounds must be rejected for the reasons given above.’

Spanish court rules there is no discrimination on social grounds. No discrimination on racial or ethnic grounds, as alleged in the case, says the court. No form of covert discrimination here against the Roma ethnic group, the court adds. The court also rules that the law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form. ‘The court must reject the idea that the recognition of the civil effects of a marital relationship created by certain specific religious rites, but not one that has been solemnised according to Roma rites and customs, may entail directly or indirectly, the alleged ethnic discrimination.”

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, a Rom of Spanish nationality, complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of her husband. She alleged that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the. Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 12 of. the Convention. The Court heard addresses by Mr Blasco Lozano, Ms Queipo de Llano López-Cózar and Mr S. Sánchez Lorente. The couple were married according to their community’s own rites. The marriage was solemnised in accordance with Roma customs and cultural traditions. On 14 October 1986 the applicant and her family were granted first-category large-family status. The couple had six children, who were registered in the family record book issued to the couple by the Spanish civil registration authorities (Registro civil) on 11 August 1983. On 24 December 2000 the applicant's husband died. He was a builder and at the time of his death had been working and paying social security contributions for nineteen years, three months and eight days, supporting his wife (registered as such) and his six children as his dependants. He had been issued with a social security benefit card, stamped by Agency no. 7 of Madrid.  applicant filed a claim with the Labour Court. In a judgment dated 30 May 2002 of Labour Court no. 12 of Madrid, she was granted an entitlement to receive a survivor’s pension with a base rate of 903.29 euros per month, her Roma marriage thus being recognised as having civil effects. Roma marriages are not registered in the Civil Register because they have not been regarded by the State as a feature of the ethnic culture which has existed in our country for centuries. ... Directive 2000/43/EC implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin is applicable to the present case, where the denied benefit derives from the employment relationship of the insured person who died from natural causes while he was still working. The INSS appealed. In a judgment of 7 November 2002, the Madrid Higher Court of Justice quashed the impugned judgment. “... A distinction must be made between the legislation that is in force and is applicable at all times and what may be considered desirable by a given sector of society. ... A marriage solemnised solely and exclusively according to Roma rites is not covered by any of the above-mentioned cases, as even though an ethnic group is concerned, the norms or formalities of that group do not produce any legal effect outside its own environment and are not enshrined in the law’s law.” Roma marriage does not correspond, in the current framework of our law, to the nature of the marriages referred to above. Section 174 of the LGSS requires that a person be the spouse of the deceased in order to benefit from the survivor’s pension, and the notion of spouse has been interpreted strictly according to an established constitutional and ordinary case-law. A couple living together de facto as husband and wife and many others who, in reality, are not married under the applicable law, are excluded from the benefit of that pension. ... A marriage can only be one that is solemnised civilly or religiously according to the terms set out above. ... The morality of the rite or its conformity with public order are not called into question. The court ruled that 'discrimination by absence of differentiation' did not arise from Article 14 of the Spanish Constitution. The court also rejected the idea that the recognition of the civil effects of a marital relationship created by certain specific religious rites, but not one that has been solemnised according to Roma rites and customs, may entail directly or indirectly, the alleged ethnic discrimination. The law establishes a general possibility – neutral from a racial and ethnic point of view – of marrying in the civil form, and that the legislature, the court said. in the case of the surviving spouse, did not prohibit such an extension of the survivor’s pension to other forms of partnership. Dissenting opinion appended to judgment no. 199/2004 found a violation of the right to equality. It referred to a case concerning the widower of a civil servant. The parties had expressly refused such registration of their marital relationship which had been solemnised in a religious form. The case-law of the Constitutional Court did not take into account the rites, practices or customs of a specific ethnic group, the dissenting judge said. The guarantee of equality required measures of positive discrimination in favour of the underprivileged minority, he added. The dissenting judge concluded as follows: “It is disproportionate for the Spanish State, which took into consideration the applicant and her Roma family by issuing them with a family record book, granting them large-family status, affording health-care assistance to her and her six children and collecting the corresponding contributions from her Roma husband for nineteen years, three months and eight days, now to refuse to recognise them’ On 3 December 2008, under the third amendment of Law no. 40/2007 of 4 December 2007 pertaining to certain social security measures, the applicant was granted a survivor’s pension with effect from 1 January 2007, as the partner of M.D. the Roma marriage. The relevant provisions of the Spanish Constitution are as follows: Article 14 “Spaniards shall be equal before the law; they may not be discriminated against in any way on account of birth, race, sex, religion, opinion or any other condition or personal or social circumstance” Article 16 “1. Freedom of ideas, religion and worship shall be guaranteed to individuals and communities without any restrictions on its expression.” The Spanish Civil Code provides for the right to marry in Spain and abroad. A surviving spouse is entitled to a survivor’s pension in the event of nullity of a marriage. This entitlement is in proportion to the period of his or her cohabitation with the insured person, provided he or she has not acted in bad faith and has not remarried. The law also allows the head of the household, his spouse and four or more children to be classified as a large family. For more information on the law, go to: www.cnn.com/2013/07/26/politics/spanish-marriage-law/index.html. Marriages solemnised according to the rites of those religious denominations are therefore recognised by the Government. Married couples can claim a survivor's pension if they live together as unmarried partners for at least six years prior to the death. The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities, opened for signature on 1 February 1995, contains the following provisions in particular. Article 1 “The protection of national minorities and of the rights and freedoms of persons belonging to those minorities forms an integral part of the international protection of human rights, and as such falls within the scope of international cooperation” Article 5 “1. The Parties undertake to promote the conditions necessary to maintain and develop their culture, and to preserve the essential elements of their identity, namely their religion, language, traditions and cultural heritage.” The measures adopted in accordance with paragraph 2 shall not be considered to be an act of discrimination. Spain signed the Convention on the day that it was opened for signature and ratified it on 1 September 1995. It came into force in respect of Spain on 1 February 1998. The Convention states that the Spanish government shall refrain from policies or practices aimed at assimilation of persons belonging to national minorities against their will and shall protect these persons from any action aimed at such assimilation. It also says that it will protect the rights of Spanish citizens who are not citizens of the Spanish Republic but of a different nation. Spain is one of seven countries to sign and ratify the Convention. The other seven are: Australia, Britain, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Norway and Portugal.

He found that the applicant's son, “who had allegedly given her the injection, had left the département to return to his dental practice abroad, in Gabon”, that “he had given his mother an injection of a substance which was medically harmless at that dosage...”. The decision was apparently served on the applicant on the same day by registered post. On 7 April 1997 the applicant went to the investigating judge's registry and, claiming that she had not received a copy of the decision, refused to sign the notice of appeal drafted by the registrar. The Indictment Division of the Court of Appeal of Saint-Denis-de-la-Réunion found that the applicant had appealed “by letter addressed to and received by the investigatingJudge's registry”, and she had gone to the registry on the same day and refused tosign the notice. She alleged that there had been a breach of Articles 592, 575-6, 593 and 646 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In a judgment of 21 April 1998, the Criminal Division ofthe Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal. The case was dismissed on the grounds that it was served out of time. The Court of Appeal ruled that the appeal of 7 April 1997 against the decision that there was no case to answer served on 14 March 1997 was ‘out of time in accordance with the conditions laid down in Article 183 of the Code of Criminal Procedure; ...’ The case was heard in the High Court in London. The verdict was returned on 8 April 1997. The case is still pending appeal in the Supreme Court of England and Wales. It was dismissed by the Appeal Court on 6 April 1998. The applicant was sentenced to three years in prison and a fine of £250,000. He is currently awaiting sentencing and his trial is expected to begin in January 2015. The Mönchengladbach District Court then issued a fresh detention order against the applicant. Borrego BorreGO, Head of the Legal Service for the European Commission and Court of Human Rights, Ministry of Justice, Agent; (b), for the Commission M. F. Martínez, Delegate. The agreement was defective because one of the parties had no capacity to conclude such an agreement. The judge added that there was nothing to prevent an agreement being concluded with the person who had the necessary capacity. The decision was at last served on the applicant in the person of her domestic help, since she herself was out at the time. The application against the decision of 7 September 1993 at Lumbier was dismissed on the ground that the neighbour, who was merely a life tenant, could not carry out the works needed to block the view without the consent of the reversioner. The applicant appealed the decision, saying that the defendant had not brought any action to have the agreement set aside. On 30 November 1993 the applicant lodged a reposición application and, in the alternative, an ordinary appeal against the decision of 7 September 1993 with the registry of the duty court in Madrid. Noticing, however, that the application should have been lodged at the Aoiz Court of First Instance, the head of the registry crossed out the stamp, thereby invalidating it. On the same day, the applicant sent, by registered letter with advice of delivery, the same repos clawón application to the court. The court dismissed the application and upheld the impugned decision, on the ground that it had not been lodged within the prescribed period of three days. The applicant filed an appeal with the Navarre Audiencia Provincial, which dismissed it in a decision of 23 December 1994. On 20 January 1995 the applicant lodged an amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court, relying on the right to protection by the courts. The application was declared inadmissible on the following grounds:. the reposición application had been determined and not at the same time as that application, and. that it was accordingly pointless to consider whether it had been lodged timeously;. the applicant was not represented by a lawyer; and. the application was filed at a post office rather than the registry of the court or with the duty judge. The rules on the postal service, as enacted in Decree no. 1653/1964 of 14 May 1964, provide: Article 205 “Acceptance of applications and documents sent to administrative institutions …” The documents and applications in question shall be submitted in an open envelope. The official who accepts the item for despatch shall stamp it with the date in the upper left-hand corner of the main document, so that the name of the post office and the date of submission are clearly visible. Mrs Pérez de Rada Cavanilles applied to the Commission on 20 June 1995. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of N. As a consequence, it had provided her with psychological assistance before and during the hearing to allow for her full examination, but to no avail. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. It had made use of all the psychological support that the presence of officials from the victims’ service could provide. The efforts were fruitless, however, and the witness’s resolved will to collaborate was prevented by one of the most horrific cases of psychological annihilation of a victim that this court has ever witnessed in its long professional experience. Only continuous breaks and recesses and an excessive effort on her part enabled her to make, in more that an hour, some progress in her statement, which came to a dramatic end as she was telling the court about the episode of a cold-water bath with which she had been tortured. N. had been tied, immersed in icy water, thrown on a bed and raped vaginally and anally. The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to N., to fifteen months’ imprisonment; (ii) breaking and entering into N’s home using violence and coercion, to two and a half years’ prison. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages. The court found that, when the applicant had been arrested at Prat de Llobregat Airport (Barcelona), he had been carrying false identification documents. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 40016/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted ILGA-Europe (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association), Liberty and Stonewall leave to intervene as third parties.

eval_texts: The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding him guilty of serious insult against the King of Spain amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to freedom of expression. The Court examined the information available to it, and decided that no hearing was necessary. The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) The applicant was represented by Mr D. Rouget and Ms J. Goirizelaia Ordorika, lawyers practising in Saint-Jean-de-Luz and Bilbao respectively. The Spanish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Blasco. The Basque Country High Court of Justice has decided to try the applicant. The prosecutor lodged a criminal complaint against the applicant for “serious insult against the King’. The applicant argued that his remarks had constituted political criticism directed against the Head of the government of the Basques Country. He said that to say that the King of Spain was the Supreme Head. of the Civil Guard did not imply any intention to undermine dignity or honour; it was merely. merely a matter of opinion. The criminal proceedings in the Basque. Country High court of Justice began on 6 April 2003. The trial is expected to last a few weeks. The judge will decide whether or not the applicant should be tried. The High Court of Justice found the applicant not guilty of the charges against him. The court found that his remarks had been ‘clearly offensive, improper, unjust, ignominious and divorced from reality’ The application had sought to express political criticism in the context of freedom of expression, one of the foundations of the rule of law and democracy. This is not an issue concerning the private life of the Head of State but one of rejection of the ties of political power deriving from the hereditary nature of the institution which he personally symbolises. The Constitution does not guarantee the right of expression solely in relation to certain points of view that are considered correct. Public prosecutor lodged an appeal on points of law to the Supreme Court. He argued that the law protected the honour of the King as a specific individual possessed of personal dignity. In the view of the public prosecutor, it was clear that the King had been performing official duties. That did not deprive him of the right to respect for his honour, he said. The Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the lower court, making several references to the Court's case-law. It sentenced the applicant to one year’s imprisonment, suspended his right to stand for election for the duration of the sentence and ordered him to pay a fine. The judge agreed with the Basque Country High Court of Justice that the remarks had not targeted the King’s private life or his personal honour. The judge pointed out that the limits of freedom of expression were wider with regard to institutions since the latter did not possess honour. In view of the seriousness of the insulting comments and the fact that the applicant had deliberately expressed them in public, the Supreme Court sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. The amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court was dismissed. The applicant lodged an appeal alleging, inter alia, a breach of his right of expression (Article 20 § 1 (a) The Supreme Court’s judgment had incorrectly weighed the competing interests at stake. The statements in question had not been disproportionate in the context in which they had been uttered. The Constitutional Court noted at the outset that the right to freedom of expression did not encompass a right to proffer insults. It pointed out in that connection that the Constitution did not prohibit the use of hurtful expressions in all circumstances. However, freedom ofexpression did not protect vexatious expressions which, regardless of their veracity, were offensive and ignominious and were not pertinent for the purpose of conveying the opinions or information in question. The Supreme Court considered that the weighing of the competing rights at stake had been carried out in an appropriate manner by the Supreme Court. The King occupied a neutral position in political debate. This implied that he was owed institutional respect of a kind that was ‘substantively’ different from that due to other State institutions. The Constitutional Court held that the applicant’s remarks, on account of their obviously derogatory nature, had clearly gone beyond what could be considered legitimate. The applicant was imprisoned on 8 June 2007 after the Supreme Court upheld a judgment of the Audiencia Nacional of 27 April 2006 sentencing him to fifteen months’ imprisonment. According to the Government, his sentence was remitted on 16 July 2009. He is currently in pre-trial detention in connection with other criminal proceedings.

Mr. Pakelli could have remained in the Federal Republic of Germany and attended the hearing, if need be with the assistance of an interpreter. The official appointment of a lawyer by the trial court covers not only the proceedings before that court but also the written stage of any appeal on a point of law. The trial court will also make a special appointment for the latter stage, if necessary. An appointment will also be made in other cases, either by the court of its own motion or at the accused’s request. An accused who is at liberty may appear in person or be represented by a lawyer at the appeal hearing (Article 350 para. 2). According to the case-law of the Federal Court, defence counsel can be assigned to him only under Article 140 para.2. The Federal Constitutional Court has held that defence counsel is to be appointed by the court of its own motion and at the expense of the State in serious cases. The court concerned may dispose of an appeal on a point of law without hearings in the following cases only: Where it finds the appeal inadmissible (Article 349 para. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure);. Where, on a reasoned application by the public prosecutor’s office, the court considers unanimously that the appeal is manifestly ill-founded;. and. Where the court finds unanimously that an appeal filed in the interests of the accused is well-founded. Appeal hearings open with the rapporteur’s address. The appellant is heard first and the last address to the court is always made by the accused. Article 350 para. 1 requires that the accused and his lawyer be informed of the date and place of the hearing. “Common defence counsel’ (gemeinschaftliche Verteidigung) does not allow several accused to be defended by a common defence counsel. The 1st Criminal Chamber followed these precedents in its judgment of 29 November 1977 in the present case (see paragraph 17 above). The Government stated that this interpretation has since been accepted by all the Criminal Chambers of the Federal Court. On 16 May 1980, the Commission granted Mr. Pakelli free legal aid on the basis of a declaration of means dated 9 September 1979 and confirmed by certificates from the competent authorities. The Commission declared the application admissible in so far as it related to the rejection of the applicant’s request that a lawyer be officially appointed for the hearing before the Federal Court. In its report of 12 December 1981 (Article 31), the Commission expressed the unanimous opinion that the applicant had been the victim of a violation of Article 6 para. 3 (c) (art. 6-3-c) and, by eleven votes to one, that it was not required to determine whether there had also been breach of the right to a fair trial.

The German Federal Foreign Office referred the applicants to the ESA Appeals Board. The Federal Labour Court dismissed the applicants’ appeal on points of law (file no. 7 AZR 600/92) in 1993. According to section 20(2) of the Courts Act, German jurisdiction did not extend to international organisations which were exempted in accordance with international agreements. The court considered that immunity from jurisdiction was an impediment to court proceedings, and that an action against a defendant who had not waived this immunity, was inadmissible. Employees of ESA could either lodge an appeal with the Appeals Board of the organisation, or the labour contract had to provide for arbitration. The Federal Labour Court considered that a rather broad competence of international organisations to regulate staff matters was not unusual. The regulations on the immunity of ESA did not conflict with fundamental principles of German constitutional law. The question of whether the applicants could claim under German public law that positive action be taken by the German government to use their influence to achieve a waiver of immunity in the present case, could not be solved in labour court proceedings. The applicants’ appeal did not raise a matter of general importance. The alleged absence of rights resulted from the particular contracts entered into by the applicants. The ESA Convention came into force on 30 October 1980, when ten States, members of ESRO or ELDO, had signed it and had deposited their instruments of ratification or acceptance. The purpose of ESA is to provide for and to promote, for exclusively peaceful purposes, cooperation among European States in space research and technology and their space applications. The Agency shall maintain the internal capability required for the preparation and supervision of its programmes. The ESA Convention provides for the creation of a European Space Agency (ESA) and for the development of European space programmes (ESA Convention). The Agency will have the power to award and award grants for space exploration. Annex I relates to the privileges and immunities of the Agency. Article XIX provides that on the date of entry into force of the ESA Convention the Agency shall take over all the rights and obligations of ESRO. Article XVII concerns the arbitration procedure in case of disputes between two or more member States, or between any of them and ESA. Article XXV of Annex I provides for arbitration with regard to written contracts other than those concluded in accordance with the Staff Regulations. A member State may submit to the International Arbitration Tribunal any dispute, inter alia, arising out of damage caused by the Agency, or involving any other non-contractual responsibility of ESA. Disputes between the Organisation and such staff members of the Organisation. the Agency and the Director General, staff members or experts in respect of their conditions of service. The Agreement concerning ESOC was concluded between the government of the Federal Republic of Germany and ESRO for the purpose of establishing a European Space Operations Centre, including the European Space Data Centre. Articles 1 to 4 of the Agreement concern the site for construction of the ESOC buildings and related matters. Article 6 provides that if the terms of employment of a staff member are not governed by the Organisation’s staff regulations, then they shall be subject to German laws and regulations. Two men applied to the Commission on 24 November 1994. They claimed they had been denied access to a court for a determination of their dispute with ESA in connection with an issue under German labour law. The Commission declared the application (no. 26083/94) admissible on 24 February 1997. In its report of 2 December 1997 the Commission expressed the opinion that there had been no violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the two separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 March 1994 and by the German Government on 29 March 1994. It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1995. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995, namely Mr F. Gölcüklü, Mr R. Macdonald, Mr A. Spielmann, Mr J. De Meyer, Mr I. Foighel, Mr M.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. Mrs Dorothea Vogt was a German national born in 1949. She was a member of the German Communist Party (Deutsche Kommunistische Partei - “DKP’) She taught German and French in a State secondary school in Jever, Lower Saxony. In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory. The Court heard addresses by Mr Trechsel, Mr Becker, Mr Jäckel, Mr Damman and Mr Meyer-Ladewig, and replies to a question put by it. Disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Vogt will be heard at a later date. The applicant had been a member of the Bremen/North Lower Saxony regional branch (Bezirksorganisation) of the DKP since the end of 1983. She had stood in the 1982 elections to the Landtag of the Land of LowerSaxony as a DKP candidate. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had taken part in and addressed the 7th party congress in Nuremberg in January 1984. The proceedings were stayed on 15 July 1985 in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary. The applicant argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. By being a member of the party and carrying out activities on its behalf she had availed herself of the right of all citizens to engage in political activity. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations and her combat against neo-fascism were in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The DKP, whose aims had always been wrongly alleged (but never proven) to be anti- constitutional, was found guilty of a breach of duty. Disciplinary proceedings against Mrs Vogt breached International Labour Organisation (ILO) Convention No. 111 concerning discrimination in respect of employment and occupation. It also violated Article 10 (art. 10) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Disciplinary Division found that the applicant had failed to comply with her duty of political loyalty and ordered her dismissal as a disciplinary measure. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The rule did not apply to measures, such as disciplinary proceedings, which initially had a different purpose and restricted the freedom to stand for election to, and to sit as a member of, parliament only as an indirect and unavoidable consequence of their implementation. The Disciplinary Division finally ordered that Mrs Vogt should be paid 75 per cent of her pension allowance for a period of six months. It did so in recognition of the fact that apart from her breach of the duty of loyalty Mrs Vog t had always performed her duties unexceptionably and enthusiastically and needed some income. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant. Mrs Vogt's conduct had been unlawful. By holding such a senior political post within the DKP, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution herself. The same approach applied in cases where a person had already been appointed to a permanent civil service post. It was not possible to support both systems at the same time. Even though Mrs Vogts sought above all to support the constitutional system, she was not allowed to do so. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. It appears doubtful whether the view of the Constitution espoused by the official and described above reflects accurately the principles enshrined in the Basic law. It is not necessary to resolve that question here. In its judgment banning the former Communist Party (KPD) (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held that the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD were incompatible with the free democratic constitutional system. The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. The attitude of civil servants who, even if they campaigned within DKP for the renunciation of aims that were contrary to the Constitution, showed outside the party, through the political offices they held, that they unreservedly supported its programme and policy, was incompatible with such a duty. Mrs Vogt had knowingly breached her professional obligations, the Disciplinary Court found. Her dismissal had therefore been justified. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (Verfassungsbeschwerde) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. The disciplinary tribunals had been entitled to find that the DKP's aims were anti-constitutional, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 21 para. 2 of the Basic Law. The basis of trust necessary for Mrs Vogt to continue to work as a civil servant was lacking, despite the fact that she had declared herself to be in favour of a change in the party's policy. The applicant's dismissal had not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. From 1 February 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 75204/01) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Mr Theodor Klasen, was born in 1933 and lived in Mülheim. He worked between 1964 and the beginning of 1974 with asbestos insulators for the T Company. During this period, the workers of this company who were exposed to asbestos dust while working had to clean their clothes themselves. This was done by the applicant's first wife Mrs Gisela Klasan. On 6 March 1991 she applied to the Düsseldorf Health Insurance Association for compensation payments, claiming that her illness was the consequence of her husband's work clothes. Mrs Gisela Klasen filed an objection against this decision which was rejected on 13 December 1991 by the Appeals Board of the Health Insurance Association. The court found that she had not been an employee herself, nor had she acted like an employee. She had cleaned her husband's clothes on ground of their living together, but not with a view to acting for her husband’s employer. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that the social courts' interpretation of Section 539 of the Social Security Act was discriminatory. The Federal Constitutional Court invited the Federal Parliament, the Federal Council (Bundesrat) and the Federal Government to submit their written observations on the constitutional complaint. Court refused to admit the complaint because it lacked reasonable prospects of success. The court held that the contested interpretation of Section 539 of the Social Security Act did not violate the applicant's constitutional rights. It also argued that it was incumbent on the legislator to determine to which extent the industrial health insurance should cover third persons. It further pointed out that a constitutional complaint could not be based on an alleged violation of the European Convention on Human Rights. This decision was notified to the applicant’s lawyer on 28 March 2001. It was announced to the public on 6 April 2001 and made public on 8 April 2001. The case was heard at the High Court in Wellington, New Zealand.

The case involved the arrest of a German man in Zürich. He was found guilty of breaching the European Convention on Human Rights. The court ruled that the decision to arrest was taken by an official who satisfied the requirements of the Convention. The decision was made by an officer who exercised judicial power, the court said. The case was dismissed on the grounds that the officer who made the decision was the same as the one who drew up the indictment. The ruling was upheld on appeal by the Federal Court of Cassation, which said that the arrest was not unlawful on the basis of the officer's status at the time of the arrest.

A Swiss court ruled in 1988 that the District Attorney of the Canton of Zürich exercises judicial power. A public-law appeal lodged against the judgment cited in the preceding paragraph, the Federal Court held on 14 March 1989 that it is possible that the district attorney may act as a prosecuting authority. The decision was taken by an official who satisfied the requirements of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the European Convention on Human Rights in other words by an officer who exercised judicial power, the court ruled. The arrest, initially regarded as being lawful, cannot subsequently become unlawful on this sole ground, it added.

In a judgment of 13 June 1988 (Ante Djukic gegen Staatsanwaltschaft des Kantons Zürich), the Cantonal Court of Cassation stated that the District Attorney of the Canton of Züich exercises judicial power. This complaint is unfounded. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. This case was allocated to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court.

The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in Spånga. In 1935 the applicant’s mother and her four siblings jointly inherited two estates from their father. The ownership of the estates, consisting of several islands in the archipelago of Stockholm, was over the years partly transferred to other members of the family. Disagreements arose between the family members. Some of them wished to divide the property (klyvning) and thus dissolve the joint ownership. The applicant disputed this and argued, inter alia, that it was her mother who had built the house and that accordingly it belonged to her mother's estate.
