eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35179/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the demolition of a house had violated her rights to the peaceful enjoyment of her possessions and to respect for her home. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 22 May 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The applicant's mother owned a number of houses on Marum 1:8. Two of the houses were used by the applicant's two sisters. A third house situated on the property was considered too small for the applicant’s needs and it was therefore decided to enlarge it. The applicant applied for a building permit to the Österåker Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden). On 9 September 1987, finding that the enlargement could not be approved as the house in question was situated too close to the shore, the committee granted a permit for the building of a new house further away from the shore. The new house was built in 1988. In 1989 practically all the other joint owners of the two estates brought proceedings against the applicant in the District Court. The applicant appealed the removal of her new house. The Supreme Court rejected her request to have the proceedings stayed. The Enforcement Office (kronofogdemyndigheten – ‘the Office’) ordered the applicant to remove the house before 3 April 1996 or risk having it demolished by the Office at her own expense. The case was referred back by the Court of Appeal to the REFA for re-examination as the latter had made procedural errors. On 14 March 1996 the Central Office of the National Land Survey gave its opinion in the division proceedings. It considered that the removal judgment did not prevent the creation of an individual plot around the house in issue. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, requesting an immediate stay of the demolition order. She claimed that she had not been given the opportunity to remove the house herself in accordance with the District Court’s judgment of 10 May 1990. She also requested a three-week respite in order to substantiate her appeal. By a decision of 31 May 1996 the applicant was ordered to complete her appeal by 12 midnight on 5 June 1996. However, at a session held on 3 June 1996 the Court. of Appeal had already examined the case and, by a decision delivered the following day, refused. the applicant leave to appeal against the District. Court's decision of 15 May 1996. The house in issue was demolished by a construction firm. The applicant had claimed that her appeal against the District Court’s decision of 15 May 1996 prevented the enforcement of the removal judgment. This claim was rejected by the Enforcement Office on 31 May 1996, referring to Chapter 3, section 21, of the Enforcement Code (Utsökningsbalken) The demolition of the house began on 3 June 1996 and was concluded ten days later. On 22 November 1996 the Real Estate Court gave judgment in the division proceedings. It decided that Marum 1:8 should be divided into six individual plots and one common plot. In this respect, the real estate court agreed with the opinion given by the Central Office of the National Land Survey on 14 March 1996. On 14 April 2000 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Court of Appeal upheld the legal-aid decision. Stating that they were unable to plead their case properly without legal aid, the applicant and her sister withdrew most of their claims in the removal case. No further appeal was lodged and the appellate court’s judgment consequently acquired legal force. The Building Committee granted the applicant building permits for the reconstruction of the demolished house and the construction of two smaller outbuildings. The court came to a different conclusion in this respect from the one reached in the original removal judgment of 10 May 1990. Accordingly, at the time of the declaratory judgment, the house had not belonged to the applicant.

Armed robbers stole 120,000 French francs (FRF) in cash from a transport company. The company employed a number of inmates from Poissy Prison who were in semi-detention or on external work assignments. An employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. The judge at the Versailles tribunal de grande instance issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for less than eight days. In accordance with Article 181 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, he ordered that the file be transferred to the public prosecutor’s office with a view to the applicant and committing him for trial at the Assize Court.

Four armed robbers wearing masks entered the premises of a transport company which employed a number of inmates from Poissy Prison. They forced the company manager, whom they had taken hostage, to open the safe, from which they stole 120,000 French francs (FRF) in cash. The investigators concentrated their inquiries on some of the prison inmates. One of them, G.D., had witnessed the offences and been threatened by the robbers. He admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn-off shotgun.

The cost of an interpreter in a German court is covered by Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. The text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court.

Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention, which forms an integral part of the domestic law, specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court’. This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while an accused is exempt from paying in advance for the expenses, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

Some courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that such expenses can be awarded against a convicted person.

eval_texts: The case of Luedicke, Belkacem and Koç was referred to the Court by the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany and the European Commission of Human Rights. On 5 October, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on 17 April that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply. On 8 May, he communicated to the Registrar a note containing ‘the applicants’ observations on the question of the application of Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention’ and Mr. Koç’s observations. The Government undertook, inter alia, responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments or statements. The oral hearings took place in public at the Human Rights Building, Stras. The Chamber decided that their Agent and counsel could plead in German at the hearings. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government and by Mr. Ermacora, Mr. Trechsel and Mr. Pawlik for the Commission. The applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings. Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court’. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. If an individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court. The text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Gerhard W. Luedicke was convicted of a road traffic offence in 1972. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. He appealed against the decision, claiming that it was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. The Court of Appeal ruled in his favour and ordered him to pay DM 1,330.90 in costs. He has since appealed again, this time to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). On 29 May 1975, his appeal was dismissed by the District Court which held, inter alia, that Article 6 para. 3 (e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. On 5 May 1977, following a request by Mr. Belkacem, the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known’ The Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The court ordered the applicant to bear the costs of the proceedings “with the exception, however, of the costs occasioned by the assistance of the Turkish-language interpreter, which costs are to be borne by the Treasury’. The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action. ... It is not its purpose to go further and alter the national legal systems ... The intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 19 April 1991. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Istvan Herczegfalvy, a Hungarian national, on 27 November 1978. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5, 8, 10 and 13. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. Istvan Herczegfalvy is a Hungarian citizen who has lived in Austria since 1964. He has served two prison sentences in succession for assaults on his wife, clients of his television repair business and public officials. The Court heard addresses by them and heard evidence from the Government, the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant. The applicant's memorial incorporated his claims for just satisfaction (Article 50 of the Convention) (art. 50), on 16 October and 20 December. On 20 June the Government informed him that they would not be submitting a memorial. Mr Herczegfalvy was detained after serving his sentence in 1977. He was transferred to a special prison at Mittersteig, Vienna. His position was equivalent to that of a curator (Sachwalter) from 1 July 1984. He has been held in a mental institution for mentally ill offenders since 1978. He is currently serving a sentence of life in prison. The application has been adjourned until April 2015, when it will be heard by the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) and the District Court (Ratskammer) The application was brought on the basis of a psychiatrist's report which had been drawn up following numerous complaints by him about prison conditions. The hearing before the Regional Court took place on 9 and 10 January 1979. The court found that the charges against Mr Herczegfalvy had been proved and ordered him to be detained under Article 21 (1) of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 45 below) The court relied on the opinions of three psychiatrists who had each diagnosed paranoia querulans which from 1975 at least had been equivalent to a mental illness. The Vienna Court of Appeal, to which the applicant had appealed, held on 29 August 1979 that it had no jurisdiction: as Article 429 (4) was the only provision which could apply, it was for the Review Chamber to hear the appeal. The Review Chamber upheld the detention in issue. Mr Herczegfalvy went on hunger strike since 2 August 1979. On 10 September 1979 he was admitted to ward 23 of a psychiatric hospital. On 14 December 1979 the investigating judge informed him that he continued to be detained in accordance with Article 429 (4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 17 January 1980 the psychiatric hospital submitted a report expressing the opinion that it was not possible to place the applicant in ordinary pre-trial detention, as his aggressive behaviour was still causing danger to those around him. Pursuant to Article 429. (4), the Review Chamber and the Court of Appeal extended the detention in question in 1980. The applicant subsequently challenged the validity of his declarations. He said that he had made them only with a view to his repatriation to Hungary. The case of Mr Herczegfalvy was brought before the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France. The court ruled that he had been detained for more than two years without an annual review of the lawfulness of his detention. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal and confirmed that the requirements for his release under Article 47 (2) of the Criminal Code were not satisfied. Claude Mazurek is a French national who was born in Avignon in 1942. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. He claimed that the applicant, as an adulterine child, could not lay claim to more than a quarter of it and that there be deposited with the notary a sum of money unlawfully withdrawn.

The applicant appealed, arguing that Article 760 of the Civil Code was incompatible with Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Nîmes Court of Appeal upheld the provisions of the lower court’s judgment ordering the estate to be divided and determining the applicant's inheritance rights. It considered, however, that the amount transferred to the applicant’‘s account should be returned to the estate because he had not proved that his mother had intended it as a gift.’ The court held that although that gift should notionally be brought into account in calculating the disposable portion of the estate, it was inappropriate as matters stood to order that it be deposited with the notary dividing the estate.

The Court of Appeal held that Article 760 was necessary in order to protect the rights of others and that it was a principle of public policy which was not contrary to the Convention. In respect of the sum which had been withdrawn by the applicant and transferred to his own account, the court held that the applicant had merely executed his mother’s intention to gift him a sum of money in addition to his share in the estate. Although that gift should notionally be brought into account in calculating the disposable portion of the estate, it was inappropriate as matters stood to order that the amount in question be deposited with the notary dividing the Estate.

The application was examined by the Court following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998. On 4 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mrs M. Dubrocard, Deputy Director, Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, and for the applicant Mr A. Ottan, of the Montpellier Bar, Counsel. Claude Mazurek was born in 1942 and lives at La Grande-Motte. His mother died on 1 August 1990 of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, Alain, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937. Alain brought an action against the applicant in the Nîmes tribunal de grande instance seeking an order that his mother's estate be divided by a notary. In a judgment of 21 January 1993 the court ordered the estate to be divided. With regard to the applicant's rights, it referred to Article 760 of the Civil Code. The court ruled that Article 760 did not discriminate against children born into a marriage. It said that the money had been intended to be given to the child's mother. But the court said the money should be returned to the mother, as it was part of the child’s inheritance. The court said that it was not intended to discriminate against the child, but to protect the interests of his parents. The decision was made in line with Article 8 and Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which protects the rights of children born to unmarried mothers and fathers. The ruling was upheld by the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on 25 June 1996. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth, but to ensure minimum compliance with the marital obligations of a married parent with regard to his or her legitimate children. The applicant’s complaint of unjustified discrimination on grounds of birth between children born in wedlock and children born out of wedlock, contrary to Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, was dismissed. In respect of the complaint that the. Court of Appeal had ordered the sum transferred to the applicant‘s account to be returned to the estate to be divided, the Court. of. Cassation held that in deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the deceased to bestow a gift on her son in. advance of the division of her estate, the court had determined an issue which it alone had jurisdiction to determine.

However, such a setting aside of decisions does not determine the question of guilt and is also so exceptional that, in my opinion, it cannot be given any significance worth mentioning in this context. The jury was constituted with 11 members, according to Article 355 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. juror W. contacted a policeman she knew and asked if she could sit on the jury even though she had been questioned by the police on one occasion. Jury member W. reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial in this case. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. I agree with the High Court that W. was prejudiced, but the question is then whether the other 10 members of the Jury became prejudiced as a result of W. serving on the jury. The jury members will regularly be told by the presiding judge that, when deciding on the question of guilt, they must only place emphasis on what is stated as evidence in court. There is no corresponding barrier to the jury members discussing the case among themselves – even continuously during the court hearing. I refer to the fact that W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation.

It noted in particular that the notion of the child's well-being was central to the entire proceedings. The child's abrupt removal from her main person of reference and her return to the United States would cause her irreparable harm.

Court emphasised that the particularity of the case lay in the fact that, in the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. Court found that the question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true.

eval_texts: The case originated in two applications (nos. 36812/97 and 40104/98) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the non-enforcement of the final return order under the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction had violated their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. The Court decided to join the applications and to communicate them to the respondent Government. The court found that the first applicant's wife had wrongfully removed the child within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. The court dismissed the mother's claim that the child's return would entail a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. It considered that the second applicant's return could not be hindered by the fact that the mother was her main person of reference and that returning could cause a massive trauma affecting her development. 26 September 2002 the Court declared the applications admissible. The case was heard in the Graz District Civil Court (Bezirksgericht für Zivilrechtssachen) and the decision was made on 20 December 1995. First applicant filed an application for enforcement of the return order of 20 December 1995. First applicant started divorce proceedings before the Oakland Circuit Court (Michigan) By a decision of 16 April 1996, the court pronounced a default judgment of divorce. Further, it awarded the first applicant sole custody of the second applicant. Second applicant should reside with first applicant in the event of her return. The court ruled that the mother could be expected to return with second applicant to the United States. The second applicant was awarded custody of her brother's son in the U.S. by the court of appeals in Graz, Germany. The child was returned to his father in the early hours of 10 May 1996, in accordance with the terms set out in the terms of the order. The case was brought by the mother of the second applicant. She applied for sole custody of her daughter. The court found that the child's well-being had to be taken into account in the enforcement proceedings. The case was referred back to the Graz Regional Civil Court, which quashed the enforcement order of 8 May 1996 and referred the case back to it. It was then transferred to the Leibnitz District Court, in the judicial district of which the applicant had purportedly established her residence. The second applicant's mother appealed against the decision of 25 June 1996, at the request of her mother, and the case was finally settled in August 1996. Austrian Supreme Court dismissed an appeal by the first applicant and set aside the enforcement order of 8 May 1996. Article 13 (b) of the Hague Convention made clear that the child's well-being took priority over the Convention's general aim of preventing child abduction. When ordering coercive measures under section 19 (1) the court had to take the interests of the child’s well- being into account, despite the fact that the return order was final. Reasons of general deterrence or, in other words, the aim of showing that child abduction was not worthwhile could not justify exposing a child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm. In the main proceedings, the courts had denied that there was any risk of psychological harm (as a result of the alleged sexual behaviour of the first applicant) exclusively on account of the child's tender age. In these circumstances, it could not be excluded that the child, who was now more than two years old and had been living solely with her mother for more than a year, would suffer grave psychological harm in the event of a return to her father. The Regional Court had rightly found that the question whether the return order could be enforced by coercive measures needed further examination, including an opinion by an expert in child psychology. It might also prove necessary to assess whether or not the mother's allegations were at all true. The second applicant was abducted in 1995 and returned to Austria on 20 December 1995. The Graz Regional Civil Court dismissed the application for enforcement of the return order on 28 May 1997. On 29 December 1997 the second applicant's mother was awarded sole custody. Following appeal proceedings the judgment became final on 31 March 1998. The court noted that Article 16 of the Hague Convention, which prohibited the State to which the child has been abducted from taking a decision on custody while proceedings for the child's return were pending, no longer applied, as the decision not to enforce the returning order had become final. The case was settled at the Austrian Court of Appeal.

The applicant was born in 1951 and is currently detained in Muret Prison (Haute-Garonne). On 22 February 1999 the Lyons Criminal Court sentenced the applicant, who had been represented by counsel at trial, to seven years’ imprisonment and ordered his permanent exclusion from French territory. The applicant appealed on points of law and filed additional submissions in which he reiterated his argument that Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not comply with the principle of equality of arms. He also challenged the finding as to his guilt. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment as to the issue of guilt and increased the sentence to twelve years' imprisonment, with a minimum term of two-thirds.

The applicant was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and ordered his permanent exclusion from French territory for drug trafficking. He was classified in law as a recidivist. Neither the applicant nor the public prosecutor appealed against the judgment within the ten-day time-limit laid down in Article 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant filed submissions urging the Court of Appeal to declare the appeal inadmissible for non-compliance with Article 6 of the Convention and the principle of equality of arms. He also challenged the finding as to his guilt. On 1 July 1999 the Lyons Court of appeal upheld the judgment as to the issue of guilt and the permanent exclusion.

The applicant was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment and ordered his permanent exclusion from French territory for drug trafficking while classified in law as a recidivist. Neither the applicant nor the public prosecutor appealed against the judgment within the ten-day time-limit laid down in Article 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant appealed on points of law and filed additional submissions in which he reiterated his argument that Article 505 did not comply with the principle of equality of arms enshrined in Article 6 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment as to the issue of guilt and increased the sentence to twelve years' imprisonment, with a minimum term of two-thirds of the sentence.

In 2000 the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law. The Court of Appeal stated that the opportunity granted to the Principal Public Prosecutor to lodge an appeal within two months from the date of delivery of the judgment was not at variance with the provisions of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In so holding, and in so far as Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not deprive the defendant of a remedy, the judges applied the law correctly ...” said the court of appeal in a judgement of 15 March 2000. The case-law had ruled that Article 546 of the code infringed Article 6 in that it afforded only the principal prosecutor the right to appeal against certain judgments concerning petty offences.

In a judgment of 15 March 2000 the Criminal Division of the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on points of law. In so holding, and in so far as Article 505 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not deprive the defendant of a remedy that could be used by the Principal Public Prosecutor, the judges applied the law correctly, said the judge. “The opportunity granted to the latter to lodge an appeal within two months from the date of delivery of the judgment was not at variance with the provisions of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights where, as in this instance, the right of appeal was also available to the defendant,” he said.

The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). On 10 January 1994 the lawyer was given leave by the President to use the Spanish language in the hearings. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr J.M. Morenilla, the elected judge of Spanish nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 June 1994. There appeared before the Court the Government (‘the Government’), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38) The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to questions from two of its members. On 23 November 1994 it declined to accept observations submitted out of time by counsel for the applicant on 13 October 1994 which related to the reimbursement of his fees in the national proceedings. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. The plant began to operate in July 1988 without the licence (licencia) from the municipal authorities required by Regulation 6. The application was brought by a woman in Lorca, Spain. She complained about a waste-treatment plant that was causing health problems. She lodged an application seeking protection of her fundamental rights. The application was heard by the Administrative Division of the Murcia Audiencia Territorial. It was ruled that the plant should be shut down, but the treatment of waste water contaminated with chromium was allowed to continue. The judge ruled in favour of Mrs López Ostra and ordered the plant to stop treating waste water. The case was heard in front of the Audiencia Territorial Commission (CAT) in March 1992. Mrs López Ostra lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court (Tribunal Supremo - see paragraph 25 below in fine) She maintained that the plant was a source of polluting fumes, pestilential and irritant smells and repetitive noise that had caused both her daughter and herself health problems. The town council’s attitude amounted to unlawful interference with her right to respect for her home and was also an attack on her physical integrity. Lastly, the applicant sought an order suspending the plant's operations. The decision of the Audiencia Territorial appeared to be incompatible with the general supervisory powers conferred on mayors by the 1961 regulations. Mrs López Ostra lodged an appeal (recurso de amparo) with the Constitutional Court, alleging violations of Article 15. The court ruled that the appeal was inadmissible on the ground that it was manifestly ill-founded. In 1990 two sisters-in-law brought proceedings against the municipality of Lorca and SACURSA in the Administrative Division of the Murcia High Court (Tribunal Superior de Justicia) alleging that the plant was operating unlawfully. On 18 September 1991 the court noted that the nuisance had continued after 9 September 1988 and that the waste-treatment plant had not been closed. SACURSA was convicted of an environmental health offence. The judge ordered that the plant should be closed until licences were obtained. However, enforcement of this order was stayed following an appeal by the town council and SACurSA. The case is still pending in the Supreme Court. The investigation file contains several medical certificates and expert opinions concerning the effects on the health of those living near the plant. The report of 27 October 1992 stated that the levels of the gas probably exceeded the permitted limits but did not pose any danger to the health. In a certificate dated 12 December 1991 Dr de Ayala Sánchez, a paediatrician, stated that Mrs López Ostra’s daughter, Cristina, presented a clinical picture of nausea. The plant was closed on 27 October 1993 and the judge confirmed the order of 15 November 1991 and the plant was temporarily closed. The applicant's daughter and her nephew showed typical symptoms of chronic absorption of the gas in question, periodically manifested in the form of acute bronchopulmonary infections. The family were rehoused in a flat in the centre of Lorca, for which the municipality paid the rent. Mrs López Ostra and her family were then moved to a house in a different part of town on 23 February 1993. train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained, in particular, that the hearings regarding the prolongation of his pre-trial detention were not held in public. By a decision of 12 October 2004, the Chamber declared the application admissible as regards the communicated complaint. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section of the Court in November 2004. The application and the Government each filed observations on the merits. Written submissions were also received from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Graz. The court based the suspicion against the applicant on the statement of the victim, who had identified the applicant in an identity parade. Given the applicant's criminal record, there was a risk that he might commit another offence similar to the one of which he was suspected (Tatbegehungsgefahr). The court stated that the applicant had nine previous convictions, mainly for property-related offences, but recently also for violent crimes. The applicant lodged an appeal against this decision. On 2 August 2000 the Graz Regional Court, having held a hearing in the presence of the parties, ordered that the applicants pre-trial detention should continue.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Graz. On 6 May 2000 the Graz Regional Criminal Court (Landesgericht für Strafsachen) ordered the applicant's pre-trial detention on suspicion of attempted sexual coercion. The court based the suspicion against the applicant on the statement of the victim, who had identified the applicant in an identity parade. The applicant appealed against this decision. The Graz Court of Appeal, sitting in private, dismissed the appeal and upheld the Regional Court's decision. On 7 August 2000 the applicant appealed again and the appeal was dismissed. He stressed that there were no reasons to maintain his pre- trial detention.

The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Graz. He was detained on suspicion of attempted sexual coercion (geschlechtliche Nötigung) The court based the suspicion against the applicant on the statement of the victim, who had identified the applicant in an identity parade. The court found that, in the light of the applicant's recidivism and his character, the prolongation of his pre-trial detention was reasonable. The applicant appealed against this decision. He submitted that there was no reasonable suspicion against him as the testimony of the only witness for the prosecution had been insufficient. The appeal was dismissed and the applicant was released.

The applicant was convicted of attempted sexual coercion and sentenced to two years' imprisonment. He lodged a fundamental rights complaint with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) against this decision. He submitted that there was no strong suspicion against him and that there were no reasons to maintain the detention on remand. The Supreme Court rejected the applicant's plea of nullity. In May 2001 the Court of Appeal dismissed an appeal by the applicant, but allowed one lodged by the public prosecutor and increased the term of imprisonment to two-and-a-half years and six months. The appeal was dismissed on 8 May 2001.

The Supreme Court rejected the applicant's plea of nullity on 8 March 2001. Written submissions were also received from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party. The Graz Regional Court ordered that the applicant's pre-trial detention should continue. There was a risk that he might commit another offence similar to the one of which he was suspected (Tatbegehungsgefahr). The applicant appealed against this decision. The Graz Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the Regional Court's decision. On 18 September 2000 the applicant lodged a fundamental rights complaint (G.) against the detention. The court found that there was no doubt about the credibility of the witness and there was therefore a reasonable suspicion against the applicant. Further, it found that reasons for detention on remand (Haftgründe) existed. On 16 October 2000 the Supreme Court, sitting in private, dismissed the complaint. It found that there was no doubt about the credibility of the witness. On 8 May 2001 the Court of Appeal increased the term of imprisonment to two years and six months. The appeal was dismissed on 8 March 2001, but the sentence was increased to three and a half years. The case was heard in front of a panel of three judges, one of whom was a judge himself. The judge found the applicant guilty of attempted sexual coercion and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment. The court of appeal dismissed the appeal on 24 October 2001. The sentence was then increased to four years and three months.

The applicant complained that he had been denied a survivor’s pension following the death of his partner, with whom he had lived in a de facto marital relationship. Judge Luis López Guerra, the judge elected in respect of Spain, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). On 11 February 2015, the President of the Section appointed Mr Blanca Lozano Cutanda to sit as an ad hoc judge. The case was heard in Madrid.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant complained that he had been discriminated against on the ground of his sexual orientation. Judge Luis López Guerra, the judge elected in respect of Spain, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court) On 11 February 2015, the President of the Section appointed Mr Blanca Lozano Cutanda to sit as an ad hoc judge. The case was heard by the Court’s Adjudicatory Chamber on 28 March 2015.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained that he had been discriminated against on the ground of his sexual orientation. Judge Luis López Guerra, the judge elected in respect of Spain, withdrew from sitting in the case. The President of the Section appointed Blanca Lozano Cutanda to sit as an ad hoc judge (Rule 29 of the Rules of Court) In substance the applicant relied on Article 14 of the. Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The application was made on 22 June 2009 by a Spanish national who had been granted legal aid.

The applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse, arguing that he had cohabited with his deceased partner for many years. The National Institute of Social Security refused to grant the applicant a survivor’s pension on the ground that since he had not been married to the deceased person, he could not legally be considered as his surviving spouse. The applicant challenged that decision before the Madrid Social Tribunal no. 33. In a judgment of 14 November 2005 the Social Tribunal ruled for the applicant. In accordance with its first additional provision all legal and regulatory provisions making reference to marriage should be understood as applicable to all marriages irrespective of the sex of its members (see paragraph 35 below).

In a judgment of 14 November 2005 the Social Tribunal ruled for the applicant. The case is about a man who cohabited with another man in a homosexual relationship from 1990 until the latter’s death on 2 July 2002. On 19 September 2003 the applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse, under section 174 (1) of the General Social Security Act. On 1 July 2005 Law no. 13/2005 amending the provisions of the Civil Code with respect to the right to enter into marriage was passed. Two days later it entered into force. This law legalised same-sex marriage in Spain. In accordance with its first additional provision all legal and regulatory provisions making reference to marriage should be understood thereafter as applicable to all marriages irrespective of the sex of its members.

The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Pozuelo de Alarcón (Madrid) The applicant cohabited with another man in a homosexual relationship from 1990 until the latter’s death on 2 July 2002. The applicant claimed social security allowances as a surviving spouse, under section 174 (1) of the General Social Security Act. The National Institute of Social Security refused to grant the applicant a survivor's pension on the ground that since he had not been married to the deceased person, he could not legally be considered as his surviving spouse. In a judgment of 14 November 2005 the Social Tribunal ruled for the applicant. In accordance with its first additional provision all legal and regulatory provisions making reference to marriage should be understood as applicable to all marriages irrespective of the sex of its members.

The Social Tribunal observed that the issue at stake was whether the applicant, as the surviving partner of a same-sex relationship that ended (following his partner’s death) before the entry into force of Law no. 13/2005, had the right to a survivor's pension. The Social Tribunal held in this regard that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex.” The tribunal held that the law should be interpreted on the basis of the first additional provision of LawNo.13/2005 as applying fully to same- sex marriage.

The Social Tribunal observed that the issue at stake was whether the applicant, as the surviving partner of a same-sex relationship that ended (following his partner’s death) before the entry into force of Law no. 13/2005, had the right to a survivor's pension. The Tribunal held in this regard that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex.” The Social Tribunal held that the solution to the legal issue raised by the applicant's case depended on whether it could be inferred that Parliament’S intention had been that surviving partners of same- sex couples who had been prevented from marrying under the former legislation could access a survivors’ pension on the same footing as survivors of different-sex marriages.

The Social Tribunal observed that the issue at stake was whether the applicant, as the surviving partner of a same-sex relationship that ended (following his partner’s death) before the entry into force of Law no. 13/2005, had the right to a survivor's pension. The Social Tribunal held in this regard that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex’. The tribunal held that it was evident that after the entry. into force in 2005, surviving spouses of same- sex marriages were entitled to survivors’ pensions on the same footing as survivors of different-sex marriages.

The applicant’s circumstances were ‘fully comparable’ to those outlined in additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/1981 of 7 July 1981. The Social Tribunal considered that treating these two groups differently would not be in harmony with the strong egalitarian intention expressed by Parliament with the passing of Law No. 13/2005. The judge added that the distinction was the main impediment to the recognition of the applicant's right to a survivor's pension. The application was rejected on the grounds that it did not comply with the Equality Act of 2004, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. The case was dismissed on appeal.

The Social Tribunal considered that the applicant’s circumstances were ‘fully comparable’ to those outlined in additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/1981. The Social Tribunal acknowledged, however, that whereas Law no., 30/ 1981 was aimed at protecting the rights of those cohabiting heterosexual couples who were prevented from marrying because divorce was prohibited at the time, Law. 13/2005 was aimed to protect the rights. of those who could not marry on account of their sexual orientation. This distinction was the main impediment. to the recognition of the applicant's right to a survivor's pension.

Law no. 30/1981 recognised the right to obtain a survivor’s pension for individuals who had been prevented from marrying a person who later died by the legislation in force until then. Law no. 13/2005 was aimed at protecting the rights of those who could not marry on account of their sexual orientation. The Social Tribunal considered that treating these two groups differently would not be in harmony with the strong egalitarian intention expressed by Parliament with the passing of Law No.13/2005. The applicant had shared a marital life with his partner until the latter's death;. the claimant had cohabited in a relationship similar to marriage with the deceased person and that the deceased had died before Law. no.30/1981 entered into force.

Social Tribunal says sexual orientation does not constitute discriminatory grounds in the application of additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/1981. In the case of the applicant’s case, the Social Tribunal relied on the constitutive effects of Law. no. 13/2005 which created new rights and was effective only from the date it entered into force. The INSS and the Treasury General of Social Security appealed (recurso de suplicación) against that judgment. The Social Tribunal recognised the applicant's right to be awarded a survivor's pension with effect from 3 July 2005. The appeal was dismissed.

The INSS and the Treasury General of Social Security appealed against that judgment to the Social Tribunal. The ruling was in favour of the claimant. The Social Tribunal recognised the applicant's right to be awarded a survivor’s pension with effect from 3 July 2005. The INSS appealed against the ruling, but the decision was upheld. The tribunal found that the ruling was consistent with the intention of the legislature. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which has jurisdiction over claims for social security benefits in Spain. The appeal was dismissed. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal and the appeal was thrown out on appeal.

The Social Tribunal stated that the first additional provision of Law no. 13/2005 sets out that provisions making reference to marriage shall apply irrespective of the sex of the spouses. It also ruled that the administration’s submission that in the area of social security benefits the governing principle was that of non-retroactivity of laws was not absolute. The INSS and the Treasury General of Social Security appealed (recurso de suplicación) against that judgment to the Social Tribunal. The Social Tribunal recognised the applicant’'s right to be awarded a survivor's pension with effect from 3 July 2005. The ruling was upheld by the Supreme Court.

Madrid High Court of Justice upheld the appeal and reversed the first-instance judgment. Court found that the legislature had not intended Law no. 13/2005 to cover same-sex partnerships which had been ended by the death of one of the partners before said law had entered into force. Court referred to constitutional case-law dating from 1994 according to which the requisite of heterosexuality for the purposes of marriage was fully constitutional. Court said that it was within the margin of appreciation of the public authorities to treat heterosexual marriages more favourably than homosexual partnerships. For the court, it was only as from the entry into force of Law. no.13/2005 that marriage between same- sex couples was recognised and that this law affected other rights for those persons who would wish to marry thereafter.

Madrid High Court of Justice upheld the appeal and reversed the first-instance judgment. Court found that the legislature had not intended Law no. 13/2005 to cover same-sex partnerships which had been ended by the death of one of the partners before said law had entered into force. Court referred to constitutional case-law dating from 1994 according to which the requisite of heterosexuality for the purposes of marriage was fully constitutional. Court said that it was within the margin of appreciation of the public authorities to treat heterosexual marriages more favourably than homosexual partnerships. New law could not be deemed unconstitutional as contrary to either any constitutional principle or to the right not to be discriminated against.

Madrid High Court of Justice upheld the appeal and reversed the first-instance judgment. Court found that the legislature had not intended Law no. 13/2005 to cover same-sex partnerships which had been ended by the death of one of the partners before said law had entered into force. Court referred to constitutional case-law dating from 1994 according to which the requisite of heterosexuality for the purposes of marriage was fully constitutional. The court said it was within the margin of appreciation of the public authorities to treat heterosexual marriages more favourably than homosexual partnerships. In this connection, the court maintained that despite the reference in the preamble of Law. no.13/2005 (see paragraph 35 below) to the discriminatory treatment to which homosexuals had traditionally been subjected on account of their sexual orientation, the aim of Parliament in passing that law was to respond to a new social reality.

The Madrid High Court of Justice found that additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/ 1981 was not applicable to the applicant’s case for two main reasons. it strictly concerned same-sex couples still in existence at that time and who would be willing to enter into marriage. The court considered that the difference between the situations before and after the passing of Law. no. 13/2005 was essentially an expression of the principle of succession of laws without constitutional implications as regards the right not to be discriminated against. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law seeking harmonisation of the case-law.

The Madrid High Court of Justice found that additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/1981 was not applicable to the applicant's case. The court considered that the difference between the situations before and after the passing of Law. no. 13/2005 was essentially an expression of the principle of succession of laws without constitutional implications as regards the right not to be discriminated against. The applicant and his partner could have never cohabited ‘as if married’ before the entry into force of LawNo.13/2005, because before then they were ineligible for marriage as they were both male. The institution of marriage was open to them in their capacity as heterosexuals.

The Madrid High Court of Justice found that this provision was not applicable to the applicant’s case. The court considered that the difference between the situations before and after the passing of Law no. 13/2005 was essentially an expression of the principle of succession of laws without constitutional implications as regards the right not to be discriminated against. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law seeking harmonisation of the case-law. Additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law. 30/ 1981 was aimed at guaranteeing a survivor's pension to those heterosexuals who had been prevented from marrying their out-of wedlock partner because divorce had not been legal at the time of the latter's death.

Relying on Articles 14 (principle of equality and prohibition of discrimination) and 24 (right to effective judicial protection), the applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision of 11 February 2009, the constitutional court declared the appeal inadmissible on the grounds that the applicant had failed to substantiate the special constitutional relevance of his complaints. (recurso de casación para la unificación de doctrina). In a. decision of 27 June 2007, the Supreme Court (Social Chamber) declared the. appeal inadsentmissible. The Supreme Court (Social Chamber) declared the appeal inadmissible on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, specifically a judgment of the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands of 7 November 2003, was not relevant. The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision of 11 February 2009, served on 17 February 2009,. the Constitutional Court declared the appeal inadmissible on the grounds that the applicant had failed to substantiate the special constitutional relevance of his complaints. (recurso de casación para la unificación de doctrina).

The case was referred to the Supreme Court (Social Chamber) and the Constitutional Court. In a decision of 11 February 2009, the Constitutional court declared the appeal inadmissible on the grounds that the applicant had failed to substantiate the special constitutional relevance of his complaints. The case was decided in favor of the applicant on the basis of Article 14 (principle of equality and prohibition of discrimination) and Article 24 (right to effective judicial protection) The appeal was settled in the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands of 7 November 2003, which was served on 26 July 2007. The ruling was decided on the ground that the decision was not relevant for purposes of comparison.

Judge Luis López Guerra, the judge elected in respect of Spain, withdrew from sitting in the case. Ms Blanca Lozano Cutanda was appointed to sit as an ad hoc judge. The case was adjourned to February 2015 for further proceedings. The decision was returned to the Court of Appeal on February 8, 2015. The ruling was unanimous. On 1 July 2005 Law no. 13/2005 amending the provisions of the Civil Code with respect to the right to enter into marriage was passed. Two days later it entered into force. This law legalised same-sex marriage in Spain. In accordance with its first additional provision all legal and regulatory provisions making reference to marriage should be understood thereafter as applicable to all marriages irrespective of the sex of its members (see paragraph 35 below) The applicant had been prevented from marrying his. partner because same- sex marriage had not been recognised in domestic law. at the time his partner died. The applicant challenged that decision before the Madrid Social Tribunal no. 33. In a judgment of 14 November 2005 the Social Tribunal ruled for the applicant. The applicant had been denied a survivor’s pension because the couple had not married. The social security administration had relied on the fact that the couple hadn’t married to refuse the applicant a pension. The Social Tribunal held that after the entry into force of Law no. 13/2005, surviving spouses of same-sex marriages were entitled to survivors’ pensions on the same footing as survivors of different-sex marriage. The court held that: “This is a wide-ranging provision which affects all the other provisions of the legal system making reference to marriage. From now onwards all references to marriage established in the law shall be understood as applying also to marriage celebrated between two persons of the same sex”. The applicant could not marry his partner because the legislation then in force prevented him from doing so. The Social Tribunal considered nonetheless that treating these two groups differently would not be in harmony with the strong egalitarian intention expressed by Parliament with the passing of Law no. 13/2005. The only method to apply it in a way which is consistent with the egalitarian intention of the legislature is to do so irrespective of the sexual orientation of the members of the cohabiting couple, the Social Tribunal said. The ruling was made by the Court of Appeal and the case was heard by the High Court of Justice. The applicant was awarded a survivor’s pension. The Madrid High Court of Justice upheld the appeal and reversed the first-instance judgment. The court found that the legislature had not intended Law no. 13/2005 to cover same-sex partnerships which had been ended by the death of one of the partners before said law had entered into force. The INSS and the Treasury General of Social Security appealed (recurso de suplicación) against that judgment to the Madrid High court of Justice (Tribunal Superior de Justicia). On 18 September 2006 the court ruled that the appeal had been successful and awarded the applicant a survivor’s pension with effect from 3 July 2005. The right thereby recognised shall currently be interpreted as providing a solution to factual situations. The court referred to constitutional case-law dating from 1994 according to which the requisite of heterosexuality for the purposes of marriage was fully constitutional. The court noted in this regard that Law no. 13/2005 had not included any provision concerning same-sex partnerships which had already ended at the time of its entry into force. The Madrid High Court of Justice found that this provision was not applicable to the applicant’s case for two main reasons. Additional provision no. 10 (2) was, as the Constitutional Court had established, of a provisional or transitory nature and had been envisaged for those persons could be said to be in similar circumstances. The applicant lodged an appeal on points of law seeking harmonisation of the case-law (recurso de casación para la unificación de doctrina) The Supreme Court (Social Chamber) declared the appeal inadmissible on the ground that the decision produced for purposes of comparison, specifically a judgment of the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands of 7 November 2003, was not relevant. In a decision of 11 February 2009, served on 17 Feb 2009, the Constitutional Court declared the applicant had failed to substantiate the special constitutional relevance of his complaints. The court contended that the applicant could never have fulfilled the more uxorio marital cohabitation requirement established by additional provision no. 10 (2) of Law no. 30/ 1981.

The President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3)

The case originated in an application (no. 7205/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged under Article 5 together with Article 14 that his continued imprisonment violated his rights under the Convention on account of the difference in treatment between prisoners serving fixed-term sentences of less than fifteen years or discretionary life sentences, where in both cases a recommendation of the Parole Board resulted in release. The President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government on 16 April 2009. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3).

The case originated in an application (no. 7205/07) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged under Article 5 together with Article 14 that his continued imprisonment following the recommendation of the Parole Board on 25 March 2002 violated his rights under the Convention on account of the difference in treatment between prisoners serving fixed-term sentences of less than fifteen years or discretionary life sentences.
