The applicant was sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment for serious crimes including attempted murder in 1994. He became eligible for release on parole on 13 March 2002 and entitled to release on 18 March 2005. On 25 March 2002 the Parole Board recommended his release on the grounds that the risk to the public had been significantly reduced. The Secretary of State rejected the recommendation on 25 October 2002, concluding that the release of the applicant would present an unacceptable risk. The applicant brought judicial review proceedings in respect of the decision of the Secretary of state to refuse his early release. The Divisional Court dismissed the applicant's judicial review claim on 9 June 2003. The Court has not been provided with details of the reasons for this decision.

The applicant was sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment for serious crimes including attempted murder. He became eligible for release on parole on 13 March 2002 and entitled to release on 18 March 2005. The Secretary of State rejected the recommendation of the Parole Board in the applicant's case, concluding that the release of the applicant would present an unacceptable risk to the public. On 17 February 2003, the applicant was granted leave to bring judicial review proceedings in respect of the decision of the Secretary of state to refuse his early release. The applicant's judicial review claim was dismissed on 9 June 2003. The Court has not been provided with details of the reasons for this decision. For the purposes of the proceedings, the Divisional Court accepted that the question of early release was not relevant.

The applicant was sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment for serious crimes including attempted murder. He became eligible for release on parole on 13 March 2002 and entitled to release on 18 March 2005. The Parole Board recommended the applicant's release on the grounds that the risk to the public had been significantly reduced. On 25 October 2002 the Secretary of State rejected the recommendation. The applicant brought judicial review proceedings in respect of the decision. The Court has not provided details of the reasons for this decision. On 9 June 2003, the Divisional Court dismissed the applicant’s judicial review claim. For the purposes of the proceedings, the Secretary. of State accepted that the question of early. release was not required for prisoners serving indeterminate sentences.

Mr Clift was granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The applicant's appeal was dismissed by the House of Lords in December 2006. The Parole Board subsequently reconsidered the applicant's case and on 25 February 2004 once again recommended his release. On this occasion the Secretary of State accepted the recommendation, and on 10 March 2004 Mr Clift. was released on licence. The application was dismissed on the grounds that release from a determinate sentence fell within the ambit of Article 5 of the Convention and that Article 14 was therefore engaged. The appeal was rejected on appeal on the basis that the parole board had acted in a proportionate manner.

Hooper J found that there was differential treatment between analogous groups. Release from a determinate sentence fell within the ambit of Article 5 of the Convention and that Article 14 was therefore engaged. The Court of Appeal endorsed the judgment of Hooper J and dismissed the applicant's appeal. The applicant was granted leave to appeal to the House of Lords. On 13 December 2006, their Lordships unanimously dismissed the appeal. They agreed that the right to seek early release, where domestic law provided for such a right, was clearly within theAmbit of articles 5 and 14 of the convention. Lord Bingham of Cornhill noted that the Convention does not require member states to establish a scheme for early release.

The applicant was granted leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The application was dismissed in 2006. Mr Clift was released on licence on 10 March 2004. The applicant was denied early release on licence. The appeal was dismissed by the House of Lords on 13 December 2006. The case was decided on the basis that release from a determinate sentence fell within the ambit of Article 5 of the Convention and that Article 14 was therefore engaged. The judge found that the differential treatment pursued the legitimate aim of reserving to a politically and democratically accountable minister the power to control the release of those serving long determinate sentences. He also said that the power was proportionate in light of the problems posed by such prisoners for public safety.

Law provided for a time at which (subject to additional days of custody imposed for disciplinary breaches) a prisoner must, as a matter of right, be released. Mr Clift does not complain of the sentence passed upon him, but of being denied a definitive Parole Board recommendation. Is his classification as a prisoner serving a determinate sentence of 15 years or more (but less than life) a personal characteristic? I find it difficult to apply so elusive a test. But I would incline to regard a life sentence as an acquired personal characteristic and a lifer as having an 'other status' I find that the right to seek early release, where domestic law provides for such a right, is clearly within the ambit of article 5.

Mr Clift was denied a definitive Parole Board recommendation. The court found that the right to seek early release, where domestic law provides for such a right, is clearly within the ambit of article 5. Mr Clift's classification as a prisoner serving a determinate sentence of 15 years or more (but less than life) a personal characteristic? I find it difficult to apply so elusive a test. But I would incline to regard a life sentence as an acquired personal characteristic and a lifer as having an 'other status', and it is hard to see why the classification of Mr Cl lift, based on the length of his sentence and not the nature of his offences, should be differently regarded.

Mr Clift was denied a definitive Parole Board recommendation. He was released from prison at an earlier, discretionary stage of his sentence. He has appealed his release from prison to the Court of Appeal. Mr Clift is serving a determinate sentence of 15 years or more (but less than life) The court ruled that the right to seek early release, where domestic law provides for such a right, is clearly within the ambit of article 5 of the Convention. But the court did not find the difference in treatment in the applicant's case to be the result of his ‘status’ such as to fall within the prohibition on discrimination in Article 14.

Prisoners are divided into broadly defined categories, or groups of people, according to the nature or the length of their sentences. As a result they are regarded as having acquired a distinctive status which attaches itself to them personally for the purposes of the regime in which they are required to serve their sentence. It must be accepted, as Lord Bingham points out, that a personal characteristic cannot be defined by the differential treatment of which a person complains. It is plain too that the category of long-term prisoner into which Mr Clift's case falls would not have been recognised as a separate category had it not been for the Order which treats prisoners in his group differently from others.

Mr Clift's case raises whether the distinguishing feature or characteristic which enables persons or a group of persons to be singled out for separate treatment must have been identified as a personal characteristic before it is used for this purpose by the discriminator. Mr Clift had already been sentenced, and he had already acquired the status which that sentence gave him before the Order was made that denied prisoners in his group the right to release on the recommendation of the Parole Board. It seems to me, on this approach, that the protection of article 14, read with article 1 of the Convention, is to secure to everyone within the jurisdiction of the High Contracting Parties the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set out in section 1.

Length of sentence does confer a status on Mr Clift which can be regarded as a personal characteristic. He had already been sentenced and acquired the status which that sentence gave him before the Order was made that denied prisoners in his group the right to release on the recommendation of the Parole Board. The question which his case raises is whether the distinguishing feature or characteristic. which enables persons or a group of persons to be singled out for separate treatment must have been identified as a. personal characteristic before it is used for this purpose by the discriminator. It seems to me, on this approach, that the protection of article 14, read with article 1 of the Convention, is to secure. to everyone within the jurisdiction of the High Contracting Parties the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms set out in section 1 of. the Convention without discrimination.

The law may look odd, but not every apparent anomaly is a breach of Convention rights. The difference of treatment between Mr Clift and people sentenced either to shorter determinate sentences or to life imprisonment is not covered by article 14 at all. The law has since been changed and one can well understand why. But it is not for us to declare legislation which Parliament has passed incompatible with the Convention rights unless the Convention and its case law require us to do so.’ The House of Lords has ruled that the Home Secretary may not be able to deport anyone who has committed a crime under the terms of article 14 of the Convention. The Commons has also ruled that it is possible to regard what he has done, rather than who or what he is, as the true reason for the difference in treatment.

The difference of treatment between Mr Clift and people sentenced either to shorter determinate sentences or to life imprisonment is not covered by article 14 at all. The law may look odd. But not every apparent anomaly is a breach of Convention rights. This one is the result of what the Home Secretary chose to do in relation to people sentenced to shorter terms of imprisonment. But it is not for us to declare legislation which Parliament has passed incompatible with the Convention rights unless the Convention and its case law require us to do so in this case. ‘It is possible to regard what he has done, rather than who or what he is, as the true reason for the difference in treatment in Mr. Clift's case.’

The law may look odd, but not every apparent anomaly is a breach of Convention rights. The real reason for the distinction is not a personal characteristic of the offender but what the offender has done. The difference of treatment between Mr Clift and people sentenced either to shorter determinate sentences or to life imprisonment is not covered by article 14 at all. The law has since been changed and one can well understand why. But it is not for us to declare legislation which Parliament has passed incompatible with the Convention rights unless the Convention and its case law require us to do so.” “It is possible to regard what he has done, rather than who or what he is, as the true reason for [Mr Clift's] case”

Lords Bingham and Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood considered whether the difference in treatment would have been justified. Lord Bingham said: “The differential treatment of prisoners serving 15 years or more had, in my opinion, become an anomaly.” Lord Brown agreed with the conclusion, saying: ‘I would accordingly resolve this issue in favour of Mr Clift and against the Secretary of State’ The case was heard at the Court of Appeal, which heard evidence from both sides of the debate. The trial was adjourned until September 4, 2013, when the jury returned its verdict. The jury was asked to return its verdict at 11.30am on September 6, 2013.

Lord Bingham and Lord Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood ruled in favour of Mr Clift. Lord Brown agreed with the conclusion of Lord Bingham. The differential treatment of prisoners serving 15 years or more had, in my opinion, become an anomaly. Anomalies are commonplace. But by 2002 it had become an indefensible anomaly because it had by then come to be recognised that assessment of the risk presented by any individual prisoner was a task with no political content and one to which the Secretary of State could not (and did not claim to) bring any superior expertise. I would accordingly resolve this issue in favour. of Mr. Clift and against the Secretary. of State.

Lord Bingham and Lord Brown of Eaton-under-Heywood ruled in favour of Mr Clift. Lord Brown said the differential treatment of prisoners serving 15 years or more had, in his opinion, become an anomaly. Lord Bingham said that by 2002 it had become an indefensible anomaly because it had by then come to be recognised that assessment of the risk presented by any individual prisoner was a task with no political content and one to which the Secretary of State could not (and did not claim to) bring any superior expertise. He decided to resolve this issue in favour. of Mr. Clift and against the Secretary. of State.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 7205/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his continued imprisonment violated his rights under the Convention on account of the difference in treatment between prisoners serving fixed-term sentences of less than fifteen years or discretionary life sentences. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The applicant was sentenced to eighteen years' imprisonment for serious crimes including attempted murder, which carried a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Under the legislative regime applicable at the time, he became eligible for release on parole on 13 March 2002. The Secretary of State rejected the recommendation of the Parole Board in the applicant's case, concluding that the release of the applicant would present an unacceptable risk to the public. As a result, the applicant was not released. For prisoners serving determinate sentences of less than fifteen years and for prisoners serving indeterminate (i.e. life) sentences, the approval of the Secretary of state following a positive recommendation of. the Paroles Board was not required. Hooper J found that there was differential treatment between analogous groups, namely those serving sentences of fifteen years or more and those serving sentence of almost fifteen years. He considered that the differential treatment pursued the legitimate aim of reserving. to a politically and democratically accountable minister the power to control the release. of those serving long determinate. sentences. The applicant was granted leave to appeal to the House of Lords. On 13 December 2006, their Lordships unanimously dismissed the applicant's appeal. They agreed that the right to seek early release, where domestic law provided for such a right, was clearly within the ambit of Article 5 of the Convention. Lord Bingham of Cornhill noted (at paragraphs 17-18): “The Convention does not require member states to establish a scheme for early release of those sentenced to imprisonment.” Mr Clift was released on licence on 10 March 2004. The Parole Board reconsidered the case and on 25 February 2004 once again recommended the applicant’s release. On this occasion the Secretary of State accepted the recommendation. The right to seek early release, where domestic law provides for such a right, is clearly within the ambit of article 5. However, unlike the lower courts, and with some hesitation, their Lordships did not find the difference in treatment in the applicant's case to be the result of his ‘status’ Lord Bingham said (at paragraph 28): “I do not think that a personal characteristic can be defined by the differential treatment of which a person complains” Lord Hope of Craighead made similar observations (at paragraphs 46-49): ‘It could be said in Mr Clift's case that the length of his sentence did confer a status on him’ Mr Clift's case raises whether the distinguishing feature or characteristic which enables persons or a group of persons to be singled out for separate treatment must have been identified as a personal characteristic. A measure of self-restraint is needed, lest we stretch our own jurisprudence beyond that which is shared by all the States Parties to the Convention. It is possible to regard what he has done, rather than who or what he is, as the true reason for the difference of treatment in Mr Clift’s case. I am persuaded, with some reluctance, that it is not open to us to resolve the second agreed issue.” Home Secretary chose to do what he was obliged by the terms of article 5 itself to do in relation to life imprisonment. It is not for us to declare legislation which Parliament has passed incompatible with the Convention rights unless the Convention and its case law require us so to do. The differential treatment of prisoners serving 15 years or more had, in my opinion, become an anomaly. That would not, in itself, be a ground for holding it to be unjustified. Anomalies are commonplace. But by 2002 it had become an indefensible anomaly because it had by then been decided that it was not legal.“The real reason for the distinction is not a personal characteristic of the offender but what the offender has done.” Lord Brown agreed with the conclusion of Lord Bingham. It was recognised that assessment of the risk presented by any individual prisoner, in the application of publicly promulgated criteria, was a task with no political content. I would accordingly resolve this issue in favour of Mr Clift and against the Secretary of State, Lord Brown said in his judgment. He added: ‘It has. come to be recognised that assessing the risk of a prisoner is not a political matter and one to which the Secretary. of State could not (and did not claim to) bring any superior expertise.’ Lord Brown added that he was ‘confident’ that Clift would get the job done. He said he would ‘resolve this issue’ in his judgement.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. Case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. By a decision of 27 November 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1), and the case was assigned again to the Second Section (Rule 52 § 1) The case was heard by the European Court of Justice.

Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. By a decision of 27 November 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) on 1 November 2001. This case was assigned into the newly constituted Second Section (Rule 52§ 1) The French Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs M. Dubrocard, Head of the Human Rights Office.

The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Ali Riza Göktan alleged a violation of Article 6 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms M.-C. Reminiac, of the Bourg-en-Bresse Bar. The French Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs M. Dubrocard, Head of the Human Rights Office, Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant was born in 1953 and currently lives in Turkey. He entered France in 1974. At the material time, he worked for a business in Strasbourg. On 15 March 1991 he and another person, M. B., were arrested by officers from the Strasbourg Regional Police Department (‘the SRPJ’) and customs officers on the verge of concluding a drugs deal with a couple, who managed to make their getaway. The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. He later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out.

The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. As for the couple who had “escaped” arrest by the police, they were in fact both customs officers, known as “Maud” and “Serge”

The applicant had been sentenced to two years' imprisonment in default of payment of a customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the order was defective. The Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. The applicant appealed to the Court ofCassation to order the prison sentence and the term of imprisonment indefault to run concurrently.

The applicant had been sentenced to two years' imprisonment in default of payment of the customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the order for his imprisonment was defective, as the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. His appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. In the present case, the express reference in the Customs Code to the Code of Criminal Procedure relates only to the length of the imprisonment indefault.

The applicant was ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment of a customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He appealed the order, arguing that the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. The Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. The applicant claimed a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, which sets out the non bis in idem rule.

Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment and a customs fine. He made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. The Court of Appeal dismissed that application on the grounds that ‘imprisonment in default possesses the legal characteristics not of a penalty, but of a means of enforcement attached to the financial penalties whose recovery they are intended to secure’ The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. After being ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In a judgment of 16 September 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons: “The appellant cannot validly argue that, by sitting in private in accordance with Article 711 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the court of Appeal infringed Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights’” The applicant has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. Mr Ali Riza Göktan (“the applicant”) alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. The Court declared the application partly admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The French Government filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The Court ruled in favour of the French Government. The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained in March 1991. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. The applicant was also ordered to pay a customs fine of FRF 400,000 that was imposed jointly and severally for the customs offence of illegally importing goods. On 27 June 1991 the public prosecutor sought an order for two years of imprisonment in default, as the customs fine had not been paid. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. However, he later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out of the Court of Cassation's list. The Court of Appeal upheld an express order for a person who has been convicted of a customs offence to remain in custody until he or she has paid the fiscal penalties imposed on him or her. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law. The applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. He claimed that he was serving two prison sentences for the same offence. He relied in particular on the Court's judgment in Jamil v France (judgment of 8 June 1995, Series A no. 317-B), in which imprisonment in default was found to constitute a ‘penalty’ for the purposes of the European Convention. Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. After being ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In a judgment of 16 September 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons. Code, which required sentences to run concurrently, had not been infringed by the trial court and could not enable a prison sentence and term of imprisonment in Default to be served concurrently. The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from.

name: Gerald Sporer
train_texts: The applicant alleged that the relevant provisions of the Civil Code relating to custody and their application by the courts had discriminated against him as the father of a child born out of wedlock. The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by an Austrian national, Mr Gerald Sporer (“the applicant’), on 12 November 2003. The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. By a decision of 25 September 2008 the Court declared the application admissible.

The case originated in an application (no. 35637/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the relevant provisions of the Civil Code relating to custody and their application by the courts had discriminated against him as the father of a child born out of wedlock. By a decision of 25 September 2008 the Court declared the application admissible.Neither party filed further observations on the merits of the case. The case was heard by a panel of judges from the European Court of Justice and the Court of Audience. The jury found the application to be admissible on the grounds of prima facie merit.

The case originated in an application (no. 35637/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the relevant provisions of the Civil Code relating to custody and their application by the courts had discriminated against him as the father of a child born out of wedlock. By a decision of 25 September 2008 the Court declared the application admissible.Neither party filed further observations on the merits of the case. The Court made its decision in September 2008 and ruled that the application was admissible, and the case was settled.

The applicant’s son K. was born out of wedlock on 26 May 2000. The applicant asked the Mattighofen District Court to transfer sole custody of K. to him under Article 176 of the Civil Code (Allgemeines Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) The judge then proceeded to discuss the factual and legal issues with the parties. The parties then concluded an agreement to the effect that, pending a decision on custody, K. would spend three days with his mother and three Days with the applicant. The court appointed Dr J.-W., an expert in child psychology, and ordered him to submit an opinion on whether the interests of the child were better served by leaving sole custody with the mother or by awarding it to the applicants.

The applicant’s son K. was born out of wedlock on 26 May 2000. The judge then proceeded to discuss the factual and legal issues with the parties. The parties then concluded an agreement to the effect that, pending a decision on custody, K. would spend three days with his mother.

The applicant’s son K. was born out of wedlock on 26 May 2000. The applicant asked the Mattighofen District Court (Bezirksgericht) to transfer sole custody of K. to him under Article 176 of the Civil Code (Allgemeines Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) The applicant and K.’S mother appeared before the District Court and were heard by the judge. The court appointed Dr J.-W., an expert in child psychology, and ordered him to submit an opinion on whether the interests of the child were better served by leaving sole custody with the mother or by awarding it to the applicant.

District Court ordered a second expert in child psychology to submit an opinion on whether or not K.’s mother was capable of taking care of him. A third expert, Dr B., was ordered to submit a decisive expert opinion on the question whether K.'s mother was able to exercise custody. A representative of the Youth Office visited K. and his mother at their home and as a result of that visit concluded that she was able of exercising custody. None of the parties made further submissions. The opinion was based on interviews which the expert had conducted with the applicant and his partner. It was served on the applicant on 17 April 2002.

The applicant and K.’s mother made detailed arguments as to why the other parent was not an appropriate person to take care of K. The court ordered a third expert, Dr B., to submit a decisive expert opinion on the question whether K.'s mother was capable of exercising custody. A representative of the Youth Office visited K. and his mother at their home and as a result of that visit concluded that she was able to exercise custody. In addition the District Court requested the Youth. Office to prepare a report. The judge ruled in favour of the applicant and gave him sole custody of the boy. The case was settled in October 2002.

K. Court on 17 April 2002. Dr J.-W. expressed the view that K.’s mother was very immature and not yet capable of taking care of him and recommended the transfer of sole custody to the applicant. The opinion was based on interviews which the expert had conducted with K.'s mother and the applicant and his partner. A representative of the Youth Office visited K. and his mother at their home and as a result of that visit concluded that she was able to exercise custody. The District Court ordered a third expert, Dr B., to submit a decisive expert opinion on the question whether K’'s mother was capable of exercising custody. On 14 October 2002 Dr B. submitted his opinion.

District Court dismissed the applicant’s request for sole custody of K. to be transferred to him by decision of 4 December 2002. The District Court noted that under Article 166 of the Civil Code the mother of a child born out of wedlock had sole custody. A transfer of custody was only to be ordered if the child's best interests were at risk. In the present case the applicant would have had to prove that K.'s mother was unable to take care of him. The decisive expert opinion by Mr B. had found it established that K’S mother was capable of taking care of her son. The applicant had failed to adduce proof to the contrary. The factual and legal issues of the case had been sufficiently clarified and a hearing would only have delayed the proceedings.

District Court dismissed the applicant’s request for sole custody of K. to be transferred to him by decision of 4 December 2002. Under Article 166 of the Civil Code the mother of a child born out of wedlock had sole custody. A transfer of custody was only to be ordered if the child's best interests were at risk. In the present case the applicant would have had to prove that K.’S mother was unable to take care of him. The District Court noted that it had not considered it necessary to hold a hearing to discuss the decisive expert opinion, since it found that opinion coherent and convincing. The factual and legal issues of the case had therefore been sufficiently clarified and a hearing would only have delayed the proceedings.

K. had been born out of wedlock, his mother had sole custody of him. He, as the child's father, could only be awarded custody if the mother put the child’s well-being at risk. In the case of a child born in wedlock the parents had joint custody and retained it upon divorce or separation. The application of different criteria when the parents of a children born out of wedlock separated lacked reasonable justification. The Regional Court found that the proceedings before the District Court had not suffered from any procedural defects. In non-contentious proceedings it was not always required to question the parties at a hearing.

K. had been born out of wedlock and his mother had sole custody of him. He could only be awarded custody if the mother put the child’s well-being at risk. In the case of a child born in wedlock the parents had joint custody and retained it upon divorce or separation. In non-contentious proceedings it was not always required to question the parties at a hearing. The application of different criteria when the parents of a children of a different sex separated lacked reasonable justification. The court ruled that its decision was immediately enforceable with the consequence that the agreement of 12 March 2002 was no longer effective.

Since K. had been born out of wedlock, his mother had sole custody of him and he could only be awarded custody if the mother put the child’s well-being at risk. In the case of a child born in wedlock the parents had joint custody and retained it upon divorce or separation unless the child's best interests required that sole custody be awarded to one of them. The application of different criteria in this case lacked reasonable justification. The decision was immediately enforceable with the consequence that the agreement of 12 March 2002 was no longer effective. The applicant appealed. He complained about a number of procedural shortcomings. He alleged, inter alia, that the District Court had failed to hold a hearing for the purpose of discussing Dr B. ’s expert opinion, and that it had not heard him in person.

In the case of a child born out of wedlock, custody was only to be transferred if the mother put the child’s well-being at risk. The applicant filed an extraordinary appeal on points of law. All Member States of the Council of Europe provide for joint parental authority by unmarried parents over their children born out of wedlock. The German Criminal Code distinguishes between penalties and measures of correction and prevention. The purpose of such measures is to rehabilitate dangerous offenders or to protect the public from them. The sentencing court orders preventive detention in addition to the penalty if someone is sentenced for an intentional offence to at least two years' imprisonment and if the following further conditions are satisfied. The penalty is determined by the law which is in force at the time of the act (Article 2 § 1 of the Criminal Code) The temporal applicability of provisions of the criminal code depends on whether they relate to penalties or measures of Correction and Prevention. The law in force on completion of an act is amended before the court's judgment, the more lenient law applies.

The order for execution of the placement in preventive detention of convicted persons must be met by a court. The perpetrator must previously have served a prison sentence or been detained pursuant to a measure of correction and prevention for at least two years. A comprehensive assessment of the perpetrator and his acts must reveal that, owing to his propensity to commit serious offences, the perpetrator presents a danger to the general public. Judicial review and duration of preventive detention can be reviewed within fixed time-limits. If the maximum duration has expired, the detainee shall be released (Article 67d § 3). On 6 March 1985 the Stuttgart Regional Court convicted the applicant of two counts of rape and abduction and of one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1984. He was then placed in preventive detention, executed in that same prison, for the first time on 27 June 1989. He had thus served ten years in preventive detained by 26 June 1999. train_texts: The case was brought against the Republic of San Marino under Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Government of the Republic complained that there had been no public hearing at first instance or on appeal. The application was declared admissible and inadmissible on 1 June 1999. The Federal Constitutional Court held that the applicant's parental rights as guaranteed by the Basic Law included an obligation for the courts to conduct custody proceedings in such a way as to obtain a reliable basis for a decision founded on the child's wellbeing. The court pointed out that it was questionable in the case at hand whether the proceedings had satisfied these requirements since the lower courts had not given any convincing reasons why the children had not been heard. However, there was no need to take a decision in this respect because in any event the applicant could not claim to have suffered a particularly serious disadvantage since his complaint did not have any prospect of success even if remitted to lower courts. The applicant made an application on behalf of and in the name of his children for the regulation of the children's contact rights with respect to their father. The application was dismissed as inadmissible on the ground that the determination of contact arrangements between the father and the children was already the subject of proceedings under file no. 5 F 272/98. The applicant argued that the grandparents were setting the children against him and obstructing the exercise of his contact rights. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint (File no. 1 BvR 2127/01) by a decision of 7 December 2005, served on the applicant in December 2005. The application was rejected by the District Court on 22 March 2001. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint that his parental rights had been violated by the decisions of the lower courts. It held that the right to determine the contact of the children with third persons was part of the right of custody which had been awarded solely to the mother. In view of the close relationship between the mother, children and the grandparents and the fact that the grandparents assumed a considerable part of child care, a prohibition of contact with the children was neither practicable nor in the children's best interest. The Court held that preventing contact between the children and their grandparents could in no way help to ensure regular contact between. the applicant and his children but would to the contrary further obstruct such an aim.

The ship Prestige, flying the flag of the Bahamas, was sailing in the Spanish exclusive economic zone off the coast of Galicia, carrying 70,000 tonnes of fuel oil. At a distance of 28 miles from Cape Finisterre it sent out an SOS after sustaining sudden and severe damage which produced a leak. The spillage of the ship’s cargo caused an ecological disaster whose effects on marine flora and fauna lasted for several months. The shores of the Atlantic coast of Cantabria and Galicia were severely polluted by the numerous waves of oil which were washed up. The oil spill blackened beaches and cliffs, destroyed marine life, adversely affected water quality and had an immediate environmental impact on numerous animal species.

The applicant was diagnosed with sexual deviance, a personality disorder and psycho-organic syndrome, which was probably a consequence of his longstanding alcohol abuse. As long as the applicant did not drink alcohol, those abnormalities did not affect his criminal responsibility as he was not drunk at the time of the offences. The applicant was diagnosed with sexual deviance, a personality disorder and psycho-organic syndrome, which was probably a consequence of his longstanding alcohol abuse. As long as the applicant did not drink alcohol, those abnormalities did not affect his criminal responsibility as he was not drinking alcohol at the time of the offences. It was found that the applicant had been in a state of diminished criminal responsibility (Article 21 of the Criminal Code, see paragraph 62 below)

The Lüneburg Regional Court decided to order the applicant’s preventive detention under Article 66 § 2 of the Criminal Code. It considered that as a result of his personality disorder, the applicant had a propensity to commit serious offences which seriously harmed the victims both physically and mentally. The court endorsed the experts’ finding that the applicant's personality disorder could no longer be treated because his sexually deviant aggressive behaviour had lasted for decades. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing the applicant in preventive detention. On 26 July 2013, the Regional Court, sitting as a chamber responsible for the execution of sentences, ordered the continuation of his preventive detention in Celle prison. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication.

The Lüneburg Regional Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention. The court found that there was a high risk that if released, the applicant would commit further violent offences for sexual gratification under the influence of alcohol. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication aimed at reducing his sadistic fantasies and his libido, and thus his dangerousness. The applicant served his full term of imprisonment, and on 12 June 2001 he was placed for the first time in preventive detention, for which he was held in a wing of Celle prison.

eval_texts: A German national was detained under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. He alleged that the retrospective prolongation of his preventive detention breached his right to liberty. The case originated in an application (no. 23279/14) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court on 18 March 2014. The application was communicated to the Government on 17 June 2014. Here we look at the circumstances surrounding the case. The applicant was born in 1943 and is currently detained in the centre for persons in preventive detention on the premises of Rosdorf Prison (hereinafter the ‘Rosdorf preventive detention centre’). He was convicted by the criminal courts five times. The applicant stabbed a female cyclist in the back in a life-threatening manner for sexual gratification. Still drunk, he had then broken into a house, strangulated a four-year-old girl and had injured her with a knife below the waist. The Regional Court found that at the time of committing the offences, the applicant had been in a state of diminished criminal responsibility. The court endorsed the experts’ finding that the applicant’s personality disorder could no longer be treated because his sexually deviant aggressive behaviour had lasted for decades. He therefore presented a danger to the general public. Public security could therefore be better safeguarded by placing him in preventive detention. The Lüneburg Regional Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s preventive detention at regular intervals. By 11 June 2011 he had served ten years in preventive detention. The Regional Court further ordered the Rosdorf Prison authorities to offer the applicant, within three months of the date on which its decision became final, a specific anti-hormonal therapy with medication aimed at reducing his sadistic fantasies and his libido, and thus his dangerousness. It noted that at the time of his last offence on 3 October 1985, his first placement in preventive Detention could not exceed ten years. It was only following the entry into force of the Combating of Sexual Offences and Other Dangerous Offences Act on 31 January 1998 (see paragraph 51 below) that the courts responsible for the execution of sentences could prolong preventive detention without any maximum duration. The Regional Court considered that the prolongation of the preventive detention of the applicant, who had been detained for almost thirty years, was still proportionate in view of the considerable threat he posed to the public. It noted that the applicant’s detention in a supervised residence, which it had suggested in its previous decision, was not possible in practice. The Regional Court found that, as required by section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code, there was still a very high risk that, owing to specific circumstances relating to his personality and his conduct, the applicant would if released commit the most serious sexually motivated violent offences. The Celle Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It confirmed that the requirements laid down in section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal Code for ordering the continuation of the applicant's preventive detention had been met. The court held that the applicant was suffering from a mental disorder as defined in section 1(1) of the Therapy Detention Act. Specific disorders affecting a person's personality, conduct, sexual preference and control of impulses were covered by the notion of ‘mental disorder’ in the Act. The decision was made on 2 September 2013, and the appeal was dismissed on 3 September 2013. The applicant argued that under the European Court of Human Rights’ well-established case-law the retrospective prolongation of a person’s preventive detention – a penalty – beyond the former ten-year time-limit breached the prohibition on retrospective punishment under Article 7 of the Convention. He claimed that the order for the continuation of his preventive detention violated his constitutional right to liberty. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant's constitutional complaint without giving reasons (file no. 2 BvR 2182/13). The decision was served on the applicant’S counsel on 7 November 2013. The decision of the Federal constitutional Court is published here. The applicant was detained under the Therapy Detention Act. He had repeatedly refused treatment with medication to diminish his libido. The applicant had participated in group therapy sessions run by a doctor and in a social skills training course. He stopped attending the group for addicts and refused to take medication for fear of side effects. Since 2 June 2013 the applicant has been detained in the new Rosdorf centre for the mentally ill. He is currently being held under Article 67d § 3 of the Criminal Code, read in conjunction with section 316f(2), second sentence, of the Introductory Act to the Criminal code. The conditions of the applicant’s preventive detention at issue are described below. The conception of preventive detention in the centre was developed in order to comply with the constitutional requirement to differentiate between preventive detention and imprisonment. Detainees are placed in apartment units measuring some 23 square metres containing two furnished rooms and a bathroom. The rooms are equipped with a controlled access to the internet including e-mail, telephone, television, CD and DVD player and radio. There are common rooms for residential groups consisting of some seven detainees, which include a kitchen, a dining room, a television room and rooms for games, handicraft work and exercise. The outdoor premises, measuring some 1,600 square metres, can be used for sports, recreation or gardening. Persons in preventive detention may work, but are not obliged to do so. The applicant has refused regular and repeated offers to start a treatment with medication to reduce his libido, which had been recommended by expert W. in 2013, for fear of side effects. In December 2014 he showed willing for the first time to take up such treatment. He proved reliable during leave from the detention centre under escort on a number of occasions under escort. He did not take part in any structured leisure activities and spent most of his day alone watching television. He declined repeated invitations to take part In group sessions of the treatment programme for offenders. The applicant no longer participated in any therapy measures from August 2014. He is being held at the Rosdorf detention centre.

Tichy, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The application was communicated to the Government on 29 January 2009. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). Elaine B. (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Cameroon, kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ She had survived her escape on a container ship, during which she ‘nearly went mad’ The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Traiskirchen centre. One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal. A few fellow Cameroonians, as well as the campaigning lawyer W.R. and his colleague R.H., are continuing to stand by her. ‘Otherwise I would have killed myself’, says Elaine. The Traiskirchen centre in Germany is home to 1,000 asylum seekers. Security officers at the centre later state in court that female asylum seekers could be paid for quick sex. They also tell of pimps rolling up to the centre in their cars. The sexual exploitation seems to have been unbearable. ‘Please help us!’ pleaded the women. The Interior Ministry stated at the time that the police were confronted with a ‘wall of silence’. The woman who claimed that she had been raped by a security officer was dismissed for sexual assault. The centre director F.S. later commented on the attacks in the washrooms of the women’s quarters by telling the court: ‘According to our information such incidents are very common’ Elaine B. describes with precision how the man locked the door and removed the key. She tells of the pains in her lower abdomen afterwards and how she washed herself with warm water for weeks. She immediately identifies the security officer in a photo. For the first interview in the interview room no trained interpreter can be found. In their minutes the police officers at times refer to Elaine B. not by her name but as ‘the nigger woman’ She is repeatedly linked to prostitution. The court heard that the woman was intimidated and seemed very anxious’, recalls District Inspector W.S., who investigated the case, a year later in court. Elaine B. denies this version of events. She says that she had other things on her mind at the time. She felt repelled by this fat man with a moustache who smelled of alcohol, she was afraid of him. If she had really been hoping to be granted asylum, why would she then have defamed the security officer? Next to take the witness stand are the employees of the bakery. Saleswoman R.Z.: ‘She gave him a kiss. She was fairly young, I’d say between 20 and 25. I couldn’t describe the woman’ When confronted with Elaine B. says: ‘I’m not quite sure whether it’s her’ No evidence is taken either from other asylum seekers or from the female staff in the women’s quarters. Judge I.K. acquits the security officer. According to the court, the bakery employees could not have identified Elaine. They have unfinished business with the African woman and attribute the basest intentions to her – without furnishing any proof. 'It cannot be established that the accused performed sexual intercourse against the will of Elaine B. be made out beyond doubt’, states the judgment. 'These have no evidentiary value' according to Judge K. Why not? Because the accused said that the underpants had been ‘beige’ Elaine B. must appear before the investigating judge ‘or be brought by force’ She could face up to five years in prison. ‘That’s just routine, nothing unusual’ says a Justice Ministry spokesman. Justice Minister K.M. has promised to do more to protect the victims of crime. Judge I.K. had no doubt about the woman's guilt. The judge ignored relevant evidence and delivered a scandalous judgment (“The judgment fails to give rise to a scandal.”) The compensation proceedings under the Media Act have been launched against the applicant company under section 6 of the media act. The Vienna Regional Court found against the applicant company. It held that the impugned statements had constituted defamation under the freedom of speech. The applicant company had sought the disqualification of Judge N.F., the judge assigned to the media proceedings, for bias. The judge had to decide on a case in which her previous lawyer was acting as representative of one of the parties. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the transcript of K.’s examination had been included in the case file and therefore no additional witness was required. On 12 December 2005 the Regional Court held another hearing in the defamation proceedings in which it examined two of the witnesses proposed by the applicantCompany. The Regional Court found that the contents of the article had given a biased account of the taking of evidence at the trial of H.P. I.K. was therefore entitled to compensation, which it set at 7,000 euros (EUR) It also ordered the applicant company to publish a summary of the judgment. According to the article, the judge had acted arbitrarily and out of racist motives and had disregarded evidence produced. The rape asserted by K. had been described as proven and the assessment of evidence by the Regional Court as absurd. K.’s assertion that she had been the victim of an assault had not been excluded but because it contradicted the statements of witnesses it had been considered to be partially implausible. The Regional Court found that the applicant company had not succeeded in proving the truth of the impugned statements. The accusation that a judge, who was under the duty to act objectively and impartially, had deliberately disregarded evidence in order to acquit an accused from the same country had to be qualified as defamation. The term scandal of justice was a value judgement, which, however, was based on assertions of fact which had been disproven in the proceedings. An error in the translation of that statement could not be excluded, but that did not allow the conclusion that there had been no basis in the file for the above finding of Judge I.K. The applicant company appealed on 8 March 2006 against the Regional Court’s judgment. On 19 June 2006 the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment. This judgment was served on the applicant's company lawyer on 29 June 2006. The amount of EUR 7,000 in compensation was appropriate. The judge ruled that the sharp critique of Judge I.K. in the impugned article, which had lacked any sufficient factual basis, had been excessive. The court also held that the judge had been wrong to criticise the applicant company. The suit was settled out of court in 2007 with the claimant receiving an undisclosed sum of money.

On 7 June 2007 the first applicant applied for a residence permit for theSecond applicant on the ground of family reunification. The Migration Office decided on 2 June 2008 to investigate the applicants’ family situation. Both applicants, as well as first applicant’s ex-wife, were interviewed. The first applicant “had abused her naivety and her good will” and “ had lied to her by hiding from her the fact that he had children” The three children, R., L. and B., entered Switzerland clandestinely in August 2009. The applicants did not appeal against the decision and it became final on 28 April 2009. They established that the applicants had not conducted themselves correctly with regard to the application, and accordingly they were no longer entitled to family reunification. The second applicant gave birth to a fourth child, E. on 12 April 2010. The first applicant informed the Migration Office that R. and L. had been living in Switzerland illegally since 15 August 2009 and that it had been urgent to bring them to the respondent State because L.’s chances of recovery were better in Switzerland. The applicants had brought the children to Switzerland illegally despite the negative decision of the Migration Office of 28 April 2009. The Migration Office also reiterated that the children’s existence had previously been concealed from the Swiss authorities, and that the paternity of the first applicant had not been established. In addition, the legal requirements for family reunification had not be met. The children had lived their entire lives in their home country of Kosovo, where they had attended school. The applicants had waited quite a while before applying for a residence permit, and they had not cited any other important family reasons for seeking reunification. It remained doubtful whether it had always been the applicants’ true intention to construct family life in Switzerland. The children were to be returned to their home country of Kosovo. They were not allowed to stay in Switzerland. The children are now staying with their parents. The decision was made to return the children to their country of origin. They have been waiting for almost two years for this decision. They say that they want to be able to live with their mother and father. The applicants applied to the Salzburg Municipal Authority (Magistrat) for a retrospective building permit. The neighbours appealed against the authorisation to reduce the minimum distance between their property and the applicants’ house. The Appeals Commission (Bauberufungs-kommission) tried to achieve a settlement between the applicants and their neighbours. The parties were asked to comment by 21 February 2001. On that date the applicants submitted comments and amended their request which was subsequently submitted to expert A. The latter submitted his opinion, after the applicants had made further necessary amendments of the plan, on 24 September 2001. The appeals Commission held an on-site hearing on 6 July 2001.

The applicants are joint owners of a house in Salzburg which they had acquired in 1996. In spring 1997 they discovered that the distance between an annex to their house and the neighbouring plot of land did not correspond to the minimum distance required by the building permit. The applicants applied for a retrospective building permit including, among other points, the authorisation to go below theminimum distance. A hearing on the applicants’ property was held on 4 November 1998. The Appeals Commission held an on-site hearing on 6 July 2001. On 17 October 2001, after a further attempt to achieve a friendly settlement had failed, the Appeals Commission requested the applicants for further comments.

The applicants are the joint owners of a house in Salzburg which they had acquired in 1996. In spring 1997 they discovered that the distance between an annex to their house and the neighbouring plot of land did not correspond to the minimum distance required by the building permit. On 24 November 1997 the applicants applied for a retrospective building permit which was granted on 7 December 1999. On 23 December 1999 the applicants’ neighbours appealed against the authorisation. The Appeals Commission held an on-site hearing on 6 July 2001. The parties were asked to comment by 21 February 2001. On 17 October 2001, after a further attempt to achieve a friendly settlement had failed, the Appeals Commission requested the applicants for further comments by 6 November.

Time-limit for filing comments was extended from 12 November until 9 December 2002. The time- limit for replying to their neighbours’ comments was also extended from 2 January until 28 January 2003. The Appeals Commission confirmed the Municipal Authority’s decision on 18 March 2003. On 2 May 2003 the applicants’ neighbours lodged a complaint to the Administrative Court. The Administrative Court dismissed the neighbours' complaint as being unfounded on 27 March 2007. The judgment was served on the applicants' counsel on 19 April 2007. At the end of the case, the appeals commission ruled that the application had been upheld and the appeal was dismissed as unfounded.

Werner Zimmermann and Johann Steiner were tenants of a flat close to Zürich-Kloten airport. In 1974, the applicants sought compensation for the damage caused by the noise and air pollution resulting from the operation of the airport. The case was referred to the Federal Assessment Commission having jurisdiction in the matter. The Commission rejected the applicants’ claims by a decision of 6 October 1976, which was served on them on 7 March 1977. The applicants then lodged with the Federal Court an administrative-law appeal against the Commission’s decision. The Federal Court sought the views of the Assessment Commission on 27 April. The latter decided that the applicants were alleging non-pecuniary damage and not damage to property.

train_texts: The San Marinese government issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The land, which was earmarked for urban development projects that were scheduled for completion by 31 December 1987, was only partially used. On 20 October 1987 the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. By a judgment of 17 August 1993, the court stated that it did not have jurisdiction to “recognise the existence of a possible right to restitution of unused land”. It found that the General Grand Council alone was entitled to rule on what was to be done with the property. Noting finally that the new land-use plan had changed the designated use of the unused land, it declared the expropriation order of 7 March 1985 void in so far as it had lapsed in respect of that particular property. The judge found that the State had acquired ownership of the plots of land in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law, on payment of compensation for expropriation. He concluded that the applicant church’s request of 20 April 1993 was inadmissible, since the government's behaviour could not be described as an implied refusal. On 27 September 1994 the Council of the XII upheld the appeal court's judgment, thus endorsing the expert's conclusion that the public-interest declaration in connection with the urban development work had transformed Beneficio Cappella Paolini's right of property into a mere legitimate interest. The council said that while section 14(3) of Law no. 15/1980 conferred not only a legitimate interest in the lawfulness of the authorities’ actions but an actual right to apply to the civil courts and obtain a declaration.

The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Vienna. He was stopped by the police at 11.05 p.m. while driving his car on a public road. After nine attempts to measure the amount of alcohol, among which only one was valid, the test was discontinued. The applicant’s conduct was considered to amount to a refusal to undergo the breathalyser test and his driving licence was temporarily withdrawn. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant's appeal. He found that according to the paper print out of the breath analyser test the applicant had made four invalid attempts out of five.

On 8 February 2006 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Administrative Court and requested an oral hearing. In his complaint he argued that the Lower Austria Regional Government had not been competent to decide on his case as he resided in Vienna. He further complained about the authority’s assessment of evidence, as the statements of the police officers who had ordered him to undergo the breathalyser test were contradictory and stated that they should be questioned on the precise circumstances in which breathalysing had been carried out. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's request for a hearing as it found that an Oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. The applicant had failed to raise any substantial arguments against these findings and had not shown that the assessment of the evidence was contradictory or implausible.

The Regional Governor concluded that refusing to undergo a breathalyser test was as serious as driving under the influence of alcohol because it prevented the authorities from verifying whether a person was actually drunk. The Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s request for a hearing as it found that an oral hearing was not likely to contribute to the clarification of the case. The applicant had failed to raise any substantial arguments against these findings and had not shown that the assessment of the evidence carried out by the authorities was contradictory or implausible. This decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 25 October 2007. On 20 April 2001 the DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) and imposed a fine.

Jehovah’s Witnesses, formerly known as Serious Bible Students, a community based upon their own interpretation of the Bible, are not outlawed in Austria. It may therefore be assumed that their objectives neither infringe the law nor offend morality (see Article 16 of the Basic Law in conjunction with Article 9 (art. 9) of the European Convention on Human Rights). Therefore, the mother's membership of that religious community cannot of itself constitute a danger to the children's welfare. The case involves the religious education of a child in Germany. The children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Their education according to the principles of this sect contravenes the law, says the court. The court says the lower courts failed to give due consideration to the children's welfare. The mother, as has been established, would refuse to consent to the. children's receiving a necessary blood transfusion. This constitutes a danger to their well-being, the court says. The Regional Court‘s failure to apply this provision is obviously in breach of the law. The parents must be able to decide without the consent of the other that the child is to be brought up in a faith different from that shared by both parents at the. time of the marriage.

Federal Law of 1985 on the Religious Education of Children (Bundesgesetz über die religiöse Kindererziehung) 1985/155 (re-enactment of the Law of 15 July 1921 on the religious education of Children) I. 939. According to Article 1 of the 1921 Act the religious. education of a child shall be decided upon by an agreement freely entered into by the parents, in. so far as the responsibility for his or her care and upbringing is vested in them. Such an agreement may be revoked at any time and is terminated by the death of either spouse. The Regional Court's failure to apply this provision is obviously in breach of the law.

According to Article 1 of the 1921 Act the religious education of a child shall be decided upon by an agreement freely entered into by the parents. Neither parent may decide without the consent of the other that the child is to be brought up in a faith different from that shared by both parents at the time of the marriage or from that in which he or she has hitherto been brought up. Since in any case the children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses, their education according to the principles of this sect (which is not, as the appellant rightly points out, a recognised religious community) contravenes the law.

Jehovah’s Witnesses believe the Bible is the word of God and must be taken as literal truth. They believe that children should be taken care of by their mother, not their father. They also believe that if a child is taken away from their mother they will be placed in care of another person. They say this is in the interests of the child, and that it would be in their best interests if they were to stay with their mother. The Bible states that any child taken away will be taken from his or her mother and put into care of someone else. This applies to children as well as adults, but it doesn't mean that all children are the same.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses believe that the bible is a literal word of God. They also believe that if they don’t obey the Bible, they will become ‘social outcasts’ They believe that it is in the name of God that children should be taken care of by their parents. The Bible is also a ‘source of truth’ for the Witnesses, they believe. ‘No one should be able to claim the right to take care of a child,’ they say, ‘except the parents.’ ‘There is no right to claim that a child should not be cared for by his or her parents’

A central feature of Jehovah’s Witness doctrine is the belief that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: ‘For we ourselves have favored adding no further burden to you, except these necessary things, to keep abstaining from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication. If you carefully keep yourselves from these things, you will be free from them.’ The Bible says: “If you keep yourself from them, they will not exist.” The Bible also says that if you don’t listen to them, the Bible says, ‘You will not be able to understand them’.

In no case are parents’ religious convictions as such a relevant criterion in deciding on parental rights and duties pursuant to Article 177 para. 2 of the Civil Code. These rights cannot be refused to a parent or withheld from him for the sole reason that he or she belongs to a religious minority. In the concrete case it needs to be examined whether the mother’s religious convictions have a negative influence on her upbringing of the children which should be taken into account. It appears in particular that Ingrid S. would not allow blood transfusions to be given to her children; that for herself she rejects communal celebration of such customary holidays as Christmas or Easter. The Regional Court rejected the appeal by decision of 14 March 1986. The mother’s religious convictions do not deprive Martin and Sandra of the possibility of celebrating these holidays in the usual way, so that no detriment to the children can be found in this regard either. Careful consideration must lead to the conclusion that in spite of more difficult social integration, as discussed above, it appears to be more in the interest of the children's welfare to grant parental rights to the mother than to transfer them to the father. The Jehovah's Witnesses, formerly known as Serious Bible Students, are not outlawed in Austria; it may therefore be assumed that their objectives neither infringe the law nor offend morality. Father's objections against assigning parental rights and duties to the mother cannot in the final instance be decisive. New points raised on appeal cannot cast doubt on the first-instance decision as regards the children’s welfare. The appellant overlooks the fact that, in view of the paramount importance of the children's welfare, the way in which they reached the place where they are currently being taken care of is not necessarily decisive. Even illegal conduct would be of relevance only to the extent that it might, in an individual case, be possible to infer therefrom a lack of suitability for care or upbringing. No expert medical opinion was sought regarding the question, which was raised anew on appeal, of blood transfusions. Mr S. lodged an appeal on points of law (außerordentlicher Revisionsrekurs) with the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) The Supreme Court overturned the judgment of the Innsbruck Regional Court, granting parental rights to Mr S. instead of the applicant. It gave the following reasons: “The appellant has not hitherto claimed that the children belonged to the Roman Catholic faith; however, he has stated, and it has in fact been established, that the mother is bringing them up according to the principles of the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ teaching”. The children do not belong to the faith of the Jehovah’s Witnesses, their education according to the principles of this sect contravenes Article 2, paragraph 2, of the 1921 Act. The lower courts also failed in their decisions to give due consideration to the children's welfare. The stress caused by being transferred to the care of the other parent, which in any case is usually transitory, has to be accepted in their own best interests. The file contains no documentary basis for the assumption that a change to another carer ‘would with a high degree of probability cause the children serious psychological harm’ ... . Even though it is preferable for young children to be taken care of by their mother, this applies only provided that all other things are equal. The Jehovah’s Witnesses form a particular religious movement. It originated in America in the 1870s. A central feature of doctrine is the belief that the Holy Scriptures in the original Hebrew and Greek are the revealed word of Jehovah God and must be taken as literal truth. The refusal to accept blood transfusions is based on several scriptural references, most notably Acts 15: 28-29, which reads: “For we ourselves have favored adding no further burden to you, except these necessary things, to keep abstaining from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication. If you carefully keep yourselves from these things ...“

The Court of Appeal upheld the refusal to approve the transfer of title. It said there was already a risk of foreign domination in the Hopfgarten area. The Court noted that 110 foreign landowners owned 5.6 hectares of land in the area. They also said it was difficult, if not impossible, for the indigenous population to find housing for themselves. The proportion of non-Austrian owners already exceeded 10 per cent and the extent of their holdings revealed a tendency towards foreign domination. The decision was dated 16 June 1977, a year after the appeal was first heard. The appeal was upheld by the Regional Authority on 3 June 1977.

The application was made by a woman who wanted to buy land in Hopfgarten, Tyrol, Germany. The Regional Authority refused to approve the transfer of title. The Authority noted that there were 110 foreign landowners in the area, and the extent of their holdings showed a tendency towards foreign domination. This caused prices to rise substantially, making it very difficult, if not impossible, for the indigenous population to find housing for themselves. For these reasons and in view of the scarcity of building plots, the Authority upheld the appeal on 3 June 1977. The appeal was upheld by the Regional Authority on the grounds that there was already a risk of foreign domination in the region.

The purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). During the course of the hearings, the Government filed a document. The Court decided on 27 March that the proceedings should continue without resumption of hearings (Rule 26). The Chamber decided under Rule 50 of the Rules of Court to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. The Government also replied to two supplementary questions which the Registrar had addressed to them on the instructions of the President. Wishing to build a holiday residence in Hopfgarten, a village in the Austrian Tyrol, she approached, with the assistance of municipal officials, the owners of a plot of land which had until then been used for agricultural purposes. Sale negotiations began in 1971 and apparently led, in 1973, to an initial contract. One year later, Mrs. Sramek paid to the vendors the greater part of the agreed price.
