In addition, the Court also authorised Mr. Pohl to speak in German (Rules 29 para. 1 in fine and 27 para. 3 in fine) The applicants are Gerhard Klass, an Oberstaatsanwalt, Peter Lubberger, a lawyer, Jürgen Nussbruch, a judge, Hans-Jürgen Pohl and Dieter Selb, lawyers. All five applicants claim that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) and a statute enacted in pursuance of that provision are contrary to the Convention. They do not dispute that the State has the right to have recourse to the surveillance measures contemplated by the legislation. They challenge this legislation in that it permits those measures without obliging the authorities in every case to notify the persons concerned after the event. The applicants claimed before both the Constitutional Court and the Commission that they were being subjected to surveillance measures. They did not know whether the G 10 had actually been applied to them. Neither as persons suspected of one or more of the offences specified in the Act nor as third parties within the meaning of Article 1, paragraph 2, sub-paragraph 2, have the applicants been subjected to such measures. There is also no question of the applicants’ having been indirectly involved in a surveillance measure directed against another person - at least, not in any fashion which would have permitted their identification. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany were prompted by this judgment to propose amendments to the G10. The parliamentary proceedings have not yet been completed. After the end of the Second World War, the surveillance of mail, post and telecommunications in Germany was dealt with by the occupying powers. Article 5 para. 2 of the Convention of 26 May 1952 on Relations between the Three Powers (France, the United States and the United Kingdom) and the Federal Republic - as amended by the Paris Protocol of 23 October 1954 - specified in fact that the Threepowers temporarily retained “the rights ... heretofore held or exercised by them’. in such cases the person concerned is notified of the surveillance measure.“ The contested legislation was introduced on 13 June 1967, as part of the Emergency Legislation. The first sought to amend Article 10 para.2 of the Basic Law; the second was designed to limit the right to secrecy. Law guaranteed the secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications with a proviso that restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. (2) Restrictions may be orderedonly pursuant to an Act of Parliament.“ The G 10, adopting the solution contemplated by the second sentence of paragraph 2 of the above-quoted Article 10, specifies. the cases in which the competent authorities may impose the restrictions provided for in that paragraph, that is to say, may open and inspect mail and post, read telegraphic messages, listen to and record telephone conversations. The surveillance measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. Measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application (Article 1 para. 5, sub-paragraph 3). The person concerned is not to be notified of the restrictions affecting him. Since the Federal Constitutional Court’s judgment of 15 December 1970, the competent authority has to inform the person concerned as soon as notification can be made without jeopardising the purpose of the restriction. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If it declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five Members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. For the Länder, their legislatures lay down the parliamentary supervision to which the supreme authorities are. The G 10 commission draws up its own rules of procedure which must be approved by the Board. According to Article 1 para. 9, sub-paragraph 5, of the G 10: “... there shall be no legal remedy before the courts in respect of the ordering and implementation of restrictive measures“ The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. For the same reason, it must be avoided that a person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The application was lodged with the Commission on 11 September. The case was described as 'a very serious matter' by the European Court of Human Rights. The application was made on behalf of a man who has been subject to surveillance by the G 10. The G 10 authorises measures of surveillance of telephone and telegraphic communications. The man is also entitled to sue the Government for damages if he has been prejudiced. He is entitled to seek the destruction or, if appropriate, restitution of documents. The person concerned can also apply to the Federal Constitutional Court for a ruling as to whether there has been a breach of the Basic Law. The court can decide by a two-thirds majority that their use is incompatible with State security. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Articles 6, 8 and 13 (art. 6, art. 8 and art. 13) of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. “... only the victim of an alleged violation may bring an application. The applicants, however, state that they may be or may have been subject to secret surveillance, for example, in course of legal representation of clients who were themselves subject to surveillance, and that persons having been the subject of secret surveillance are not always subsequently informed of the measures taken against them.“  case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion ‘criminal charge’ Delegates of the Commission made the following concluding submissions to the Court: “May it please the Court to say and judge whether the applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act’” “Whether, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the applicants. could claim that they were victims of a. violation of the rights set forth in the Convention, considering that it gives no guarantee to persons whose communications have been subjected to secret surveillance. that they will be notified subsequently of the measures taken concerning them.“

The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present his own case. The President of the Chamber refused leave and requested the applicant to appoint to represent him an advocate authorised to practise in any of the Contracting States and resident in one of them.

On 26 April 1998, the Court ruled that the case should be dismissed.

The Constitutional Court’s judgment was served on the applicants’ counsel on 25 February 2004. The purpose of the Registered Partnership Act (Eingetragene Partnerschaft-Gesetz) was to provide same-sex couples with a formal mechanism for recognising and giving legal effect to their relationships. The rules on the establishment of a registered partnership, its effects and its dissolution resemble the rules governing marriage. Like married couples, registered partners are expected to live together. The Registered Partnership Act, Federal Law Gazette (Bundesgesetzblatt) vol. I, no. 135/2009, came into force on 1 January 2010. Section 2 of the Act provides as follows: “A registered partnership may be formed only by two persons of the same sex (registered partners) They thereby commit themselves to a lasting relationship with mutual rights and obligations” The rules on the establishment of a registered partnership, its effects and its dissolution resemble the rules governing marriage. Like married couples, registered partners are expected to live together. The law does not provide for special rules for married couples. It is unnecessary to examine whether, and in which areas, the law unjustifiably discriminates against same-sex relationships.

The Registered Partnership Act provides registered partners with the same status as spouses. Unlike married couples, registered partners are not allowed to adopt a child. Rules on the choice of name differ from those for married couples. Artificial insemination is also excluded (section 2(1) of the Artificial Procreation Act – Fortpflanzungsmedizingesetz). However, some differences between marriage and registered partnership remain, apart from the fact that only two persons of the same sex can enter into a registered partnership. The most important differences, however, concern parental rights. The law uses the term “last name” where a registered couple chooses a common name, but “family name’ is used in reference to a married couple’s common name.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30141/04) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged in particular that they were discriminated against as, being a same-sex couple, they were denied the possibility to marry or to have their relationship otherwise recognised by law. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 February 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms B. Ohms, Federal Chancellery, Deputy Agent, Ms G. Paschinger, Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs, Mr M. Stormann and Mr K. Mayer. Two men tried to marry in Austria in 2002. Court said marriage could only be contracted between two people of the same sex. Couple appealed, but the appeal was rejected by the Court of Appeal. The case was decided in favour of the couple on a technicality. The appeal was dismissed on the basis that the case was a matter of law, not of law on same-sex marriage. The decision was upheld on appeal by the Supreme Court of Austria. The application was rejected on the grounds that the marriage was not legally valid, and that the couple were not of same sex, as their marriage was to be a private one. The couple were allowed to marry. Austrian Constitutional Court dismissed the applicants’ complaint. The European Court of Human Rights found in its Cossey [v. the United Kingdom] judgment of 27 September 1990 that the restriction of marriage to this ‘traditional’ concept was objectively justified. The essence of marriage is, moreover, not affected in any way by the fact that divorce (or separation) is possible and that it is a matter for the spouses whether in fact they are able or wish to have children. Neither the principle of equality set forth in the Austrian Federal Constitution nor the European Convention on Human Rights require that the concept of marriage, as being geared to the fundamental possibility of parenthood should be extended to relationships of a different kind. Same-sex relationships fall within the concept of private life and enjoy the protection of Article 8 of the [Convention]. This does not give rise to an obligation to change the law of marriage. It is unnecessary in the instant case to examine whether, and in which areas, the law unjustifiably discriminates against same-sex. relationships by providing for special rules for married couples. The purpose of the Registered Partnership Act (Eingetragene Partnerschaft-Gesetz) was to provide same- sex couples with a formal mechanism for recognising and giving legal effect to their relationships. In introducing the said Act, the legislator had particular regard to developments in other European States.  registered partnership. involves cohabitation on a permanent basis. It may be entered into between two persons of the same sex having legal capacity and having reached the age of majority (section 3) A registered partnership must not be established between close relatives or with a person who is already married or has established a still valid registered partnership with another person (section 5). Like married couples, registered partners are expected to live together like spouses in every respect, to share a common home, to treat each other with respect and to provide mutual assistance. The partner who is in charge of the common household and has no income has legal authority to represent the other partner in everyday legal transactions. European Union law does not recognise same-sex marriage. The right to marry and to found a family shall be guaranteed in accordance with national laws governing the exercise of these rights. A few countries, e.g. in the Netherlands and in Belgium, marriage between people of the same sex is legally recognised. Others, like the Nordic countries, have endorsed a registered partnership legislation, which implies that most provisions concerning marriage are also applicable to these unions. The name ‘registered partnership’ has intentionally been chosen not to confuse it with marriage and it has been established as an alternative method of recognising personal relationships. This new institution is, consequently, as a rule only accessible to couples who cannot marry. International courts and committees have so far hesitated to extend the application of the right to marry to same-sex couples. A number of directives are also of interest in the present case. The state of relevant legislation in Council of Europe member States is unclear. Six out of forty-seven member States grant same- sex couples equal access to marriage, namely Belgium, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. In addition, the following thirteen member States do not grant same.-sex couples access to. marriage, but have passed some kind of legislation permitting them to register their relationships: Andorra, Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Iceland, Luxembourg, Sweden. In two States, namely Ireland and Liechtenstein, reforms intending to give same-sex couples access to some form of registered partnership are pending or planned. Croatia has a Law on Same-sex civil unions which recognises cohabiting same-Sex couples for limited purposes. In most of the States concerned, registered partners obtain a status similar to marriage. The possibilities for registered partners to undergo medically assisted insemination or to foster or adopt children vary greatly from one country to another. Other consequences include the use of the partner’s surname, refusal to testify, entitlement to compensation following the wrongful death and lawful organ donation.

The applicant’s arrest was made on the night of 12/13 March 1981 in Lausanne. He was immediately transferred to Champ-Dollon prison in Geneva. The Argentine authorities had sent radio-telegrams to the authorities of the Swiss Confederation on 10 and 11 March asking for help in identifying the five persons thought to be responsible for kidnapping a Uruguayan banker, K, in Buenos Aires on 19 February. The kidnappers had demanded a ransom and had required K's wife and sister to go first to Paris, then to Zürich.

The Federal Court was involved in extradition proceedings in two sets of circumstances. If the arrested person protested against the extradition itself by raising an objection based on the Act, a treaty or a declaration of reciprocity (section 23), the Federal Court could rule on the merits of the extradition. The Office was also responsible for ruling on any request for provisional release lodged by the person who was detained with a view to extradition. It could authorise his release if it appeared that the circumstances so required (section 25, first paragraph). The Office could still, for important reasons of political expediency, refuse to extradite the person concerned. In the latter event - which was very rare -, the hearing took place in public, unless there were serious reasons to the contrary.

The Office could grant release if this appeared to be required by the circumstances (section 25, first paragraph) If the Court refused to authorise extradition, the Office was bound by that decision. On the other hand, if the Court authorised extradition, it could still, for important reasons of political expediency, refuse to extradite the person concerned. Lastly, it was for the Office to give instructions for the handing over of the person extradited.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36378/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been unable to obtain legal representation under the legal-aid scheme to bring proceedings against a lawyer. By a decision of 16 April 2002 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. It was allocated to the Third Section (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber which would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

The case originated in an application (no. 36378/97) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention in that he had been unable to obtain legal representation under the legal-aid scheme to bring proceedings against a lawyer. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. By a decision of 16 April 2002 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court's decision was published in December 2002.

The case was brought by a man who was not entitled to legal aid. He claims that he was unfairly dismissed from his job. The case was eventually settled in favour of the man. The judge ruled that the man did not have a right to sue the government. The court ordered the man to pay back the money he lost. The man, who has not been named, appealed the decision and the case was settled out of court. The matter was referred back to the bar council. The bar council decided that the case should be heard by a judge rather than a jury. The decision was upheld by the court and the man was allowed to appeal the decision.

Three lawyers were assigned to the case by the bar council. The last of the lawyers, who had no connection with the case, withdrew in November 1995. The case was eventually transferred to the legal-aid office, who refused to take the case any further. In March 1996, the judge ruled that the case should be sent back to the bar to be decided. The judge wrote to the lawyer again, but this time the case was put on hold until the next day. The lawyer was then forced to drop the case and take it to the court again. The court ruled the case had been dropped because the lawyer did not have the right to stay in the case.

Three lawyers were assigned to the case by the bar council. The last of them withdrew from the case in November 1995. The case was not heard from again until March 1996. The judge ruled in favor of the fourth lawyer in the case on June 14, 1996. In March 1997 the case was dismissed and the case returned to the legal-aid office. The court heard the case again on March 31, 1998, when it was decided that the case should be heard by a different judge. The decision was made to dismiss the case and the judge ruled that the previous hearing had been unfair to the defendant. The hearing was adjourned until April 1998, at which point the case against the third lawyer was dismissed.

Consequently, he was advised to make a fresh application if he wished to pursue his claim against Mr T.

train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Venezuelan and Colombian national. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his extradition to the United States of America would expose him to a risk of treatment contrary to Article 3. On 10 July 2017 the Grand Chamber of the Court declared that case inadmissible. The Chamber decided, after examining the request of the applicant, that there is no need to relinquish jurisdiction in favour of the Grand chamber under Rule 72 of the Rules of Court. The parties were informed that the examination of the case was suspended, pending the outcome of the proceedings in the case.

The applicant was born in 1982 in Venezuela and is currently detained in Valdemoro Prison. He has been living in Spain with his family since 2003. He was charged with conspiracy to import one or more kilograms of heroin into the United States in violation of Title 21, United States Code, sections 952(a), 960(a)(1) and 960(b)(1)(A), and 963. Each of those offences carried a possible maximum term of life imprisonment. The applicant lodged an appeal against that decision. On 19 December 2014 the Plenary of the Criminal Section of the Audiencia Nacional ruled against that appeal.

eval_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 68919/10) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lenz, a lawyer practising in Stuttgart. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H.-J. Behrens, Ministerialrat, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 3 June 2013 the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective remedy was communicated to the Government. On the same day the President of the Section sitting in a single-judge formation declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The remaining leapfrog appeal on points of law (Sprungrevision) was dismissed on 13 December 2005 by the Federal Social Court. On 20 January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (no. 1 BvR 170/06) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The complaint did not raise a pressing constitutional question as the relevant provision of the social security legislation had meanwhile been amended. The Government informed the Court that in response to the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany ( no. 46344/06, 2 September 2010) an Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was to be introduced. The application was denied. In December 2011 the Court informed the applicant of the enactment of the new domestic remedy and drew his attention to the transitional provision of that Act. On 6 February 2012 the applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long, even taking the position and function of the Federal Constitutional Court into account. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. On 1 October 2012 the complaints panel of the Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The court noted that the actual duration of the proceedings – four and a half years – was unusually long, but not excessive. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution and it served further purposes beyond the administration of individual justice. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The decisions and judgments of the Federal Constitutional Court had binding inter omnes legal effect and for this reason had to be drafted with the utmost diligence, the court said. However, the two cases shared sufficient similarities to justify the decision of the former judge rapporteur. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. The Remedy Act introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation shall amount to €1,200 for every year of delay. Complaint of undue delay must be lodged in writing. Complaint must set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length of the proceedings. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. The decision is not subject to appeal.’2. Transitional provisions under section 23 of the Remedy Act (see for details Taron, § 27, and Garcia Cancio, § 36, both cited above), stipulated that, in the case of terminated proceedings whose length might still become or had already become the subject of a complaint before that court, it was not necessary to raise a complaint.

The court martial took place on 3 and 4 April 1995 and the applicant, who was legally represented, pleaded not guilty. The school had approximately 180 pupils, none of whose fees were paid out of public funds, and received no direct financial support from the Government. In September 1985 Mrs Costello-Roberts sent the applicant, who was then aged seven, to an independent boarding preparatory school in Barnstaple, Devon. In the school’s prospectus it was stated that a high standard of discipline was maintained, but no mention was made of this. The school in question operated a system whereby such punishment was administered upon acquisition of five demerit marks. On 3 October 1985 the applicant received his fifth mark for talking in the corridor and for being a little late for bed. The headmaster decided that the only answer to the lack of discipline was to give him three “whacks’ on the bottom through his shorts with a rubber-soled gym shoe. In a letter to his mother he wrote “come and picke me up I have had the wacke’. The school initially denied that he had been punished, but this was denied by the Government. On 5 November, the headmaster wrote to the Governors of the school to express his “grave concern’ about the use of corporal punishment. The applicant's mother complained to the police some time between 4 and 16 November 1985, but was told that there was no action they could take without any visible bruising on the child’s buttocks. A complaint by her to the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children received a similar response. The headmaster was of the opinion that the applicant “strung his parents along“, taking home stories about bullying and the like “which he has clearly made up but which equally clearly his parents believe’. It was argued in Strasbourg, on behalf of the applicant, that he had been extremely disturbed by the slippering, which turned him from a confident, outgoing seven-year-old into a nervous and unsociable child.

The two remaining applicants, Ms Danuta Korsak and Mr Tadeusz Łagowski, were not parties to the proceedings as they had either donated or sold their shares. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 and 14 of the Convention. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. The trial ended on the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the jury to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.” The applicant was legally represented at the trial. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ress, Mr Mansfield and Mr Garnham. Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. Prosecution counsel recalls that defence counsel did not raise strong objections to the approach which the judge indicated he intended to pursue. However, defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Defence counsel based his recollection on the grounds of appeal and advice on appeal which he drafted shortly after the trial on 10 December 1991. Neither of these documents suggests that defence. counsel made an express request to the judge to discharged the jury. Judge's recollection is that both counsel agreed to his proposed course of action (see paragraph 11 above). The jury, being unable to reach a unanimous verdict, were recalled by the judge. He informed them that the time had come when he could accept a verdict of at least a majority of ten. At 4.06 p.m. the jury returned and delivered a ten to two majority verdict finding the applicant guilty. The applicant was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment. The appeal proceedings were heard at the Court of Appeal in London. The judge ruled that the trial judge had wrongly failed to make any enquiry into the note with a view to determining whether one of the members of the jury should be discharged on the grounds of racial prejudice and that this failure gave rise to the appeal. Leave to appeal was refused by the single judge on 28 February 1992. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The court continued: “Matters of this kind raise delicate issues. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. In our judgment His Honour Judge Hammond dealt with this matter sensitively, sensibly and correctly, and cannot be faulted for a conclusion that the jury should continue the deliberations which they had given their oath to undertake. We, therefore, find no ground for complaint and we dismiss this application’

The applicant, Ms Alison Halford, was born in 1940 and lives in the Wirral. From 1962 until her retirement in 1992 she worked in the police service. Ms Halford was appointed to the rank of Assistant Chief Constable with the Merseyside police in May 1983. As such she became the most senior-ranking female police officer in the United Kingdom. She applied unsuccessfully on eight occasions during the following seven years to be appointed as Deputy Chief Constable, in response to vacancies arising. Ms Halford alleges that certain members of the Merseyside Police Authority launched a “campaign’ against her in response to her complaint to the Industrial Tribunal. This took the form, inter alia, of leaks to the press, interception of her telephone calls and the decision to bring disciplinary proceedings against her. Mr Justice MacPherson found that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Police Authority had acted ultra vires and, without imputing ill-motive to them, held that there had been an element of unfairness. Ms Halford was given an ex gratia payment of 10,000 pounds sterling (GBP) by the Chief Constable. As Assistant Chief Constable, Ms Halford was provided with her own office and two telephones, one of which was for private use. She alleges that calls made from her home and her office telephones were intercepted for the purposes of obtaining information to use against her in the discrimination proceedings. It was agreed that she would retire from the police force on medical grounds (arising out of an injury to her knee in 1989). In addition, the Home Office agreed to implement various proposals put by the Equal Opportunities Commission, inter alia to update and review selection procedures for senior posts within the force. The Government accepted that the applicant had adduced sufficient material to establish a reasonable likelihood that calls were intercepted. The judge discussed the case and ordered the juror who had written the complaint not to join the other jurors. The judge received two letters from the jury the next day. The first letter was signed by all the jurors including the juror who had sent the complaint. The second letter, which the judge commended, was written by a Juror who appeared to have thought himself to have been making the jokes. The juror in question explained at length that he might have done so, that he was sorry if he had given any offence, and that he he was not the one who had made the joke. The case was adjourned and the judge listened to submissions in open court. The defence asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge decided to call the jury back into court. The jury found the applicant guilty, but acquitted G.C., who was also Asian. On 20 April 1995 the judge imposed on the applicant a sentence of five years' imprisonment. The applicant was given leave to appeal against conviction. In his appeal he raised, inter alia, the following ground: The judge should have reacted to the juror's complaint by dismissing the jury. The juror who had written the complaint should not have been segregated from the other members of the jury in the early stages. The judge was right to confront the jury with the problem and ask them to consider it. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court found that the judge did not err in reaching the conclusion that there was no real risk of bias. The judge dealt with the possibility of tensions among the jurors perfectly sensibly in the direction he gave to them. However, it would be unrealistic to suppose that the jury would not have wanted to know who the author of the complaint was. Other members of the jury, as this led to his identification, were also asked to give evidence in the trial. The jury's decision will be returned in a few weeks' time and the case will be heard in front of a panel of judges and jury members. The trial is expected to last at least three more days before it is adjourned until the jury's verdicts are returned. The verdicts will then be returned to the jury.

Olubukunola Obasa was a social worker with the London Borough of Islington. She made a formal complaint in 1991 alleging harassment and refusal of a promotion on grounds of race. However, with regard to the applicant's transfer request, the Council committee was concerned at the lack of evidence that any serious consideration was given to this matter. The matter was adjourned, the applicant making no objection to this adjournment. In her application, she relied on events going back to the commencement of her employment in 1989. Determination of the merits was considered to require detailed evidence and the matter was reserved for a further hearing.

The investigators confirmed that they were aware of the criminal proceedings pending against the applicant. They added that paragraph 7 of Schedule 2 restricted the disclosure of information obtained by a financial investigator.

The applicant was charged with failing without reasonable excuse to comply with the financial investigator's requirement to answer questions or otherwise furnish information. On a request by the investigators, on 25 June the applicant's representatives informed the investigators that the applicant would not attend the interview. The interview did not take place. On 25 February 1999, the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of GBP 200. On 5 July 2002, the Belfast County Court allowed the applicant’s appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation.

The Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation and the same investigation. The only outstanding matter was whether the applicant should have attended the interview and then refused to answers questions, or, as he did, refuse to attend the interview once he failed to receive the assurances he had asked for.

On 25 February 1999, the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of GBP 200. The Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. The judge noted that the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had dealt with a similar case (Clinton v. Bradley [2000] NI 196) which related to the same legislation and the same investigation. The appeal was dismissed on 5 July 2002, with the judge noting that the judge had also dealt with the similar case in 2000. The applicant had refused to answer questions at an interview, and he had not been interviewed by the police, or charged with any offence. In Clinton v. Bradley, the Northern Ireland Court of Appeal had held that as Parliament had put in place certain express limitations on the use of information obtained by investigators, it could not have intended that the person concerned could put forward the risk of self-incrimination as a “reasonable excuse”. Lord Justice Carswell, giving judgment, considered, in the light of R. v. The case was heard by a Chamber of Judges from October to November 2005. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant has been submitted. It confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” and that he had had the opportunity to be advised by an officer of his choice. The CO referred the case to the Higher Authority and remanded the applicant in close arrest. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. The applicant was given a four-page document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him immediately thereafter. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except that he was likely to suborn witnesses. It was undesirable in the interests of discipline that he be allowed to consort with his comrades due to the seriousness of the alleged offence. On 22 February 2000 the CO of the MCTC released the applicant from close arrest and he was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. A return date was fixed for 3 March 2000. The application was served on the CO on 19 February 2000. On 2 March 2000, the same CO swore an affidavit setting out the reasons for the applicant's release. He stated: 'I decided, on balance, following a thorough review of the suspect's case, that he should be released.’ The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. All three defendants were acquitted. The judge ruled that the applicant should be posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK. He was issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses. The court martial ruled that 'the interests of justice could be met by releasing the Applicant into open arrest even though the allegation against him was that he had committed rape and indecent assault...and despite the fact that there was evidence that he, with others, concocted a story and interfered with a witness'

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 1176/10) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings leading to his conviction he had not been afforded a fair hearing by an impartial tribunal. On 17 July 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. By a judgment of 5 the High Court ruled in favour of the applicant and the Norwegian Government. The case was heard at the Oslo Court of Appeal on 21 March 2013. The judge described the case as ‘a case of alleged sexual assault’ and ruled that it was a case of attempted rape. In February 2009, the Borgarting High Court (lagmannsrett), hearing the applicant’s appeal with a jury, convicted him on the attempted rape charge and sentenced him to one year's imprisonment. It ordered him to pay 60,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK) (approximately 7,500 euros at that time) in compensation to Ms A for non-pecuniary damage. The High Court also noted that Mr B had testified that he had not noticed anything conspicuous about Ms A; she had been cheerful and friendly and her clothes had not been in disorder. However, this did not suggest, in the High Court's view, that she had not was exposed to sexual abuse causing a great burden on her. Counsel for the defence requested that J be disqualified from taking part in the further proceedings on grounds of lack of impartiality. The public prosecutor expressed understanding for the motion without taking a stance. The High Court observed that “the jury member had formed a picture [bilde] of the victim from many years ago where she at the time had experienced her as a quiet and calm person” It decided that a member might be disqualified if the person in question had particular reasons for identifying himself or herself with the victim or if there were any other circumstances to the effect that he or she had a prejudging attitude. However, that was not the situation in the present case. Juror J took part in the entire trial before the High Court, including the jury’s deliberations and vote on the charge of attempted rape. High Court had special regard to the fact that the parties to the case had requested that J recuse herself, but it found the absence of partiality so clear in this case that this could not be decisive. By a judgment of 26 June 2009 the Supreme Court, by three votes to two, rejected the applicant's appeal. The majority did not consider that the juror's knowledge of the victim from her attendance at birthday parties and class outings with the victim in itself indicated an identification with the Victim or weakened in any other way the confidence in her impartiality. J's information about Ms A had emerged after she had given evidence to the High Court for one hour. At that point, the jury, including J, had a good opportunity to form an independent and updated picture of the victim as a person. That defence counsel and the assistant advocate had requested that J withdraw could not be decisive. There were no particular circumstances capable of calling into doubt J’s impartiality for the purposes of section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act, as interpreted in the light of Article 6 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The minority considered that the case concerned a serious and stigmatising accusation against the defendant. There was no basis for such a conclusion and there was in any event no reason for attaching weight to such a possibility. It was correct to add that she had experienced the victim as a “quiet and calm person”. The timing of J’s affirmation could easily have given the impression that J expressed a positive assessment of the victim. That J had expressed a view on how she had perceived her “at the time”, was of secondary importance. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, “the standpoint of the accused [was] important but not decisive” in this case the “fear” of lack of impartiality by the applicant had been “objectively justified” (see Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy, 7 August 1996, § 58, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑III).

The applicant is a United Kingdom national, who was born in 1944 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HMP Maidstone. On 16 April 1997, the Chief Constable of South Wales authorised the installation of covert recording devices at the applicant's cottage. Over 160 hours of tapes were obtained between the period of 25 April to 9 June 1997, on which latter date the applicant and his wife were arrested. On 15 June 1998, the applicant was convicted of charges inter alia of conspiracy to import controlled drugs and possession of controlled drugs in connection with importation of marijuana and cocaine from overseas. A confiscation order was imposed on him on 24 September 1998 in the sum of 50,169.18 pounds sterling (GBP)

Rule 13 of the special provisions of the tenancy agreement stipulated the following: “The tenant undertakes not to erect, without specific permission, placards, signs, sunblinds, outdoor aerials and such like on the house” The agreement further stipulated, as a general condition, that the tenants were obliged to take proper care of the flat and to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house.

The applicants' landlord demanded that the satellite dish be dismantled. The applicants did not comply and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement with effect from 31 July 2004. The landlords claimed that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenants' tenancy agreement. The couple, of Iraqi origin, have three children, who are now eighteen, sixteen and eight years of age. The case was heard by the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm. The verdict was returned in favour of the applicants and the tenants are suing the landlord for damages.

The Board found that it was not a breach of the Landlord's obligations to protect the tenants' interests in using a satellite dish. The appeal was dismissed on appeal on 21 October 2004, with the Board's decision to be appealed again on 6 October 2005, with a new order to be issued to the landlord. Also, the liability for damage to persons and property could not reasonably be incurred unless it were able to prevent it. The applicant was born in 1943 and lives in Solihull. His wife died on 23 March 1999. On 16 September 2000 the applicant made a claim to the Inland Revenue requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow, namely Widow’s Bereavement Allowance (“WBA”), for the years 1998/99 and 1999/2000. On 29 September 2000 he was informed that he was ineligible for WBA as he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under United Kingdom law.

The second applicant, Mr Hueth Wilson, was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. Expert psychiatric evidence recommended that he should be made subject to a hospital order coupled with a restriction order without limit of time. Due to an absence of any beds in hospitals providing the level of security that the trial judge considered necessary, the judge felt unable to make the orders and passed, instead, a discretionary life sentence. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. On 9 January 2001, the MHR Tribunal recommended his discharge. The applicants had appealed against their treatment in hospital for mental illness. Their case was reviewed by the MHR Tribunal on 13 June 2000. The Tribunal did not recommend discharge of the second applicant. The applicants were not eligible for review by the discretionary lifer panels empowered by section 34 of the Criminal Justice Act 1991 to order their release on licence. The right to a hearing under the 1991 Act was conferred only on persons who were solely subject to that Act, and not on those who were mental patients. The Court of Appeal reversed the High Court's decision in part in 1994. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal against the decision in 1995.

The applicant is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HM Prison Rye Hill, Warwickshire. He is barred by section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983 from voting in parliamentary or local elections. He sought a declaration that this provision was incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights. His application was heard before the Divisional Court on 21 and 22 March 2001, together with the application for judicial review of two other prisoners, Mr Pearson and Mr Feal-Martinez, who had applied for registration as electors and were refused by the Registration Officer. Lord Justice Kennedy concluded that in Europe only eight countries, including the United Kingdom, did not give convicted prisoners a vote.
